records.question_issues: The question calls reproducibility and best practice "dual needs" that the architecture "addresses". The paper never uses that framing and never links the two in one argument. It treats them as separate features. Reproducibility and portability come from Nextflow, Conda, Docker or Singularity containers, nf-core guidelines, pinned pipeline versions, tests and CI. Analytical practice comes from GATK best-practice pre-processing, tool selection criteria, QC metrics and Gold Set benchmarking. The only best-practice standard the paper names is the GATK recommendations, and it claims them only for read alignment and pre-processing. A broader reading of "scientific best practices" (QC, benchmarking, leaving filtering to the user) is reasonable but is an interpretation. Because the question is conceptual and open-ended, correct answers could pick different subsets of these features. One evidence sentence (Conda/DockerHub) starts on page 3 and finishes on page 4, with the "Amendments from Version 1" box and Table 1 printed between the two halves. It is quoted as one sentence and given page 3.

records.short_answer:
Reproducibility: Sarek is implemented in Nextflow and adheres to the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines. To ensure reproducibility, all required tools are installed in Conda and pushed to DockerHub, so Sarek and its dependencies can be used from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version (2.5.2) from GitHub with the corresponding container, and fetches the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. A small test dataset and a suite of tests verify the installation, and they are also used for Continuous Integration testing with GitHub Actions. The complete run was executed by a single command with no manual intervention. The paper concludes that, thanks to its design, Sarek installs easily and reproducibly on all POSIX compatible systems. The abstract adds that support for Docker and Singularity containers as well as Conda environments makes Sarek ideal for easy deployment on any POSIX-compatible computers and cloud compute environments.

Best practice: Sarek follows the GATK best-practice recommendations for read alignment and pre-processing (BWA-MEM alignment, then GATK deduplication and recalibration). Beyond pre-processing, it includes a wide range of software for the identification and annotation of both germline and somatic variants. Its tools are selected for being high quality, well-maintained and robust. It generates a wide range of quality control metrics, aggregated across samples with MultiQC. Using the intersection of GATK4 Mutect2 and Strelka2, Sarek gave F1 score = 0.80 for SSMs and 0.58 for SIMs. That is in the top range of the 18 somatic variant calling procedures in the original benchmarking study, which indicates that the workflow operates as intended. The paper sets two limits. Sarek leaves it to the user to combine and filter results from different callers. Careful parameter tuning, downstream variant filtering and qualitative assessment by the user remain important.

records.short_answer: Snakemake uses workflow-inherent information to calculate a hash value for each job, prior to actually generating the file. The hash captures exactly how the output file is generated. For a job eligible for caching, the hash is a SHA-256 hash value calculated from the job's code, parameters, raw input files and software environment, plus the hashes of its dependencies. The scheme is blockchain-style because the hash function is applied recursively: for each dependency, a hash value is included in the hash of the job, which is the hashing principle behind blockchains. As a result, the hash describes everything that affects the content of the job's output files, including the input generated by jobs it depends on. The output files are stored under this hash in a central cache, such as a folder on the same machine or in a remote storage. If a rule is marked as eligible for caching, Snakemake can obtain its output from the cache when the file has been created before in a different workflow or by a different user on the same system. Subsequent runs of the same job (with the same dependencies) in other workflows can then skip the execution and take the output files directly from the cache. This saves computation time, as well as disk space: on local machines the file can be linked instead of copied. The hash is only descriptive if the workflow developer ensures that the cached result is generated in a deterministic way. For example, downloading from a URL that yields data which may change over time should be avoided.

records.short_answer:
Scheduling: Snakemake solves the scheduling problem at the start of execution and again whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending. The first releases used a greedy scheduler. The current implementation solves a mixed integer linear program (MILP) whenever there are free resources. The MILP optimizes four criteria in lexicographical order: (1) prefer jobs with high priority, (2) maximize the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), (3) delete existing temporary files as soon as possible, and (4) reduce the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. The order is enforced by multiplying each criterion sum by a value at least as high as the maximum the terms to its right can reach. Constraint (2) ensures the selection does not exceed the available amount of each resource.

Cluster and cloud: with middleware such as SLURM, PBS, LSF or Kubernetes, Snakemake does not need to govern all resources at a global level. Some resources are handled by the middleware, and constraint (2) can be dropped for them. Snakemake can pass the resource requirements to the middleware, which can use them to choose the best fitting machine. By default runtime, threads, memory and disk usage are local resources passed to the middleware; all other resources are global and are still governed by Snakemake via constraint (2). The number of jobs queued or running at a time is limited by the same kind of constraint.

Submission overhead: by default every job is submitted separately to the queuing system. For short-running jobs this can cause considerable overhead, as jobs wait in a queue, and may add delays or cost when accessing files from remote storage or network file systems. To minimize it, Snakemake can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs by assigning rules to groups. Connected subgraphs with the same group are submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job (a group job) instead of each job separately. For each group, the number of connected subgraphs spanned per submission can be defined (one by default), so the partition size can be adjusted to the computational platform. A group job's resource usage is computed by sorting its jobs topologically, summing resource usage per level and taking the maximum over all levels. For runtime it is the other way round: the maximum per level, summed over all levels.

records.question_issues: The question is open-ended ("how does ... leverage architectural and methodological changes"), so more than one reasonable selection of changes could be given. The paper's own summary (abstract) names two: the CRAM format for storage and increased intra-sample parallelization for runtime, on a Nextflow DSL2 rewrite. It also lists FastQ sharding with fastP, interval grouping and scatter-gather, a parameter to skip germline calling, mosdepth in place of Qualimap, and spot instances on AWS Batch. The paper gives the cost reduction differently in different places: 70% in the abstract, 69% in the introduction, costs reduced "to approximately 30%" in the Results (Table 2: $68.04 to $20.82), and "reduced the costs to 50%" in the Discussion. The paper says CO2 emissions are kept low or reduced but gives no CO2 measurement.

records.short_answer:
nf-core/sarek 3.1.1 is a full rewrite as a modular re-implementation in the Nextflow DSL2 framework, focused on reducing required compute resources. The abstract names two main changes: the CRAM format for storage and increased intra-sample parallelization for runtime.

Parallelization: FastQ files are split into shards with fastP (optional adapter trimming) and mapped in parallel, so alignment runs on smaller machines. Median mapping runtime falls to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs, and scatter-gathering covers all applicable variant callers. Runtime was lowest at 21 interval groups. Going from 21 to the 124-group default raised BQSR storage by a factor of five, so the default is being set to 21.

Storage: merging, duplicate marking and CRAM conversion run in one process. CRAM cuts pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage. Less scattering reduces storage by a further factor of 5, which lets the pipeline run on smaller systems.

Other changes: Qualimap is replaced by mosdepth, and a new parameter skips germline-only calling for paired samples. Combining trimming, QC and sharding plus tailored interval splitting reduces CPU hours by 66%.

Cloud: on AWS Batch with spot instances (Tower Forge, fusion mounts), one normal sample cost $20.82 with 3.1.1 against $68.04 with 2.7.2. Runtime fell from 46h8m to 12h4m and CPU hours from 1118.4 to 342.5, a reduction of about 70% in CPU hours and 84% in runtime. The paper states the cost saving four ways: a 70% cost reduction (abstract), a 69% reduction versus 2.7.2 (introduction, about $20 per sample), costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% (Discussion). It says this keeps costs and CO2 emissions low but gives no CO2 figure.

That figure is about CPU hours for the combined changes, not median mapping runtime, so it does not answer this question.

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with three limits. (1) The paper never measures I/O overhead. Its I/O case is an argument: separate tools read and load the data several times, while fastp does every operation in a single scan; separate UMI tools also need their own run, which consumes additional I/O. (2) The speed benchmark (Table 1) ran every tool on a single thread, and the paper gives no multi-thread comparison because some of the other tools do not support multi-threading. No experiment credits the 2–5 times speed-up to any single design choice, and the multi-thread gain is something fastp "may" show. (3) The question can be read narrowly (architecture: all-in-one single scan, C/C++, multi-threading with packs and per-thread contexts) or broadly (also module-level choices: duplication arrays in place of FASTQC's hash table, 64-bit integer keys, the two-step overrepresented-sequence method). Both readings are covered here. The paper also gives two values for the UMI speed-up: "approximately 3 times faster" than UMI-tools or umis (Section 2.6) and 2.7 times faster than umis and 6.1 times faster than UMI-tools (Section 3.3); both are quoted. The extraction prints C++ as "Cþþ" and "=" as "¼"; quotes keep them as printed. The array size 2^24 is printed as "224" and is left out.

records.short_answer:
fastp is much faster than its peers because of a set of design choices. The paper argues its I/O advantage but never measures I/O.
The problem it addresses: traditional preprocessing chains separate tools (FASTQC, Cutadapt, Trimmomatic), so the data are read and loaded multiple times, which makes preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient; most of those tools are written in Python or Java with limited multi-threading support. The paper states the I/O inefficiency of separate tools in the abstract, the introduction and the UMI preprocessing section (separate UMI tools need individual execution that consumes additional I/O and computational resources), but shows no I/O measurement.
The design choices:
1. All-in-one, single scan: quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning, polyG/polyX tail trimming, UMI preprocessing and other operations run in a single scan of the FASTQ data.
2. Written in C/C++ with a solid multi-threading implementation, which the authors say makes it much faster than its peers.
3. Overall design for multi-threading parallel processing: reads are packed with a size of N = 1000, each pack is consumed by one thread in the pool, each thread keeps an individual context of statistics (per-cycle quality profiles, per-cycle base contents, adapter trimming results, k-mer counts), and these are merged after all reads are processed.
4. UMI preprocessing integrated with little overhead: fastp runs approximately 3 times faster than UMI-tools or umis even when performing other tasks simultaneously (Section 3.3: 2.7 times faster than umis, 6.1 times faster than UMI-tools).
5. Duplication evaluation: duplication keys are stored in a duplication array D and a counting array C instead of FASTQC's hash table, for much faster access, with key2 as a 64-bit long integer for fast comparison.
6. Overrepresented sequence analysis: an efficient two-step method.
Result: fastp is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt despite performing far more operations, measured with all tools on a single thread; in multi-thread mode it may show even higher performance, but no multi-threading comparison is provided. No experiment credits the speed-up to any single design choice.

records.short_answer: fastp uses different algorithms for the two data types. For single-end data, adapter sequences are detected by assembling the high-frequency read tails: it computes k-mers (k = 10) of the first 1 M reads, takes sequences with occurrence frequency >0.0001 as adapter seeds (low-complexity sequences removed), and extends them with a tree-based algorithm (forward extension to check validity, then backward extension to obtain the complete adapter), assuming only one adapter exists in the data and adapters exist only in read tails. For paired-end data, fastp finds the overlap of each pair (an algorithm derived from AfterQC) and considers the bases that fall out of the overlapped region as adapter content; this overlap analysis can trim adapters with even only one base in the tail. A user-given adapter sequence also behaves differently: for SE data it disables automatic detection; for PE data it is used for sequence-matching-based trimming only when fastp fails to detect a good overlap in the pair.

records.short_answer: MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and builds a single summary report that visualizes output from multiple tools across all samples, so global trends and biases can be identified quickly. Collecting the data in one report gives a fast way to scan key statistics, and a general statistics table gathers metrics from different tools for each sample. Shared plots allow accurate comparison between samples and detection of subtle differences not noticeable when switching between different files. Data visualization aids batch effect detection and minimizes the risk of confounding factors. Plots are resizeable and interactive, and a report toolbox lets samples be renamed, hidden and highlighted; highlighting helps identify groups of samples behaving in an irregular manner. For large projects MultiQC parses data for thousands of samples within minutes and adapts the report output. For reports with hundreds of samples it renders plots as images with MatPlotLib instead of HighCharts. The reports reveal overall analysis success, make abnormal samples easy to identify and give the overview required to spot failing samples. Routine use aids quality control early in data processing, reducing the risk of batch effects and other downstream analysis problems.

records.question_issues: The question can be answered from the text but is mildly open-ended, because "diverse sequence features beyond simple genomic mapping" is not defined. The paper's own list (Section 2.1 and the Fig. 1 legend) credits the MMP search with three feature types: splice junctions; mismatches and indels; and poly-A tails, library adapters and poor-quality tails. The suffix-array MMP search is also credited with multimapping reads. Chimeric alignments, such as the BCR-ABL fusion, come from the later clustering/stitching phase (Section 2.2), not from the MMP search, so a correct answer should not attribute them to it. Splice junctions are the MMP search's core use, so the "beyond" in the question is loose. In the pymupdf text on page 2, the sentence "The MMP search in STAR is implemented through uncompressed suffix arrays" is scrambled (one word per line, out of order). It describes implementation, not features, and is not quoted. The MMP definition sentence is also not quoted, because its formula extracts with garbled symbols ("Ri þ 1").

records.short_answer:
STAR runs the MMP search sequentially. It applies the search only to the part of the read that is still unmapped, which finds several kinds of feature:
- Splice junctions: a read with a splice junction cannot be mapped contiguously, so the first seed maps to a donor splice site. The repeated search on the unmapped portion then maps to an acceptor splice site. This gives precise locations of splice junctions in a single alignment pass, with no a priori knowledge of where the junctions are.
- Mismatches and indels: the MMP search enables finding multiple mismatches and indels. When mismatches stop the search before the end of the read, the MMPs serve as anchors in the genome that can be extended.
- Tails: when extension does not yield a good genomic alignment, poly-A tails, library adapter sequences or poor sequencing quality tails are identified.
- Multimapping reads: for each MMP, the suffix-array (SA) search can find all distinct exact genomic matches.
The search runs in both forward and reverse directions and can start from user-defined points in the read. This helps find anchors for reads with errors near the ends. The MMP search itself finds only seeds that match the genome exactly. The stitching procedure that follows aligns reads with many mismatches, indels and splice junctions.

records.short_answer:
The paper says that correcting fragment GC content bias improves the reliability of downstream DE analysis. Left uncorrected, such biases can cause high false positive rates in DE studies. With Salmon's estimates, the paper reports:
(1) Higher sensitivity at the same FDR. The main text gives 53% to 250% higher. The Figure 1c legend gives 53%–450% greater than kallisto and 210%–250% greater than eXpress, on Polyester simulated data whose two 8-sample groups differ in fragment GC bias.
(2) Fewer false-positive DE calls. On 30 GEUVADIS samples where the groups differ only by sequencing center (a technical confound), Salmon makes fewer than half as many DE calls as the other methods at an expected FDR of 1%.
(3) At the gene level, the number of genes called DE falls by a factor of about 2.6.
(4) Dominant isoform switching seen with kallisto or eXpress is eliminated under Salmon's GC bias aware estimates, and Salmon reduces the isoform switching rate across thresholds and gene categories.
Caveat: bias correction was enabled for all methods, and the results text credits the gains to the dual-phase inference algorithm and the sample-specific bias models together.

records.question_issues: The question can be answered from the text, but it is open-ended. "Describe the algorithmic components and optimization techniques" has no single fixed list, so a correct answer could weight the speed mechanisms differently: quasi-mapping, streaming asynchronous mini-batches, sparse updates, rich equivalence classes in a concurrent cuckoo hash map, and the cost of bias modelling. The core is clear: three components (lightweight mapping, an online phase and an offline phase over equivalence classes). "Ultra-fast alignment-free tools" is the question's own wording. The paper calls only its own quasi-mapping "ultra-fast". Its speed benchmark puts Salmon at about 23 min and kallisto at about 20 min (600 million reads, 30 threads). The paper does not describe how quasi-mapping works internally (it cites ref. [17]). The overview (Supplementary Fig. 1) and the pseudo-code (Supplementary Algorithm 1) are supplementary material and are not in the text.

evidence.sentence: Our novel quantification procedure, called Salmon, achieves greater accuracy than tools such as kallisto and eXpress, employs sample-specific bias models that account for sequence-specific, fragment-GC and positional biases, and simultaneously achieves the same order-of-magnitude speed benefits as kallisto and Sailfish.
evidence.supports: Overall claim: greater accuracy than kallisto and eXpress, sample-specific bias models, and the same order-of-magnitude speed benefits as kallisto and Sailfish; frames the answer

evidence.sentence: Salmon consists of three components: a lightweight-mapping model, an online phase that estimates initial expression levels and model parameters, and an offline phase that refines expression estimates (Supplementary Fig. 1).
evidence.supports: The three algorithmic components

evidence.sentence: This two-phase inference procedure allows Salmon to build a probabilistic model of the sequencing experiment that incorporates information — like terms contributing to the conditional probability of drawing a fragment given a transcript — not considered by Sailfish [9] and kallisto [10].
evidence.supports: Accuracy: the two-phase inference supports a richer model than Sailfish and kallisto

evidence.sentence: Unlike pseudoalignment, Salmon’s lightweight mapping procedure tracks, by default, the position and orientation of all mapped fragments.
evidence.supports: Accuracy: the mapping keeps position and orientation of mapped fragments

evidence.sentence: These probabilities are used to estimate auxiliary models and bias terms, and to update abundance estimates, and are subsequently aggregated into weights for the rich equivalence classes used during offline inference.
evidence.supports: Per-fragment probabilities feed the auxiliary/bias models and the rich equivalence-class weights

evidence.sentence: Salmon’s rich model accounts for the effects of sample-specific parameters and biases that are typical of RNA-seq data, including positional biases in coverage, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ end of sequenced fragments, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols, and the fragment length distribution.
evidence.supports: Accuracy: the biases and sample-specific parameters the model accounts for

evidence.sentence: Salmon can quantify abundance either via a built-in, ultra-fast read-mapping procedure (quasi-mapping) [17], or using pre-computed alignments provided in SAM or BAM format.
evidence.supports: The ultra-fast mapping procedure is quasi-mapping

evidence.sentence: When run in quasi-mapping mode, Salmon takes as input an index of the transcriptome and a set of raw sequencing reads (i.e., unaligned reads in FASTA/Q format) and performs quantification directly without generating any intermediate alignment files.
evidence.supports: Quasi-mapping quantifies directly without intermediate alignment files

evidence.sentence: This saves considerable time and space, since quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment.
evidence.supports: Speed gain from quasi-mapping

evidence.sentence: Salmon is designed take advantage of multiple CPU cores, and the mapping and inference procedures scale well with the number of reads in an experiment.
evidence.supports: Multi-core design and scaling

evidence.sentence: Salmon can quantify an experiment of approximately 600 million reads (75bp, paired-end) in ≈ 23 minutes (1384 seconds) using 30 threads— this roughly matches the speed of the recently-introduced kallisto, which takes ≈ 20 minutes (1198 seconds) to complete the same task using the same number of threads on the same machine (a 24 core machine with hyper-threading and 256Gb of RAM; each core is Intel® Xeon® CPU E5-4607 v2 2.60GHz).
evidence.supports: Measured speed compared with kallisto

evidence.sentence: The online phase uses a variant of stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference [19].
evidence.supports: Online-phase inference method

evidence.sentence: The offline phase applies either a standard EM algorithm or a variational Bayesian EM algorithm [20] over a reduced representation of the data represented by the equivalence classes until a data-dependent convergence criterion is satisfied.
evidence.supports: Offline-phase inference over equivalence classes

evidence.sentence: The parameters for all auxiliary models are learned during the streaming phase of the inference algorithm from the first N′ observations (5,000,000 by default).
evidence.supports: Auxiliary models learned from the first 5,000,000 observations

evidence.sentence: These auxiliary terms can then be applied to all subsequent observations.
evidence.supports: Learned auxiliary terms reused for later observations

evidence.sentence: Typically, the extra computational cost required to apply bias correction is rather small, and the learning and application of these bias weights is parallelized in Salmon (for example, when processing sample ERR188021 of the GEUVADIS dataset using 16 threads, the full fidelity bias modeling added 2 minutes (119 seconds) to the non-bias-corrected quantification time.
evidence.supports: Bias correction cost is small and parallelized

evidence.sentence: Moreover, since the bias model works by evaluating the bias along bases of the reference transcriptome, it scales in the number of active (i.e., expressed) transcripts rather than in the number of reads, so the extra cost of bias modeling is almost entirely independent of the number of fragments in an experiment.

records.short_answer:
The paper claims that Salmon achieves greater accuracy than tools such as kallisto and eXpress, employs sample-specific bias models (sequence-specific, fragment-GC and positional biases), and achieves the same order-of-magnitude speed benefits as kallisto and Sailfish. Salmon has three components: a lightweight-mapping model, an online phase that estimates initial expression levels and model parameters, and an offline phase that refines the expression estimates.

Speed: mapping uses a built-in, ultra-fast procedure called quasi-mapping. It quantifies raw FASTA/Q reads directly, without intermediate alignment files. This saves considerable time and space, because quasi-mapping is faster than traditional alignment. The online phase is a streaming variant of stochastic, collapsed variational Bayesian inference. It updates read-count estimates after each mini-batch (1,000 alignment groups by default), and mini-batches are processed asynchronously and in parallel. The only synchronization is an atomic compare-and-swap loop that updates the global transcript weights. The paper says that, because the updates are stochastic and additive, this has little-to-no detrimental effect. The updates are also sparse, so they can be performed efficiently. During the online phase Salmon also builds a highly-reduced representation: rich fragment-level equivalence classes, held in a concurrent cuckoo hash map that many threads can query and write with very little contention. The offline phase runs a standard EM algorithm or a variational Bayesian EM algorithm over the equivalence classes until a data-dependent convergence criterion is met. Equivalence classes have been shown to greatly reduce the time needed for this iterative optimization. The auxiliary models are learned from the first 5,000,000 observations by default and then applied to all later ones. Salmon is designed to take advantage of multiple CPU cores.

Accuracy: unlike pseudoalignment, the mapping tracks, by default, the position and orientation of all mapped fragments. The two-phase inference supports a model that includes terms not considered by Sailfish and kallisto. That model covers positional coverage biases, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution. The equivalence-class weights carry the full model's conditional probabilities without revisiting every fragment. The extra cost of bias correction is typically small (full bias modeling added 119 seconds with 16 threads on sample ERR188021), and its learning and application are parallelized. Its cost scales with the number of expressed transcripts rather than reads, and stored cumulative GC counts per transcript make GC computation efficient.

Result: Salmon quantified about 600 million 75 bp paired-end reads in about 23 minutes (1384 seconds) using 30 threads. On the same machine with the same number of threads, kallisto took about 20 minutes (1198 seconds).

records.question_issues: The question's framing is only partly right. For fold changes it fits the paper: the paper ties strong LFC variance and stronger shrinkage directly to low read counts. For dispersion it does not. The paper says dispersion shrinkage is needed because of small sample sizes ("two or three replicates ... resulting in highly variable dispersion estimates for each gene"). The strength of that shrinkage depends on how close true dispersions are to the fit, and on the degrees of freedom. The paper never says it depends on count level. Low counts enter the dispersion part in two places only. First, the prior is centred on a trend fitted against average expression strength. Second, the Methods say that when μ ≲1/α the data give little information on α, so the estimator's sampling variance is large. That passage explains the shape of the trend, and the paper adds that overestimating α in the low-count range has little effect on inference. An answer claiming that dispersion shrinkage scales with count level would go beyond the paper. Apart from this, the question can be answered from the text.

records.short_answer:
Both shrinkage steps follow one principle: empirical Bayes priors set the amount of shrinkage from the amount of information the data carry for the estimated quantity.

Dispersion: with two or three replicates, the dispersion estimates for each gene are highly variable. DESeq2 assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion. It first gets gene-wise maximum-likelihood estimates, then fits a smooth curve against average expression strength. It shrinks the gene-wise estimates toward the values predicted by the curve, combining the likelihood with the trended prior to give maximum a posteriori (MAP) dispersion estimates. The strength of shrinkage depends on how close true dispersion values tend to be to the fit, and on the degrees of freedom. It decreases as the sample size increases. The width of the prior is estimated from the data, and the fitted curve aids estimation in less information-rich settings. Estimates below the curve are raised, which helps avoid false positives from underestimated dispersion. A gene-wise estimate more than 2 residual standard deviations above the curve is used instead of the shrunken one. On low counts, the paper says that when μ ≲1/α the observed data provide little information on α, so the sampling variance of the estimator is large. Overestimating α in that low-count range has little effect on inference, because the Poisson component dominates the variance there.

Fold change: LFC estimates have strong variance for genes with low read count, because ratios are noisier when counts are low. DESeq2 fits ordinary GLMs to get maximum-likelihood estimates (MLEs) of the LFCs, then fits a zero-centered normal distribution to the MLEs over all genes. That distribution is the prior in a second round of GLM fits, and the MAP estimates are kept as the final LFCs. Shrinkage toward zero is stronger when a gene has little information, because counts are low, dispersion is high or there are few degrees of freedom. The amount of information is indicated by the observed Fisher information, not simply by the mean count. Such genes have flatter profile likelihoods, so the zero-centered prior pulls the high-uncertainty MLE closer to zero. This removes the problem of exaggerated LFCs for low counts. For genes with less than one read per sample on average, LFCs hardly deviate from zero. The paper describes this as a bias-variance trade-off: lower variance in exchange for a bias toward zero. As the degrees of freedom increase, the shrunken estimates converge to the unshrunken estimates.

records.question_issues: Partial false premise. The question says the datasets are "significantly larger than the human genome", but the text never says this. The scaling test (page 8, Fig 3) uses files made by repeating human chromosome 1 N times. The legend says only that the labels give file size relative to chromosome 1 (241.4 Mb). The values of N, and so the actual file sizes, appear only in the Fig 3 image. The text therefore never states that any test file is larger than the human genome (Dataset B, file size ~2.9 G). The paper's sentence "the memory usage increased with file size and stayed at approximately 780 Mb" is internally ambiguous: it may mean that memory rose and then levelled off. It is quoted as printed. The mechanisms come from the Implementation (page 3) and Methods (page 4) sections, and the paper does not explicitly link them to the scaling result. records.short_answer: Most SeqKit subcommands do not load all FASTA/Q records into memory. Removing duplicate sequences by content does need whole sequences in memory, so SeqKit uses an MD5 digest to represent sequence content, which greatly reduces memory usage. Some subcommands ("sample", "split", "shuffle" and "sort" on page 4; "subseq", "split", "sort" and "shuffle" on page 3) read the files twice in two-pass mode, which uses the FASTA index for rapid access of sequences and reduces memory usage (FASTA format only). The sequence parser uses a custom buffered file reading algorithm instead of Go's "bufio", which increased speed and significantly lowered memory usage. Most CPU-intensive processes are parallelized by multiple Goroutines. In tests on files made by repeating human chromosome 1 N times, memory stayed at approximately 780 Mb for reverse complement and duplicate removal, and peak memory stayed at approximately 750 Mb for shuffling and sorting with the FASTA index. The authors conclude that peak memory usage is determined by the length of the longest sequence record, so SeqKit can handle large FASTA and FASTQ files as data size grows.

records.question_issues: The paper never describes a trade-off between user accessibility and computational efficiency, and it never says that one design choice balances the two. The question's framing is interpretive. The answer is built from separate statements: the implementation (mainly Python, with the alignment algorithm in C as a Python extension module "for speed"), the accessibility statements (user-friendly, easy-to-use command-line tool; automatic detection of gzip compression; should work wherever Python is available; full documentation through "cutadapt --help"), and the Performance section (O(nk) theoretical cost; in practice, reading and parsing the input take more than half of the time; about 1 million reads per minute). The paper does not say that Python was chosen for accessibility, nor that the C module was chosen because alignment dominates the theoretical cost; an answer asserting either causal link goes beyond the text. The question can also reasonably be read as asking only about the Python/C split (evidence 0).

records.short_answer: Cutadapt is mainly written in Python, but for speed the alignment algorithm is implemented in C as a Python extension module. On accessibility, it is a user-friendly, easy-to-use command-line program that supports a variety of file formats, automatically detects gzip compression of input or output files, has full documentation via "cutadapt --help", and should work on any platform for which Python is available. On efficiency, in theory trimming is dominated by computing alignments, O(nk) (n = total characters in all reads, k = sum of adapter lengths); in practice, reading and parsing the input files take more than half of the time. With 35 bp colour-space reads and an adapter of length 18, it trims approximately 1 million reads per minute (0.06 ms per read) on a single core of a 2.66 GHz Intel Core 2 processor.

The paper characterises four targets: partial p72, complete p54, partial CD2v and partial B602L/CVR. The Methods primer sentence calls three of them "Three different genomic targets" and adds CD2v separately, so the number of targets can be read as three or four. The Abstract and the Conclusion say "five variants based on the number of deleted KCPPPK motifs" (evidence 17, 19). The motif is also spelt three ways: KPCPPP, PCPPPK and KCPPPK. (3) The tree topologies and support values (Figs 2, 3, 5) and the per-isolate profiles (Table 2) are only in figure images or the table. The prose gives only the resulting assignments. The id suffix "CO2" has no counterpart in the paper or the question.

records.short_answer:
The researchers characterised four gene targets: the partial P72, the complete p54, the partial CD2v and the partial B602L genes. They sequenced nineteen partial p72 and p54 genes, fourteen partial CD2v genes and twenty partial B602L, and aligned the sequences with MUSCLE in MEGA software version 7. Each gene gave a different level of classification.

Genotype (p72): they built a Neighbor-Joining tree in Mega 7 with the Maximum Composite Likelihood method and 1,000 bootstrap re-samplings. The dataset held 93 nucleotide sequences (398 characters): 19 from this study plus GenBank sequences, with at least one representative of each of the 24 known ASFV genotypes and historical samples from Burkina Faso and neighbouring countries. All 2018 Burkina Faso ASFV clustered within genotype I.

Subgroup (p54): they built a Minimum Evolution tree with the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm. The dataset held 63 taxa (453 characters), including 19 study sequences and representatives of the 18 p72 genotypes for which a p54 sequence is available. All isolates belong to the genotype Ia subgroup. The alignments split them further into two sub-groups by complete p54 length (552 bp and 564 bp).

Serogroup (CD2v): they built a maximum-likelihood tree of the partial CD2v amino acid sequences with the predetermined CpREV + G model. The dataset included representatives of the eight known serogroups and ASFVs clustering outside them. All sequenced isolates belong to serogroup 4. By the number of deleted PCPPPK units, the isolates fell into groups with 0, 2, 3 or 4 missing KPCPPP units. The Abstract and Conclusion instead give five variants based on deleted KCPPPK motifs.

CVR (B602L): each CVR was translated and its tetramers matched with previously reported codes. The 20 CVRs gave four TRS variants, with 32, 24, 23 and 12 TRS.

Combined result: ASFVs of genotype I, serogroup 4, caused four outbreaks in October 2018 in Burkina Faso. CD2v can serve as an additional tool for discriminating ASFV isolates.

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with three caveats. (1) Software is named only for assembly and editing (Vector NTI 11.5), alignment (MUSCLE in MEGA 7) and the p72 Neighbor-Joining tree (Mega 7). The paper does not name the program behind the p54 Minimum Evolution tree or the CD2v maximum-likelihood tree, so an answer that credits MEGA 7 with those two trees goes beyond the text. (2) "Phylogenetic methods" covers a different method for each gene (p72 NJ, p54 ME, CD2v ML), so a full answer lists all three. (3) The paper contradicts itself on where the CVR variants occur and when. The Results say the Kossodo 23-TRS profile was "identical to the pattern found in the fourth outbreak ... in Tampouy". Table 2 gives all three Tampouy isolates (BKF_2018_19 to _21) the 32-TRS string, and the Discussion says the 32-TRS Kossodo isolate BKF_2018_05 matched Tampouy. The Results date the Saaba index outbreak to September 28, 2018. Table 2 dates the Saaba isolates 23-Sep-18 and the Kossodo isolates 28-Sep-18, and the Discussion gives onset "between September 23 and September 28, 2018". The number of CVR variants (four) and their repeat counts (32, 24, 23, 12) are the same in the Abstract, Results, Table 2, Discussion and Conclusion.

records.short_answer:
Software: the raw sequences were assembled and edited in Vector NTI 11.5 Software. Multiple sequence alignments were done with MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7.

Phylogenetic methods, one per gene:
- p72: a Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree built in Mega 7 using the Maximum Composite Likelihood method.
- p54: a Minimum Evolution tree using the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm. The initial tree came from the Neighbor-joining algorithm, and all positions with less than 95% site coverage were removed.
- CD2v: a maximum-likelihood (ML) tree of the partial amino acid sequences using the CpREV + G model.
Each tree was tested with 1000 bootstrap replicates.

CVR: each CVR nucleotide sequence was translated into amino acids, and the tetramers were matched with previously reported codes. The 20 CVRs gave four variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS), with 32, 24, 23 and 12 TRS. Three of the four shared motifs beginning with "ABNAAA" and ending with "CBNAFA". Where each variant was found:
- 12 TRS: Saaba (the index outbreak), Nioko II and Kossodo.
- 24 TRS: only at Nioko II.
- 23 TRS and 32 TRS: Kossodo.

Tampouy: the Results say the Kossodo 23 TRS pattern was identical to Tampouy's. Table 2 lists the Tampouy isolates as 32 TRS, and the Discussion matches Tampouy to the 32 TRS Kossodo isolate.

All four variants differ from the ten found in samples from 2007 to 2010, which makes fourteen variants identified in the country.

key_concepts.phrase: MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7
four variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS)

records.question_issues: Answerable, with four caveats. (1) The question equates Galliformes with chickens. The paper's chicken-side groups are layer-type and meat-type poultry, and meat-type includes turkey farms (Table 3; p7 says the meat-type category "also contained many broiler and turkey farms"). Clinical signs are compared as layer-type vs meat-type vs ducks, or by age group (juvenile/adult chickens vs juvenile/adult ducks). (2) "Mortality detection thresholds" can be read two ways. Reading (a) is the study's own measure: how often the MR > 3 cut-off was reached the day before notification. Reading (b) is the reporting thresholds in Dutch legislation and the literature, which differ for chickens and ducks. Both are answered here. (3) Under reading (a), the abstract and discussion say ducks reached MR > 3 less often, but the paper reports that the differences between poultry types were not statistically significant (Table 6). The adult-duck figure rests on a single farm with mortality data (0 of 1). (4) The paper contradicts itself twice. Nervous and locomotor signs on duck farms are 67.7% in the p7 text but 14/21 = 66.7% in Table 5. Juvenile ducks with MR > 3 are 53% in the p10 text but 7/12 = 58.3% in Table 6. Both versions of each are quoted.

records.short_answer:
Clinical signs: ducks more often showed neurological (nervous) and locomotor signs and reproductive tract signs. Nervous and locomotor signs were seen on 67.7% of duck farms in the text (66.7% in Table 5), against 48.4% of meat-type and 15.0% of layer-type farms. Reproductive tract signs were seen in 100% of ducks, against 19.4% of layer-type and 28.6% of meat-type farms. Reduced feed intake was also seen mainly in ducks. Layer- and meat-type poultry more often showed mucosal membrane and skin signs, including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva (55.0% and 67.8%, against 4.7% of duck farms). These signs were more frequent in juvenile than adult chickens. Respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry (61.3%, against 37.5% of layers and 23.8% of ducks). Gastrointestinal signs were more frequent in adult than juvenile chickens, and the opposite held in ducks.

Mortality: in both chickens and ducks, mortality increased exponentially within four days before notification. The trend fluctuated more in ducks and meat-type poultry than in layers, and duck mortality showed more peaks. Ducks reached a mortality ratio (MR) > 3 against the previous week's average less often than chickens. The day before notification, 54% of duck farms reached it, against 83% of layer-type and 80% of meat-type chicken farms, but these differences were not statistically significant. Adult ducks reached it least often (0 of 1 farm). In chicken flocks, high mortality was the main reason for notification. In ducks, mortality remained limited, and notifications were more often based on a decrease in feed or water intake or egg production.

Reporting thresholds: the Dutch rules require chickens to be reported at MR > 3, meaning mortality tripled for two consecutive days against the average of the week before. Ducks must be reported at daily mortality >0.15% for two consecutive days, or >0.5% for one day combined with a 5% decrease in feed intake. The literature suggested daily mortality thresholds of 0.13% for layers, >0.17% for broilers and 0.3% for ducks, and a >9% drop in egg production for breeder ducks. The authors conclude that reporting criteria should differ between poultry species and age groups.

records.question_issues: Partly answerable. The paper gives no formula for the MR. It says MRs were calculated "using the method described by Gonzales and Elbers (2018) [25]" and leaves the detail to that reference. records.short_answer: The MR was calculated from NVWA farm production charts with daily mortality records, which were retrieved for 63 of 92 farms. The percentage of daily mortality was calculated per house. Then 0.1 was added to all percentages so that log10 could be taken, and log10(0.1) = −1 indicated no mortality (0%). For each flock, the MR of the day before notification was calculated using the method described by Gonzales and Elbers (2018). The MR compares mortality with the average mortality of the previous week. The method had also been used by Schreuder et al. (2021), but this study adjusted it slightly, using a threshold of >3 instead of >2.9. This threshold matches Dutch legislation, which requires notification when daily mortality is >3 times the average mortality of the preceding week for two consecutive days. Each farm was scored as increased (MR above the cut-off value of 3), not increased (MR < 3), or unknown/unclear (MR could not be calculated). The MR could not be calculated for 36 of 92 farms.

records.short_answer: Both the test and the skinfold-thickness threshold change the estimated prevalence substantially. With CIDT at 3 mm, 11 of 160 cattle were positive, an apparent prevalence of 6.8% (95% CI: 4.35%–9.41%). At the 4 mm threshold (the WOAH positive decision threshold), CIDT gave 0.6% (95% CI: 0%–1.2%). The paper gives that count as 1 positive in Table-2 and as three positives in the prose. SITT at 4 mm found 3 positives out of 160, an AP of 1.8% (95% CI: 0%–3.6%). The Abstract reverses the two 4 mm figures. The authors conclude that the 3 mm threshold increased the sensitivity of bTB detection, and that AP at ≥3 mm was significantly higher than at ≥4 mm for CIDT. At the CIDT 3 mm threshold, body condition score significantly influenced prevalence. They cite an Ethiopian study in which CIDT performed best at a threshold strictly >2 mm, and they recommend applying thresholds of 3 mm in Cameroon rather than 4 mm.

- CIDT at a 3 mm threshold: 11 positive, 6.8% (95% CI: 4.35%–9.41%).

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with three caveats. (1) The paper names three software packages. Microsoft Excel 2010 organised the data. IBM SPSS Statistics was used "to analyze data" in general, and its version is given two ways in the same sentence ("20.0" and "Version 27.0"). R 2.10.0 is the only package tied explicitly to the univariate and multivariate (logistic regression) analyses, so R is the answer for the regression models. (2) "Verify the independence of the identified risk factors" is best read as the multicollinearity check by variance inflation factor (VIF). The paper's wording there is odd: VIF was tested "to avoid model convergence", and the result sentence says all VIFs close to one indicate that "collinearity was not explored", which presumably means no collinearity was found. That wording is quoted as printed and not reinterpreted. (3) The paper also reports a likelihood ratio statistic (LRT) in Table-6 and says all possible interactions with the final model were examined. These are secondary metrics or steps, so they are included as supporting evidence.

records.short_answer: The univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were run in R 2.10.0 statistical software (R Core Team). Only variables with p < 0.2 entered the multivariate analysis. The model was refined by a top-down step-by-step analysis using the Akaike information criterion (AIC; the lower the AIC, the better the model): AIC fell from 85.07 in the original model to 45.83, and the procedure stopped when deleting any other variable would increase the AIC. Table-6 (identification of variables with significant effects on the initial model) also reports a likelihood ratio statistic (LRT) per variable, and all possible interactions with the final model were examined. Independence of the risk factors was checked as multi-collinearity with the variance inflation factor (VIF): all VIFs were close to one (forage reason 1, cattle herder 1.212942, age >10 years 1.106897, tuberculous organs seizure 1.172151). The multivariate model reported adjusted ORs (AORs) and p-values. Elsewhere the paper says Microsoft Excel 2010 was used to organize data and IBM SPSS Statistics (version printed as 20.0 and as 27.0) to analyze data.

records.question_issues: The question's premise, "even when average coverage targets are met", does not match the paper. The recommended 70% target was rarely met: only 3% of village campaigns reached it (evidence 13). Vaccination still controlled rabies without reaching it (evidence 10). The heterogeneity result is comparative. At the SAME average (non-focal, wider-district) coverage, more heterogeneous coverage gives higher focal incidence. The worked example uses a mean of 40%, not a met target (evidence 5, 6). So the question can be answered as "same average coverage, different spatial distribution", but not as "the target was met and rabies still persisted". Two caveats belong in a complete answer. First, the heterogeneity effect was detected only in models that leave out prior incidence beyond the focal village, because prior incidence masks it (evidence 0, 3). Second, the estimated power p lay beyond the range the authors expected a priori (evidence 4). The paper links heterogeneity to outbreaks and continued circulation (evidence 1, 7, 12). It does not directly measure persistence inside low-coverage patches.

evidence.sentence: Removing the masking effects of prior non-focal incidence shows that, for the same average prior non-focal (wider-district) vaccination coverage, increased heterogeneity in coverage among the non-focal villages leads to increased focal incidence.
evidence.supports: Core result: at equal average coverage, more heterogeneity raises focal incidence, seen only once prior non-focal incidence is removed

evidence.sentence: These effects led to outbreaks following years when vaccination campaigns missed many villages, whereas when heterogeneity in coverage was reduced, incidence declined to low levels (<0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually and no human deaths) and short vaccination lapses thereafter did not lead to resurgence.
evidence.supports: Consequence: outbreaks after villages were missed; low incidence and no resurgence once heterogeneity was reduced

evidence.sentence: If p>1, the power mean is biased towards higher susceptibility villages and rises above the arithmetic mean; i.e. for the same total number of unvaccinated dogs, the effective susceptibility is higher when those dogs are distributed unevenly.
evidence.supports: Mechanism as modelled: an uneven distribution of unvaccinated dogs raises effective susceptibility

evidence.sentence: We find that incidence increases with power mean susceptibility in bordering and non-bordering villages only when prior incidence at those scales is not included (Table 1, Fig. 4A).
evidence.supports: Condition under which the heterogeneity effect is detected

evidence.sentence: In those models we estimate p to be substantially larger than one (Table 1, Fig. 4B) and beyond what we a priori expected to be the feasible range (Fig. S6).
evidence.supports: Estimated p > 1, so heterogeneity raises effective susceptibility; caveat about the feasible range

evidence.sentence: The power mean susceptibility model without prior incidence beyond the focal village predicts, for example, that if half the bordering and non-bordering villages had prior coverage of 30%, with the other half having 50%, then the focal village incidence would be 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times greater than if prior coverage had been homogeneous at 40%.
evidence.supports: Quantified effect at the same mean coverage (40%)

evidence.sentence: If we further increase heterogeneity by assuming half the villages had prior 20% coverage and the other half 60%, then focal incidence is expected to be 2.6 (95% CrI: 1.9-3.4) times the homogeneous scenario.
evidence.supports: Greater heterogeneity at the same mean gives a larger increase in incidence

evidence.sentence: Under endemic rabies circulation, we find that outbreaks occur following multi-year periods when clusters of villages remain unvaccinated.

evidence.sentence: We therefore conclude that, while high coverage should be the target for rapidly controlling disease, policymakers should not be deterred from introducing dog vaccination when achieving 70% coverage is challenging; if persistent spatial gaps are minimal, sub-optimal coverage still has major benefits due to rabies’ low transmissibility [44] relative to human diseases that require higher levels of vaccination [61].
evidence.supports: Spatial gaps matter: with minimal gaps, sub-optimal coverage still works

evidence.supports: Premise check: rabies was controlled without meeting the target

evidence.sentence: In contrast, high coverage in a small area has only limited impact if the rest of the population is poorly vaccinated, consistent with the findings of previous simulation studies[38,63].

evidence.sentence: Returning to our three initial hypotheses for why rabies continues to circulate despite control efforts, we conclude that: 1) spatial heterogeneity in dog vaccination was detrimental for control, and vaccination was only effective in interrupting endemic circulation when implemented consistently, underlining the importance of monitoring fine-scale coverage to promptly identify and address gaps; 2) mean coverage over the district was relatively low, but once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless – a promising result given hard-to-reach populations with fast demographic rates; 3) Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district are frequent and now represent a major source of residual transmission.
evidence.supports: Overall conclusion on heterogeneity and continued circulation

records.short_answer: The spatial distribution of coverage matters, not only its average. For the same average prior non-focal (wider-district) vaccination coverage, increased heterogeneity in coverage among non-focal villages leads to increased focal incidence. In the power mean susceptibility model, p was estimated to be substantially larger than one. With p>1, the same total number of unvaccinated dogs gives a higher effective susceptibility when those dogs are distributed unevenly. Against homogeneous 40% prior coverage, a 30%/50% split is predicted to raise focal incidence 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times. A 20%/60% split raises it 2.6 (95% CrI: 1.9-3.4) times. Outbreaks followed multi-year periods when clusters of villages remained unvaccinated. High coverage in a small area has only limited impact if the rest of the population is poorly vaccinated. Spatial heterogeneity in dog vaccination was detrimental for control, and vaccination interrupted endemic circulation only when implemented consistently. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, although mean district coverage stayed relatively low. Two caveats. The effect was seen only once the masking effects of prior non-focal incidence were removed. The estimated p lay beyond the range the authors expected a priori. The premise does not hold for this study: only 3% of village campaigns reached the 70% target, and vaccination controlled rabies without reaching it.

high coverage in a small area

records.short_answer: The authors reconstructed transmission trees using the treerabid package in R. The algorithm probabilistically assigned a progenitor to each case with no known rabid biter. A possible progenitor had to have an earlier symptoms onset date, and its serial interval and distance from the case had to be smaller than a selected quantile of those distributions (the pruning threshold). The main analysis used the 97.5% pruning threshold. Where no progenitor qualified, the case was assumed to be an incursion. Probable incursions were the cases identified as an incursion more often than they were assigned to any other progenitor across 1,000 bootstrapped trees. The number of incursions stayed relatively constant (mean of 7 annual incursions). The proportion of cases identified as incursions sharply increased, from 3% pre-2018 to 26% post-2018 (>20% of cases since 2019), and peaked at 50% in 2022.

records.question_issues: The question is answerable from the text, but "why" can be read two ways. (a) Why the paper judges herd immunity insufficient: the 68.8% measured in 128 vaccinated small ruminants is below the FAO-WOAH recommended threshold of 80% herd immunity. (b) Why immunity falls short: the paper offers possible causes (logistics, cold chain, vaccine handling and distribution, awareness), but only as speculation ("may be due to"). The record answers (a) as the core and gives (b) as the paper's suggested explanation. The paper reports no zone-wide immunity estimate. The 68.8% comes from the sampled vaccinated animals and is called a "seroconversion rate" (Results), an "overall seroprevalence" (Results) and a "protection level" / herd immunity (Discussion).

records.short_answer: Herd immunity measured in 128 vaccinated small ruminants was 68.8% (reported as the seroconversion rate). That is below the FAO-WOAH recommended threshold of 80% herd immunity, so the study concludes that herd immunity in vaccinated animals is inadequate. The authors suggest the shortfall may be due to logistical challenges in vaccination efforts: inadequate cold chain management, poor vaccine handling and distribution practices, and insufficient awareness and communication during vaccination campaigns.

records.question_issues: "Clinical history" is not a term the paper uses. It is read here as the herd history of abortion and of retained fetal membranes (RFM), which the paper records as yes/no variables. The paper is internally inconsistent in several places that bear on the answer. (1) Small ruminants, multivariable RFM: the text gives OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42), but Table 2 gives 8.2 (2.4–29), the same value as the univariable Table 1. (2) Camels, univariable RFM: the text and Table 3 both give OR 22 with 95% CI 5.9–8, an interval that does not contain the point estimate. (3) Camels, multivariable RFM: the text gives only the CI (12.7–60) and p < 0.05. Table 4 gives OR 35 (12.7–60,) and p = 0.004. (4) Camels, history of abortion: it is significant in the univariable analysis (OR 3.9, p = 0.02) but not in the multivariable Table 4 (OR 0.7, p = 0.80). The Discussion still says camel seropositivity was 'significantly associated with RFM and history of abortion' and does not say which analysis it means. (5) The Discussion gives p < 0.001 for RFM, while the tables print 0.00*. (6) The 'Not aborted' camel count is 250 in Table 3 and 259 in Table 4. (7) Pregnancy in camels is physiological status, not history, so it is left out of the answer. Its values also disagree: the text gives OR 3.3 (1.4–15), but in Table 3 that value sits on the 'Lactating' row, and the 'Pregnant' row reads 5.3 (0.7–20), p = 0.01.

records.short_answer:
In both species, a history of retained fetal membranes (RFM) was the history factor significantly associated with Brucella seropositivity. Together with herd size, the paper names it a risk factor for brucellosis in animals.

Small ruminants: 33.3% of animals with a history of RFM were seropositive, compared with 1.5% of those without (univariable OR 8.2, 95% CI 2.4–29). For the multivariable model, the text gives OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42) and Table 2 prints 8.2 (2.4–29). History of abortion was not significant (23% vs 3.1%, OR 3, 95% CI 0.9–9.7, p = 0.08).

Camels: in the univariable analysis, both history of abortion (10.2% vs 2.8%, OR 3.9, 95% CI 1.2–13) and RFM (35.7% vs 2.5%, OR 22) were significant. In the multivariable model only RFM stayed significant (OR 35, 95% CI 12.7–60, p = 0.004). Abortion did not (OR 0.7, p = 0.80). Even so, the Discussion says camel seropositivity was associated with both RFM and history of abortion.

The authors explain the link this way: when Brucella causes abortion, the placenta is frequently retained, so retained fetal membrane is a sequel of brucellosis.

records.short_answer:
Laboratory sequence: the 1,000 serum samples were first screened for anti-Brucella antibodies with the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT). Any visible agglutination counted as positive. Camels were tested with 30 μL of RBPT. Sheep and goats got a modified RBPT, one volume of antigen to three volumes of serum (e.g. 25 μL with 75 μL), to improve sensitivity. All RBPT-positive sera were then tested at Jigjiga Veterinary Diagnostic and Research Laboratory. The Methods say animal sera went to a commercial cELISA (Abbexa) and human sera to an IgG ELISA (Abbexa). The Discussion instead says RBPT and c-ELISA were used for camel and human sera. A sample was seropositive only if it tested positive on both RBPT and cELISA, and a flock or herd was seropositive if at least one animal was positive on both tests. The two tests were used serially. RBPT was the screening test for its high sensitivity, and competitive ELISA excluded false-positive cross-reactions to keep specificity at its maximum.

Statistics: data were entered into Microsoft Excel and analysed in R (version R-3.3.0). Univariate logistic regression first identified putative risk factors. Variables with p ≤ 0.2 in that step went into a multiple (multivariable) logistic regression, estimated by maximum likelihood. The candidate variables were age, sex, species, RFM, parity, abortion, physiological status, flock/herd size and migration. When two variables showed strong collinearity (p < 0.05), one was excluded on grounds of biological plausibility. Stepwise backward elimination selected the variables for the final model, and strength of association was assessed with odds ratios.

records.question_issues: The question can be answered from the text, with two caveats. (1) The "biological evidence" the question asks for is partly a methodological argument in the review (Section 3.4, page 8). The 28-day definition came from a single 4-week study, which counted cattle still virus-positive at the end as carriers. The biological part is that cattle which cleared infection did so considerably earlier, and that a transitional stage falls at about 14–21 dpi, or 7–14 dpi in vaccinated cattle. All of this evidence concerns cattle only. (2) The paper describes the pig/ruminant difference as the presence or absence of a carrier state. It gives no mechanism for that difference and lists it as an open question on page 18: "Why are ruminants, but not suids susceptible to persistent FMDV infection?" The contrast is stated in two places, the Figure 2 legend (page 5) and Section 3.4 (page 8), and the two agree.

records.short_answer:
Pigs: no FMDV carrier state. Pigs efficiently clear FMDV from all tissues after recovering from the clinical phase.

Ruminants: FMDV can cause a prolonged persistent phase of subclinical infection, with continuous low-level virus replication in distinct epithelial compartments. In cattle these are in the upper respiratory tract; in sheep and African buffalo, the upper gastrointestinal tract. This is the carrier state. In ruminants, persistence follows either clinical or subclinical infection, regardless of vaccination or immune status.

The 28-day threshold: the carrier state is commonly defined as isolating FMDV from oropharyngeal fluid (probang) samples for more than 28 days after infection. Three points in the review undercut that threshold.
- It came from a single historical experimental study limited to 4 weeks, which assumed that cattle still virus-positive at the end of the study were carriers.
- Cattle that cleared infection had done so considerably earlier, a finding confirmed by more recent publications.
- A transitional stage, in which animals either clear the virus or become carriers, occurs at about 14–21 dpi in clinically affected cattle, and about 7–14 dpi in cattle clinically protected by vaccination.

The review concludes that the 28-day threshold holds no specific biological relevance, but may still be useful for practical purposes.

records.question_issues: "Relative frequency" can be read two ways: how often infection has been detected in mammals versus humans, or how often each clinical presentation occurs within each group. The paper answers both only qualitatively. For mammals it lists species and says "most" presented with severe neurological disease, with no count of infected mammals. For humans it gives "less than 10" cases and says "most" were mild or asymptomatic. The paper names no specific human symptoms observed in clade 2.3.4.4b cases. Acute febrile respiratory disease and unexplained neurological disease appear only as criteria for when clinicians should suspect HPAI, so that sentence is not used as evidence. Conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal symptoms are attributed to other avian H5 strains, not to clade 2.3.4.4b. The figure of over 860 humans infected with about 50% mortality refers to H5N1 before 2020, not to this clade, and is excluded. The paper also says the observed mammal picture is skewed towards severe disease because wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals. v2.3 (11 October 2026, F2): that sentence is now evidence 8 and the answer reports it as the presentations in which clinicians should consider HPAI infection.

records.short_answer: Mammals: clade 2.3.4.4b H5N1 has infected multiple species, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Most infected mammals presented with severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Milder disease was likely also present (and likely more prevalent), because wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, and identified infections are assumed to represent only a minority of spillovers. Humans: this clade has been identified in less than 10 humans. Most cases have been mild or asymptomatic (the first case, in the United Kingdom, was mild; a second, in the United States in April 2022, was asymptomatic), but in recent months severe cases have occurred, all with direct exposure to poultry. The paper reports no symptom profile for the clade 2.3.4.4b human cases, but it advises clinicians to consider HPAI virus infection in any individual with acute febrile respiratory disease or unexplained neurological diseases after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10 to 14 days; it notes that conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal symptoms have also been reported in humans infected with other avian H5 strains. Comparison: detected mammal infections span many species and are mostly severe neurological disease, while human infections are few (less than 10) and mostly mild or asymptomatic.

records.short_answer: Breed selection: most studies focus on a few cosmopolitan and highly selected breeds. Local breeds from rural areas are largely neglected or frequently overlooked, despite their demonstrated resistance to harsh environmental circumstances. The paper names ovicaprine and chicken breeds from rural areas of developing countries as largely neglected. It says this focus lacks representativeness in terms of diversity and functionality. Taxonomic focus: research has mostly focused on bacteria, the most-studied microbial group. Other microorganisms (protists or protozoa, fungi, archaea and viruses) have received far less attention, and knowledge of them is scant. They usually get attention only when they are parasites of commercial relevance. Research on commensal protozoa and on the fungal component of the gut microbiome is still limited.

records.question_issues: Part of the premise is false. Paper 21 is a narrative review. It has no Methods section and analyses no livestock microbiome data of its own. The question can only be answered as "the sequencing techniques and bioinformatics tools the review describes", mainly in Section 2 (Next-Generation Sequencing Techniques: 2.1 Amplicon Metabarcoding, 2.2 Shotgun Sequencing, 2.3 Metatranscriptomics) and Section 6 (Metagenome and Functional Profile Prediction). The question is also open-ended, so where the list stops is a judgement call. The core items are the three Section 2 techniques and every software tool the paper names (QIIME, Tax4Fun, BLAST+, HISAT, ABioTrans, PICRUSt, PICRUSt2, FaproTax, Tax4fun2). Some items could reasonably go either way: the reference databases (GenBank, Greengenes v13_8, SILVA 138, RDP18), KEGG pathway analysis, and pyrosequencing and nanopore technology, which the paper names only when citing chicken and cow studies. Approaches mentioned in passing without a named tool (culturomics, metaproteomics) are left out.

evidence.sentence: The advent of innovative nanopore technology, which enables large-scale research to highlight the most abundant resistance genes that may have a signiﬁcant inﬂuence on animal, human, and environmental health, has spurred the rapidly expanding interest in the cow resistome [155].

records.short_answer:
The paper is a review and has no methods of its own. It describes these next-generation sequencing techniques and tools:
(1) Amplicon metabarcoding, a PCR-based method with dual indexing. It targets the V2-V3 and V3-V4 16S rRNA hypervariable regions for bacteria, the V4 and V9 18S rRNA regions for protists, and ITS1 and ITS2 for fungi. Its reference sequences come from GenBank, Greengenes v13_8, SILVA 138 and RDP18. QIIME does 16S-based taxonomic assignment, and Tax4Fun predicts functional profiles from 16S sequences.
(2) Shotgun sequencing, with BLAST+ for building customized reference databases.
(3) Metatranscriptomics, especially RNASeq, with the software HISAT and ABioTrans.
(4) Functional-profile prediction with PICRUSt, PICRUSt2, FaproTax, Tax4Fun and Tax4fun2, often combined with KEGG pathway analysis.
In passing, the review also names comparative metagenomic pyrosequencing (chicken studies) and nanopore technology (cow resistome).

key_concepts.phrase: Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology pipeline (QIIME)
Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with three caveats. (1) The study measures the weaning effect on individual MAGs: MaAsLin2 compares samples taken immediately before weaning with samples taken 7 days postweaning. The question's "transition from nursing to weaning" matches that comparison. (2) The genus-level pattern (Bacteroides and Escherichia decrease; Blautia, Prevotella and Roseburia increase) comes from cited earlier studies (refs 38-40). The paper adds only that many of its differentially abundant MAGs were assigned to these genera, and gives no per-genus direction for its own data. An answer that presents that pattern as this study's measurement overstates it. (3) The full list of differentially abundant MAGs is in Table S5, the NMDS plot in Fig. S1 and per-MAG abundances in the Fig. 1 bars. None of these is in the text, so the answer rests on the taxa the text names. Text layer: both extractions print the plus-minus sign as '6' in '(0.25 6 0.07%)'. It is quoted as printed.

records.short_answer:
The diet changes abruptly at weaning, from liquid and milk-based to solid and based on cereal grains. By 7 days postweaning, the relative abundance of a large number of MAGs had shifted significantly (MaAsLin2, immediately before weaning versus 7 days postweaning).

Decreases: 69 MAGs fell in relative abundance. The most differentially abundant were Limousia pullorum, B. fragilis, E. coli, P. hyovaginalis and P. vulgatus. C. coli and S. pasteurianus MAGs were also enriched in preweaned piglets. Six MAGs above 0.1% in nursing piglets were not detected in the same pigs 7 d later: B. thetaiotaomicron, Bulleidia sp., Enterococcus faecalis, Mediterraneibacter torques, Parvimonas sp. and P. hyovaginalis. One E. faecalis MAG was relatively abundant in nursing samples (0.25 ± 0.07%, printed '0.25 6 0.07%') and was not detected in any postweaning sample. It may represent a strain unique to nursing piglets.

Increases: 140 MAGs rose in relative abundance, including Copromorpha sp., Clostridium sp000435835, Fusicatenibacter saccharivorans, Intestinibacter sp., Oliverpabstia intestinalis, Phascolarctobacterium sp004558595, Prevotella sp002251295, Prevotella sp004556065 and Ruminococcus sp003011855. They also included uncultured potential butyrate producers (CAG-83 sp., Aphodosoma sp900769035, Copromorpha sp., Egerieousia sp004561775, UMGS1668 sp004556975).

Genus level: earlier studies (38-40) report that weaning lowers Bacteroides and Escherichia and raises Blautia, Prevotella and Roseburia. Many of this study's differentially abundant MAGs were assigned to these genera, but several belonged to taxa not known to be associated with weaning.

On an NMDS plot of Bray-Curtis dissimilarities, the preweaned samples appear separate from the postweaned samples of other studies.

records.question_issues: Answerable from the Methods ("Bioinformatics", page 10), the Results (page 2) and the Abstract (page 1). Two points for sign-off. (1) In both text extractions the comparison signs in the Methods are mis-encoded: "<" appears as "," and ">" appears as ".". The text therefore reads "quality score , 15", ". 90% complete" and ", 5% contamination". The evidence quotes them as extracted. The Results and the Abstract give the completeness and contamination thresholds in words ("greater than 90% completeness and less than 5% contamination"; "at least 90% complete and had less than 5% contamination"), and the short answer uses those words. No sentence states the trimming threshold's direction in words, so the short answer gives it as a quality-score threshold of 15. (2) "Identify" can mean recovering the MAGs (assembly and MetaBAT 2 binning) or classifying them (GTDB-tk). Both are included. The paper also reports a second dereplication at 95% ANI that gives 758 putative species. The 1,150 non-redundant MAGs come from the 99% ANI secondary clustering.

records.short_answer: Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic v. 0.38 (quality score threshold 15 over a sliding window of 4 bp, minimum length of 50 bp), which also removed sequencing adapters. Host reads were removed by alignment to the Sus scrofa genome (Sscrofa11.1) with Bowtie2 v. 2.4.2-1. MEGAHIT v. 1.29.0 co-assembled the metagenomes and also assembled each one individually. Before co-assembly, samples were normalized with BBNorm (BBTools v. 38.79). Reads were mapped back to the assemblies with Bowtie2, and contigs with a minimum length of 2,000 bp were binned with MetaBAT 2. CheckM v. 1.1.2 assessed the bins, and MAGs with greater than 90% completeness and less than 5% contamination were retained. This gave 2,327 MAGs from the individual assemblies and 85,145 from the co-assemblies, 87,472 in total, from 738 Gb of sequencing data. dRep v. 3.2.2 dereplicated these MAGs with primary clustering at 90% and secondary clustering at 99% ANI. The result was 1,150 non-redundant MAGs (potentially unique strains), which were used for all subsequent analyses. With 95% ANI for secondary clustering, 758 putative species were produced instead. Taxonomy was assigned with GTDB-tk 2.0.0 and GTDB release 207.

records.short_answer:
The CD methods detected more ASVs than the CI methods at every stage: 415, 675, 808 and 823 ASVs against 378, 482, 565 and 555 at the lactation, nursery, growing and finishing stages. Diversity increased over successive growth stages under both methods, and Shannon diversity rose with age under both. Simpson evenness followed different patterns under the two methods.

The overlap is only partial. 171, 264, 301 and 313 ASVs were shared by CD and CI. On average, 45.2, 54.8, 53.3 and 56.4% of the CI-detected ASVs were observed on the plates, so approximately half of the ASVs were recovered by culture. About 44 to 54% of the CI-detected ASVs remain to be cultured. CD also found 244, 411, 507 and 510 new ASVs that CI did not detect. Each method therefore captures ASVs the other misses, and together they yielded 622, 893, 1,072 and 1,065 ASVs at the four growth stages.
