records.short_answer:
RMP profiles the proportions of taxa, while QMP tracks changes in absolute abundance (AA) and shows the real community dynamics. Microbial loads changed over time and space in the gut. RMP ignored the absolute growth or decline of microbes, failed to detect real microbial changes, and biased both the developmental trajectory and the microbial interactions.

Community variation: AA was relatively stable over time compared with the RMP results. Firmicutes AA was relatively stable in the four gut segments, but its RA varied more, especially in the duodenum and cecum. Ascomycota showed the opposite development trend under QMP and RMP. QMP showed similar Lactobacillus numbers across segments after 7 DHP, whereas RMP showed its abundance as extremely low in the cecum. The same held for Candida. The correlation coefficients (Figure 2B) were only 0.622 (bacteriome) and 0.459 (mycobiome). RA exaggerated the proportion of variation explained by individual, segment and DPH, so RMP overestimated community structure variations and the influencing factors.

Microbial interactions: the comparison used genus-level Spearman's correlation. The QMP and RMP correlations were consistent in 82.1%, 66.0%, 78.7% and 86.8% of cases for the bacteriome (duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum) and in 81.1%, 73.8%, 78.6% and 56.0% for the mycobiome. RMP overestimated bacterial positive correlations: 402 vs. 196 (duodenum), 1164 vs. 678 (jejunum) and 1050 vs. 725 (ileum), but 668 vs. 683 in the cecum. RMP missed fungal positive correlations: 400 vs. 775, 997 vs. 1338, 865 vs. 1044 and 1048 vs. 2270. Overall, RMP missed many significant positive taxon–taxon interactions found in QMP, especially for the fungal community. The authors conclude that quantitative approaches are necessary.

missed positive correlations for the mycobiome
ignored the absolute growth or decline

records.question_issues: The question can be read two ways. "Primary assembly processes" can mean the broad split between deterministic and stochastic processes (bacteria 56.7% deterministic, fungi 55.1% stochastic), or the individual processes (homogeneous selection and homogeneous/homogenizing dispersal). The paper reports both, so the answer gives both. The paper is also inconsistent with itself in places; all of these are quoted as printed. (1) The Results say "Homogeneous dispersal", while the Methods and the Figure 3 legend say "homogenizing dispersal". (2) The Figure 3D legend defines heterogeneous selection as βNTI < −2 and homogeneous selection as βNTI > 2, which is the reverse of the usual βNTI convention. (3) The fungal figures do not add up exactly: homogeneous selection is 44.0% against a deterministic total of 44.9%, and homogeneous dispersal is 50.3% against a stochastic total of 55.1%. The text does not break down the remainder. (4) The full breakdown by process appears only in Figure 3D, which is an image.

evidence.sentence: To assess the relative importance of determinism and stochasticity in microbiome assembly, a two‐step procedure was applied considering β‐nearest taxon index (βNTI) and Bray–Curtis‐based Raup–Crick Index (RCBray) values, including heterogeneous selection, homogeneous selection, dispersal limitation, homogenizing dispersal, and undominated [25].

evidence.sentence: The results indicated that deterministic processes (56.7%) played a more important role than stochastic processes (43.3%) in bacterial communities, and stochastic processes (55.1%) played a more important role than deterministic processes (44.9%) in fungal communities (Figure 3D).
evidence.supports: Bacteria mainly deterministic and fungi mainly stochastic, with percentages

evidence.sentence: Homogeneous dispersal (32.7% for bacteria and 50.3% for fungi) and homogeneous selection (56.7% for bacteria and 44.0% for fungi) were the two processes that governed the assembly of bacterial and fungal communities.
evidence.supports: The two governing processes and their shares in each kingdom

evidence.sentence: The bacteriome was more impacted by deterministic processes, and the mycobiome was more affected by stochastic processes.
evidence.supports: Abstract statement of the bacterial versus fungal contrast

evidence.sentence: Deterministic processes dominated the bacterial community assembly, and stochastic processes governed the fungal community assembly.
evidence.supports: Discussion restatement of the contrast

evidence.sentence: (D) Relative importance of different ecological processes (heterogeneous selection: βNTI < −2, homogeneous selection: βNTI > 2, dispersal limitation: |βNTI| < 2 and RCBray > 0.95, homogenizing dispersal: |βNTI| < 2 and RCBray < −0.95, and undominated: |βNTI| < 2 and |RCBray| < 0.95) along the broiler gut microbiota.

records.short_answer: The study used a two-step procedure based on the β-nearest taxon index (βNTI) and the Bray–Curtis-based Raup–Crick Index (RCBray), calculated with the R package iCAMP (v1.3.4). It sorted assembly into five processes. Two are deterministic: heterogeneous selection and homogeneous selection. Three are stochastic: homogenizing dispersal, dispersal limitation and undominated. Bacterial communities were mainly deterministic (56.7% deterministic versus 43.3% stochastic). Fungal communities were mainly stochastic (55.1% stochastic versus 44.9% deterministic). Two processes governed assembly. Homogeneous selection accounted for 56.7% in bacteria and 44.0% in fungi. Homogeneous dispersal accounted for 32.7% in bacteria and 50.3% in fungi.

records.question_issues: The question can be answered from the text, with these caveats. (1) The paper describes the Chr3 effect in two ways. The abstract and Discussion say the Chr3: 116.5 Mb locus (Chr3:116,575,934) affects RFI only indirectly, through the abundance of microbes. The Results and the Fig. 4 legend say the two BTA3 QTL (Chr3:116,575,934 and Chr3:117,335,980) were "directly and indirectly" associated with RFI. The text never says which SNP has a direct edge to RFI; that detail is only in the Fig. 4 image. An answer giving either reading has support in the text. (2) The paper names the mediators by genus in the abstract and Discussion (Syntrophococcus, Prevotella, an unknown genus of Class Bacilli) and by ASV in Results (ASV1047, ASV666, ASV57). Table 1 lists ASV1047 only as "NA/NA". The paper never says that ASV1047 is the Bacilli genus, so matching the two is an inference. (3) The paper does not say whether the effect raises or lowers RFI, and it gives no mediation effect sizes in the text. It also proposes no specific mechanism for how the Chr3 locus acts on these microbes. It gives only Prevotella's metabolic roles and says that Prevotella interacts with other microorganisms. (4) [Eubacterium] brachy group ASV2236 also co-localises with the RFI pQTL at 116.5-117.3 Mb, but the network does not name it as a mediator. (5) The question ID contains "CO2", but neither the question nor the paper is about CO2. Copying note: the PDF text layer has non-breaking spaces before "Mb" and after "Figure", and an en space after "Fig. 4." and "Table 1.". The non-breaking spaces are kept in the evidence sentences.

records.short_answer: The causal network was learned with the IAMB algorithm and Fisher's Z test. It shows that the cow genome at Chr3: 116.5 Mb (SNP Chr3:116,575,934) affects RFI indirectly. The effect is mediated by the abundance of rumen microbes: Syntrophococcus, Prevotella and an unknown genus of Class Bacilli. Results says the two BTA3 QTL (Chr3:116,575,934 and Chr3:117,335,980) were directly and indirectly associated with RFI, mediated by the rumen microbiome (ASV1047, ASV666 and ASV57). In the genomic scans, 116.5-117.3 Mb on BTA3 was an RFI pQTL and one of the regions with the strongest SNP effects on RFI. Prevotella ASV57, Syntrophococcus ASV666 and [Eubacterium] brachy group ASV2236 had significant SNP in the same region. So the microbes are mediators: the host genome affects their abundance, and through them it affects RFI. Prevotella can use starch, protein, hemicellulose and pectin to produce acetate, succinate and propionate. It interacts with other microorganisms and affects dairy cow feed efficiency.

key_concepts.phrase: directly and indirectly associated with RFI

records.short_answer: Causal structure was learned with the Incremental Association Markov Blanket (IAMB) algorithm, used in conjunction with Fisher’s Z test for conditional independence (α = 0.10), with all network analyses in the R package bnlearn. Stability of the causal networks was evaluated using Jackknife resampling: leaving out one observation per time from the dataset, each edge of the original network was evaluated for presence (presence or absence in the resampled network) and direction (same direction as the original edge, opposite direction, or undirected arc), expressed as the frequency at which a given edge was presented and with the same direction in the resampled networks. Most edges were present in more than 65% of the resampled networks.

records.short_answer:
Gut bacteria ferment dietary fiber (host-indigestible carbohydrates) into SCFAs, chiefly acetate, propionate and butyrate. Dietary fiber intake therefore influences SCFA levels and composition. Colonic cells absorb SCFAs through monocarboxylate transporters, passive diffusion or bicarbonate exchange. Inside these cells, SCFAs are converted to acetyl-CoA or propynyl-CoA, which produces ATP. SCFAs the colonic cells do not metabolize travel through the portal circulation to the liver, where they serve as an energy substrate. Only small amounts reach the systemic circulation. There they increase insulin secretion, maintain energy homeostasis and improve the function of the liver, skeletal muscles and adipose tissue.

The review cites four links from SCFAs to fat:
- Acetate-dependent GPR43 stimulation in white adipose tissue improved glucose and lipid metabolism.
- In rabbits, acetate reduced intramuscular triglyceride levels by increasing fatty acid uptake and fatty acid oxidation, and PPARα was associated with this reduction in fat.
- Low-fat pigs had more butyrate-producing bacteria and more SCFA formation, especially butyrate, which alleviated fat deposition.
- SCFA administration into the ileum of growing pigs inhibited mRNA expression of fatty acid synthase (FAS) and acetyl-CoA carboxylase in the longissimus dorsi.

The review concludes that through these effects on muscle and fat tissue, SCFAs influence meat quality.

records.question_issues: The paper is a review, so "the gut microbiome studies cited" can be read at two scopes. Read narrowly, it matches the review's own sentence "Gut microbiome studies showed that..." (Lei et al., 2021), and the answer is four genera: Ruminococcaceae_NK4A214_group, Parabacteroides, Christensenellaaceae_R-7_group and Ruminiclostridium. Even there the review is hedged: these genera "might corelate" with higher IMF content, and it never says "positively correlated". Read broadly, the scope takes in every pig study the IMF section cites. That adds Romboutsia (Wu et al., 2021, colonic samples) and, in Enshi pigs, Prevotellaceae UCG-001, Alistipes and Clostridium sensustricto 1 (Tang et al., 2020). Only the Tang et al. sentence uses the words "positively correlated". The record answers at both scopes. Four related statements are left out of the evidence. (1) Fang et al., 2017 (p.6) names Prevotella, Treponema, Bacteroides and Clostridium only as the genera to which "IMF-associated OTUs" belonged, and gives no direction. (2) The Romboutsia sentence about mice that received Jinhua pig microbiota describes mice, not pigs. (3) The Prevotella copri sentence is about fat accumulation, not IMF. (4) Roseburia, Prevotella, Coprococcus and Faecalibacterium are cattle findings. Figure 2 lists the genera related to IMF, but only as an image, so its contents cannot be read from the text.

records.question_issues: (1) The paper does not name a metric. It states only that the gut microbiome "explained nearly 11% of the variation in ﬁnishing weight", so the answer is the share of variation explained. The term "microbiability" does not appear. (2) The second part is ambiguous about species. The question asks for host "genes" (plural) in a pathway for intramuscular fat "accumulation". In the rabbit passage (page 5) the paper names one host gene, PPARα, and links it to acetate REDUCING intramuscular triglyceride and intracellular fat, which is a reduction, not accumulation. The paper's only explicit list of host genes in a microbe-driven fat accumulation pathway comes from pigs (page 3): Prevotella copri acts through the TLR4 and mTOR signalling pathways and upregulates Fabp9, Scd1, Scd2 and Scd3. The same pig paragraph also names reduced ANGPTL4 expression in mice that received Jinhua pig microbiota. (3) Figure 2 lists "genes and pathways" affecting IMF, but only in the image, so its contents cannot be read from the text. Two readings are reasonable: PPARα (rabbit) or Fabp9/Scd1/Scd2/Scd3 (pig). The record gives both and labels each by species.

records.short_answer:
Whenever iNAP exports a network matrix (adjacent or bipartite), it also generates the files needed for visualization. These files can be imported directly into Cytoscape or Gephi, and the output format is chosen for one or the other.
- Cytoscape: a .sif file, which imports directly, plus a node attribute file (.txt) and an edge attribute file (.txt).
- Gephi: a node attribute file (.csv) and an edge attribute file (.csv).
The node attribute file holds node features. The edge attribute file shows the positive/negative association between nodes and the coefficient values.

A "Generate node attribute for visualization" step combines two sets of results into a formatted node property file for Cytoscape and Gephi:
- node-level properties: degree, betweenness and closeness;
- module results: within‐module connectivity (Z) and among‐module connectivity (P), which classify species into network hubs, module hubs, connectors and peripherals, plus an exported Z–P plot.
In Figure 3, nodes are coloured by taxonomic group (Cytoscape) or by module compartment (Gephi).

For further interpretation:
- Topological structure can reflect ecological implications, for example modular structure indicating similar functions.
- Mantel and partial Mantel tests relate network topological structure to environmental factors.
- Module‐EigenGene analysis outputs a web page of tables and plots covering each module's eigengene, the hierarchy structure and module correlations to environmental factors.
- Auxiliary tools convert a sif file exported from Cytoscape back into a bipartite or adjacent matrix for further analysis.

records.question_issues: The question says iNAP "recommends" methods, but the paper's wording is weaker. For nontemporal data sets the methods "could be alternative options", and for temporal data sets they "might be candidate methods". RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's correlations appear in both lists, so they do not belong to one data type. The same split is drawn in Figure 1 ("Non-Temporal datasets" and "Temporal datasets"), whose labels survive in the text layer only as a jumble of labels, not as a sentence.

evidence.sentence: For nontemporal data sets, SparCC, SPIEC‐EASI, and RMT‐based Pearson's and Spearman's could be alternative options, while for temporal data sets, eLSA/LA and RMT‐based Pearson's and Spearman's approaches might be candidate methods to generate network matrices.
evidence.supports: The core answer. Nontemporal: SparCC, SPIEC-EASI and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's. Temporal: eLSA/LA and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's. The sentence starts on page 2 and ends on page 3 with "matrices."

evidence.sentence: Extended local similarity analysis (eLSA) [12] and liquid association (LA) [13] explore time‐dependent microbial associations for time series data.
evidence.supports: Spells out eLSA and LA and says they handle time series data.

evidence.sentence: For Pearson's or Spearman's correlation‐based methods, molecular ecological network analyses (MENA) [8] identify a threshold based on random matrix theory (RMT) to filter fewer but still robust microbial associations [9], which can be conducted automatically.
evidence.supports: Spells out RMT: for the Pearson's and Spearman's correlation methods, random matrix theory sets the threshold.

evidence.sentence: Sparse correlations for compositional data (SparCC) [10] and sparse inverse covariance estimation for ecological association inference (SPIEC‐EASI) [11] also perform well to infer microbial associations and provide python‐based script and R packages, respectively.
evidence.supports: Spells out SparCC and SPIEC-EASI, the two methods listed only for nontemporal data.

evidence.supports: In the protocol (Method 3: eLSA), the LSA method is the one that handles temporal data sets.

evidence.sentence: If the data set is temporally dynamic, a sample description file to show the replicates and time points is required as well.
evidence.supports: In Method 4 (RMT-based correlations), temporal data also need a sample description file.

records.short_answer: For nontemporal data sets, iNAP gives SparCC (sparse correlations for compositional data), SPIEC-EASI (sparse inverse covariance estimation for ecological association inference) and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's correlations as alternative options. For temporal (time series) data sets, it gives eLSA/LA (extended local similarity analysis and liquid association) and RMT-based Pearson's and Spearman's approaches as candidate methods to generate network matrices. In the RMT-based methods, a threshold based on random matrix theory filters the correlations. These methods appear in both lists, and when the data set is temporally dynamic they need a sample description file giving the replicates and time points.

records.question_issues: The question is open-ended and general ("the choice of bioinformatic pipeline", "different sample types"). The paper answers it for one comparison only: an OTU-based pipeline against an ASV-based pipeline, on thermophilic anaerobic digestion (AD) reactors (control, experiment, inoculum) and psychrophilic PWASS. The answer is limited to those pipelines and sample types. Because the question is open-ended, a correct answer can rest on different subsets of the findings (alpha diversity, phylum and genus composition, NMDS and Permanova, the proposed mechanism). Several detailed results appear only in Figures 1 to 4 and are summarised in the text. The paper's Permanova statements are hard to reconcile. Results p9 (evidence 13) and Discussion p13 (evidence 24) say that when factors were nested within pipeline the null hypothesis could no longer be rejected, in both the AD-only and the full dataset. Discussion p12 (evidence 22, 23) says that on the whole dataset pipeline alone is not significant but becomes significant once its interaction with treatment is included. Table 3, given only as significance codes, shows pipeline '***' for AD-only without interaction and '.' for AD and PWASS. All of these statements are quoted.

records.short_answer:
Comparing an OTU-based and an ASV-based pipeline, the paper finds that both gave comparable results that would generally allow the same interpretations, and phylum-level composition was overall in good agreement. Still, community composition differed between 6.75% and 10.81% per treatment on phylum level, based purely on the pipeline. Biologically driven variability between samples affected the two pipelines differently.

- Thermophilic AD reactors: diversity trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. Inverse Simpson values were almost identical. Both pipelines allow the same interpretation of alpha diversity. Some genera (Firmicutes, Chloroflexota, Patescibacteria, Hydrothermae) still differed, and several genera were not picked up by one or the other pipeline.
- Psychrophilic PWASS: diversity indices diverged. The Shannon Wiener index was similar, but other estimators strongly differed, with a partial trend reversal for some (especially evenness). Inverse Simpson differed at times by a factor greater than two. Between-pipeline variability in composition was much greater than in the other treatments. Aeromonas differed by as much as 3% of the total community, or by 400% (4% ASV, 1% OTU).
- Statistics: on the AD-only dataset, NMDS and Permanova showed that the choice of pipeline significantly influences the reported composition. Pipeline differences were greater than treatment differences, even over more than 170 days. The ASV pipeline showed the time and co-substrate drift more clearly. On the whole dataset, pipeline alone was not significant, but it became significant once its interaction with treatment was included. With factors nested within pipeline, the null hypothesis could no longer be rejected. On the reduced dataset, this would suggest that pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, which has no foundation in experimental reality.
- Cause the authors propose: temperature was the prominent factor. The ASV algorithm calculates error rates on a subset of samples, mostly thermophilic AD samples, and applies them to every sample, including psychrophilic ones, where the results diverged.
- Consequence: pipeline-dependent differences in taxonomic assignment could lead to different conclusions and interfere with downstream analysis such as network analysis or predictions of ecosystem service. The differences were not limited to the PWASS.

(1) The OTU pipeline has two full-dataset values: 67,015 unrarefied (OTU Based 1) and 50,065 rarefied with vegan (OTU Based 2). The question asks for one OTU number, so a correct answer should give both, or at least name which one it uses (the unrarefied 67,015 is the plainest reading). (2) Section 3.2 on the same page gives other counts that could be mistaken for the answer: "73,003 unique sequences after clustering at a 97% identity threshold" for the OTU pipeline and "2,327,901 unique sequences" for DADA2. These are unique-sequence counts at an earlier stage, not the Table 1 "Number of Taxa"; the paper does not explain why 73,003 differs from 67,015. "Prior to filtering" is read as the "full Dataset" row, before the 0.001% relative-abundance threshold and before Genus-level agglomeration. The Merged column has no full-dataset value.

records.short_answer:
OTU pipeline: it follows the method of Dyksma et al. Cutadapt trimmed adapters (minimum adapter overlap of 6 bases, adapter error rate of 0.1). BBMerge merged reads at default merging strictness with a quality trim threshold of 10. VSEARCH did dereplication and chimera removal, then clustered sequences into OTUs at 97% similarity. The SINA classifier assigned taxonomy (minimum length 100 bp, quality score filter of 20 at the 3′ end) against the SILVA REF99 SSU reference database version 138.1.

ASV pipeline: DADA2 v1.18.0 under R version 4.1.0, following the DADA2 workflow for Big Data: Paired-End (1.4 or later). Changes to that workflow: reads trimmed left 17 bases to remove residual primers, truncQ lowered to 2, truncLen removed, and minFoldParentOverAbundance increased to 8 for chimera removal. Taxonomy came from the SILVA REF99 SSU reference database version 138.1. This pipeline does not cluster: a quality-based error correction mode replaces the 97% clustering.

Both pipelines: an abundance threshold of 0.001% was applied to the OTU and ASV datasets to remove rare taxa.

The paper says the replacement of OTUs by ASVs "has been proposed" (Callahan et al., 2017) and lists the advantages of ASVs. records.short_answer:
OTUs are clusters of reads that differ by less than a fixed dissimilarity threshold (usually 3%). The clustering is done either de novo or against a reference database (closed-reference). OTUs have no innate biological meaning: each is a "cloud" of similar sequences, not a single species or genus. They are artifacts of either a subjective threshold (de novo) or the reference database (closed-reference). As a result, de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses any biological information that is not in the database.

ASVs can differ by as little as one nucleotide and have no fixed threshold. They are produced by a model-based approach that separates sequencing errors from bona fide biological variation without constructing OTUs. The paper gives these advantages:
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, so ASVs generated independently from different samples can be validly compared (cross-study tractability).
- They capture unique biological sequence variation from all phylogenetic lineages, without the limits of closed-reference databases (database-independent biological veracity).
- They avoid the computationally intensive clustering step. Their time and memory requirements are relatively light and scale linearly, which suits routine large-scale microbial monitoring.

For these reasons, replacing OTUs with ASVs has been proposed. The paper notes one concern: ASVs may inflate diversity, because a single bacterial genome can produce multiple ASVs (Schloss, 2021).

records.question_issues: The paper never compares how the two approaches handle variance in a single passage. "Sample variance" appears only in the rarefaction sentence ("rarefying equalizes sample variance by adding artificial uncertainty"). For the scaling methods the paper describes how each factor is computed and says only that the methods "have been shown to be robust to differences between samples and maintain the differences in relative abundance". It makes no statement about variance as such, so that half of the contrast rests on this weaker wording. The sentence "In this method, the ASV numbers are multiplied by a value or proportion..." starts on page 11 and ends on page 12, interrupted by the Figure 4 legend. records.short_answer: Rarefaction randomly subsamples ASVs or OTUs within each sample without replacement to a preselected depth that is the same across all samples. Every sample ends with the same number of ASVs, and samples below the rarefaction level are removed. This discards valuable data and loses statistical power by removing sequences, and rarefying equalizes sample variance by adding artificial uncertainty. Scaling normalization does not subsample. It multiplies the ASV numbers by a value or proportion. In DESeq2 (median of ratios), the scaling factor is the median ratio of an ASV's count over its geometric mean across all samples. TMM (Trimmed Mean of M-values) uses one sample as a reference and compares the weighted mean of log ratios of an ASV within a sample with that reference. These methods have been shown to be robust to differences between samples and to maintain the differences in relative abundance.

records.question_issues: The question can be answered from the text, but its wording is loose in two places. (1) It sets "16S rRNA" against "PacBio long-read" as if they were separate targets. In the paper both are amplicon approaches on the 16S gene: the PacBio Shoreline StrainID amplicon covers 16S-ITS-23S. The paper's "16S" arm is short-amplicon Illumina sequencing with three primer sets, and one of them (27F/534R) "was excluded from downstream taxonomic analyses" (Fig. 2 legend). (2) The abstract describes a five-way comparison: "3 types of 16S short amplicon sequencing, PacBio long-read amplicon sequencing, and amplification-free shotgun metagenomics". The question groups these into three approaches. The answer follows that grouping and reads "16S rRNA" as the short-amplicon approach, as the abstract and Discussion do.

records.short_answer: 16S short-amplicon sequencing was adequate for community studies. It captured spatio-temporal dynamics and community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Primer choice and amplicon length changed some values, such as diversity measures and the number of assigned taxa, but had no impact on the spatio-temporal patterns between sample types, farms and time points. It cannot provide the resolution required for species or strain identification. PacBio long-read amplicons underperformed on the quantitative resolution of spatio-temporal patterns, because the low number of reads prohibited community statistics. Still, the 10,041 reads identified 204 species, and the approach was suited to identifying functional services (e.g. nitrification cycling) and detecting pathogens. Shotgun metagenomics corroborated the amplicon findings and extended the picture beyond prokaryotes (75.55%) to eukaryotes (23.97%), archaea (0.24%) and viruses (0.24%), including fungi and bacteriophages. The authors call it the most thorough approach. All datasets agreed on the major prokaryotic players (Actinobacteriota, Bacteroidota, Nitrospirota, Proteobacteria). The approaches gave overlapping and highly complementary results, and each contributed data the others could not provide.

records.short_answer:
Earth (V4) primers gave higher alpha richness than MiSeq (V3-4) primers, even though the MiSeq primers identified more taxa. Richness ranged 1070–2240 with Earth and 441–1962 with MiSeq.

Average richness, Earth vs MiSeq:
- Farm A biofilter water: 2166 vs 1504.
- Farm A tank water: 1934 vs 1477.
- Farm A young biofilm: 1135 vs 465.
- Farm A mature biofilm: 1497 vs 829.
- Farm B tank biofilm: tank1 1793 vs 1665, tank2 1805 vs 1815.

Farm B tank 2 is the one place where MiSeq was slightly higher. The paper's figure legend nonetheless says Earth was higher across all sample types.

The authors call these minor differences in ASV richness. They did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns or the biological conclusion. Amplicon choice did not affect community composition at higher taxonomic levels. Composition and spatio-temporal patterns were very similar between the two amplicons. Subtle phylum biases remained: Chloroflexi was favored by Earth, and Myxococcota and Plantomycetota by MiSeq. These biases did not affect the inferred overall community structure, which was virtually identical for both amplicons according to MDS analyses. With Earth primers the pattern was identical but sat in a distinct area of the morphospace. The authors conclude that relative differences in community composition can safely be compared across primers, but they recommend against comparing absolute statistics from different primers.

did not impact the spatio-temporal patterns

records.short_answer:
The review calls AR a One Health issue because livestock, humans and the environment are interconnected, which opens channels for transmission of antibiotic resistant bacteria (ARB). AR is linked to each domain through reckless and excessive antibiotic use in agriculture, livestock farming and human medicine. The interconnections create pathways for bacteria, mobile genetic elements (MGEs) and antibiotics themselves, and movement between compartments promotes the spread of AR. Each domain contributes:
- Humans: careless antibiotic use drives ARB and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs), which pass to other humans through direct contact, food, water and environmental surfaces.
- Livestock: antibiotic use contributes to resistant bacteria, which reach humans through direct contact and food products. They reach the environment through livestock waste, and pathogens pass into the environment through air, slurry and feces from livestock, acting as a source of ARGs.
- Environment: environmental contamination is a major factor in dissemination. Residues from the pharmaceutical industry, livestock husbandry, hospitals, fecal waste from humans and animals, and agricultural runoff make it a hidden source of resistant organisms. ARB persist in soil and water and can potentially spread to animals and humans who contact contaminated sources.
The cycle closes when bacteria released in the feces of livestock and humans act as an environmental reservoir before reintroduction into the livestock-human cycle. At the human-animal-environment interface, AR bacterial clones, MGEs and ARGs carry the dissemination. MGEs (plasmids, transposons, integrons) act as vehicles, and together these components promote horizontal genetic exchange. Changes in one domain can have far-reaching effects on the others, and the Fig. 1 legend shows pathways running in every direction among the three domains. The review notes that it is not yet clear how much livestock-derived routes contribute compared with human-derived routes.

records.short_answer:
Origin: the misuse or overuse of antibiotics in animal production has led to ARB and ARGs. The animal gut microbiota is a reservoir of ARB and ARGs, and antibiotic use is the main cause of ARG prevalence. Insertions, integrations and transposons lead to horizontal transfer of ARGs among microbes, and spread between farm animals and humans is mostly attributed to the transfer of mobile ARGs. About 75% of antibiotics (70% in another passage) are not absorbed and are excreted via feces and urine, contaminating the surrounding environment. Manure used as fertilizer increases resistant bacteria and resistance genes in the environment.

Pathways to humans (three groups):
(1) Direct contact with farm animals. Farm workers have an increased risk and can transfer ARB and ARGs between persons; ESBL-producing E. coli and K. pneumoniae were found in 9.8% of workers versus 5% of the Dutch population.
(2) Exposure to animal manure, wastewater or aerosol. Manure and wastewater are hotspots for animal-to-human transmission. Animal waste and slaughterhouses are an occupational risk to workers (MDR E. coli in up to 50% of butchers). Bioaerosols from swine confinement buildings carry zoonotic pathogens and ARGs from feces and may cause respiratory infections in pig farmers. Natural wind carries ARB and ARGs from farms to environmental dust, ARGs disperse up to 10 km, and MDR bacteria and ARGs reach workers and residents in the surrounding environment via inhalation into the respiratory tract.
(3) Consumption of uncooked or contaminated animal products (meat, eggs, milk), a key route of extraintestinal MDR pathogens, especially E. coli and Salmonella; the food chain is one of the important sources of transmission between animals and humans.

records.short_answer: The GOHF gives recommendations for using a One Health approach to improve multisectoral collaboration, and thereby enhance the prevention and control of zoonotic diseases. It is a five-step framework: engagement, assessment, planning, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. A visualization (Fig. 2) sets out the steps and their corresponding activities, which give countries a structure for developing the capacity to coordinate zoonotic disease programming across sectors. Users may enter at any step based on their current capacity. A toolkit (Supplementary Tables S1–5) compiles available resources matched to each step and activity, so users can identify their progress on the visualization and then use the toolkit to advance. The GOHF is applied across technical domains: laboratory, surveillance, joint outbreak response, prevention and control, preparedness, communication, and government and policy. It is not intended to be prescriptive. It is meant to be broadly applicable to common zoonotic diseases, in high-income and low-middle income countries, from the local to the international level. Its intended outcome is improved capacity to control zoonotic diseases and other threats at the human–animal–environment interface. Instead of building independent programs for priority zoonotic diseases, it is intended to deepen One Health capacity throughout the system. Ideally this leads to a gradual transition towards a comprehensive One Health system that can combat a diversity of health threats.

records.short_answer: None of the 12 tools examined, ATLASS and NEOH included, was developed specifically to evaluate OH integration into AMR and AMU surveillance systems, and none covers all the information required at all five levels of the ISSE framework. ATLASS was developed for national AMR surveillance in the food and agriculture sectors. It mostly addresses the animal components of surveillance systems and gives no guidance on how to evaluate integration with the other sectors (human and environment). Table 4 shows it covering parts of Levels 1, 2, 3 and 4. NEOH was developed for OH evaluation: it measures the degree of OH implementation (knowledge integration) in projects or programs. Its metrics were not developed specifically to evaluate OH integration into surveillance systems, but they can be applied to surveillance systems as a complementary approach. Table 4 shows it covering Level 1 and parts of Levels 2 and 4. Several tools mention the importance of measuring impacts, but none includes specific guidance for evaluating the global health and economic impact of OH integration. The authors found it difficult to link the existing tools to the ISSE levels, most likely because none was designed to evaluate OH surveillance systems, and the tools' metrics and methods were only partially relevant to most ISSE evaluation questions.

records.short_answer:
Integration is measured at the first evaluation level, which evaluates the integration of a OH approach across the different components of the surveillance system. The evaluator first answers three questions with a descriptive qualitative methodology: focus groups or individual interviews with key informants from the surveillance team, external end-users and AMR/AMU experts. That information is then used to assess the overall level of integration on a semi-quantitative scale (Table 3). Integration is treated as a continuum (multiple levels of integration), not a dichotomy. The scale defines six levels of OH integration, 0 to 5, for each of four surveillance activities: data collection, analyses, interpretation and dissemination. The levels are defined with respect to the type of information integrated, the integration into operations and processes (e.g., standardization of measures), and the integration of multiple institutions, disciplines and perspectives. Table 3 gives criteria for each level, for example the lowest and highest:
- Data collection: level 0 means the system does not collect data from sources other than humans. Level 5 means AMR data in >1 bacteria species from >1 animal source including retail food, AND from at least one collection point in the environment, AND AMU data in ≥1 animal species and humans.
- Data analysis: level 0 means separate, non-standardized analyses by different analysts in ≥2 organizations. Level 5 means conjoint analysis by a team of analysts, with formal statistical testing and multivariable statistical approaches or modeling.
- Data interpretation: level 0 means there are no formal integrated analyses. Level 5 means a team with multispecies/multidisciplinary/multiperspective expertise, including external collaborators/stakeholders from different sectors.
- Information dissemination: level 0 means animal and human information goes separately to animal and human health stakeholders. Level 5 means conjoint reporting by one organization, with means of dissemination adapted to different end-users.

key_concepts.phrase: data collection, analyses, interpretation, and dissemination

records.short_answer: Knowledge is limited. The outcomes of integration are poorly described and evidenced, and information on them is rarely available in the literature. A few papers describe some outcomes. Immediate outcomes: improved knowledge about ABR, surveillance capacity to detect correlation in ABR across sectors and between ABU and ABR, and level of awareness on ABR and ABU. Intermediate outcomes: a more responsible use of antibiotics by prescribers (Swedres-Svarm), a decrease in the quantity of antibiotics used in animals and humans (CIPARS, DANMAP, NethMAp/MARAN), new research projects with a One Health perspective (NethMap/MARAN), and the One Health perspective in sectoral or intersectoral policies (DANMAP, NARMS). To a lesser extent, ultimate outcomes were identified as changes in ABR levels (CIPARS). In the example, CIPARS detected a strong correlation between ceftiofur-resistant Salmonella Heidelberg from retail chicken and human infections across Canada. As a result, the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, and resistance to this antibiotic in salmonella decreased. Where outcome information exists, the direct causal link with integration is difficult to establish. The information is usually provided by people in charge of the surveillance system, who may lack objectivity. Reliable information was found only for systems at an advanced stage of maturity that have undertaken external evaluations. For less performant and more recent systems, outcome claims seem more aspirational than based on observed facts. Few systems have been formally evaluated for effectiveness and impacts, partly because of a lack of adapted tools and methods. Better integration does not systematically bring greater surveillance performance. The authors call for more evaluation of the impacts of integrated surveillance systems, and of the outcome of the integration models.

records.short_answer: The typology came from a multiple-correspondence analysis (MCA) followed by a hierarchical cluster analysis (HCA). The MCA used a subset of variables of the full database, which has 39 variables. Variables were selected if information could be retrieved for most of the systems and if they could discriminate between the systems. A Fisher exact test was applied to variables suspected of being highly correlated. "Collection points" was excluded from the MCA because it correlated too closely with "populations/commodities under surveillance". The HCA was applied to the Euclidean distance matrix of the first three axes of the MCA, which represent 44% of variance. A k-means clustering algorithm was used to check the robustness of the HCA. Table 2 marks 16 of the 39 variables as selected for the MCA: variables 2, 4, 8, 10, 14, 15, 18, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31, 32, 37, 38 and 39. The 14 systems grouped into four distinct clusters.

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with three caveats. (1) The paper is a commentary, so the mechanism is the authors' conceptual argument and no model sits behind it. (2) The disease-incidence part rests mainly on the Figure 1 legend (page 4, adapted from Karesh et al. [20]). The epidemic curves themselves are only in the figure image, but the legend text states the effect: early detection and control efforts reduce incidence in people and animals. (3) The economic arguments are spread across Sections 1 to 3 and describe prevention, prediction and coordination before or at emergence. The paper does not describe cost reduction during a single spillover event, so an answer could reasonably stress early detection and prediction, or coordination and efficiency. The concrete savings in Table 1 (over €1 million for West Nile virus, 26% operational cost) are illustrations, not the mechanism asked about.

evidence.sentence: (B) Early detection and control efforts reduce disease incidence in people (light blue) and animals (dark green).
evidence.supports: Disease incidence: early detection and control efforts reduce incidence in both people and animals (Figure 1B legend).

evidence.sentence: (A) Transmission of infection and ampliﬁcation in people (bright red) occurs after a pathogen from wild animals (pink) moves into livestock to cause an outbreak (light green) that ampliﬁes the capacity for pathogen transmission to people.
evidence.supports: The spillover scenario without intervention: a pathogen moves from wild animals into livestock, and the livestock outbreak amplifies transmission to people (Figure 1A legend).

evidence.sentence: A One Health approach can be invaluable for establishing and improving local, national, and global surveillance for early detection of zoonotic disease events and facilitating prompt sharing of data for a coordinated response.
evidence.supports: How early detection is achieved: surveillance across levels and prompt data sharing for a coordinated response.

evidence.sentence: The beneﬁts of taking a multisectoral One Health approach to zoonotic diseases include strengthening systems and coordination across the human health, animal health and the environment, improving the efﬁciency and effectiveness of disease management, which can reduce cost, supporting outbreak investigation and response, and facilitating evidence-based decision making for improved public health outcomes [1].
evidence.supports: Multisectoral coordination improves the efficiency and effectiveness of disease management, which can reduce cost, and supports outbreak investigation and response (sentence runs from page 3 onto page 4).

evidence.supports: Cross-sector collaboration lets countries prepare for, detect, assess and respond to zoonotic diseases.

evidence.sentence: Coupled with data variables from preparedness, investigation, and response, a coordinated One Health surveillance system can be used to project disease progression and predict as accurately as possible the magnitude and time of a potential outbreak, based on a range of mathematical model assumptions and an understanding of pathogen transmission dynamics.
evidence.supports: Data-driven element: a coordinated surveillance system can project disease progression and predict the magnitude and time of a potential outbreak.

evidence.sentence: Strengthening systems and coordination across the human, animal, and environment interface can save costs by preventing duplication of activities and providing a positive return on investment.
evidence.supports: Economic damage: coordination saves costs by preventing duplication of activities and gives a positive return on investment.

evidence.sentence: Existing studies have shown that reduced risks from zoonotic diseases also reduce indirect societal losses, such as poorer nutrition and restriction of tourism and trade, which, if included, would bring the global costs of recent zoonotic disease events to tens of billions of dollars [1,22].

records.short_answer: Infection is transmitted and amplified in people after a pathogen from wild animals moves into livestock and causes an outbreak there, and that outbreak amplifies transmission to people (Figure 1A). Early detection and control efforts reduce disease incidence in people and animals (Figure 1B). A One Health approach supports early detection through local, national and global surveillance of zoonotic disease events, with prompt sharing of data for a coordinated response. Sustainable collaboration across all sectors and disciplines lets countries prepare for, detect, assess and respond to these diseases. A coordinated One Health surveillance system can also project disease progression and predict the magnitude and time of a potential outbreak. On economic damage, the paper gives four routes. Improving the efficiency and effectiveness of disease management can reduce cost. Strengthening systems and coordination across the human, animal and environment interface can save costs by preventing duplication of activities and providing a positive return on investment. Analytically driven approaches can predict potential outbreaks at a much lower economic cost than responding after the pathogens might have emerged. Reduced risks from zoonotic diseases also reduce indirect societal losses, such as poorer nutrition and restriction of tourism and trade.

records.question_issues: The paper uses the phrase "business case" in one sentence only (page 2, section "Breaking silos for a safer Africa"). That sentence cites reference [4] and the paper gives no cost analysis of its own. The question's framing is imprecise in one respect: the business case is made for "zoonotic disease prevention actions", not for the One Health approach as such. The paper does place it next to its argument that many sectors must act at the human, animal and environment interface with scarce resources. The economic-loss sentences (evidence 2 to 4) describe the burden the business case addresses. They are not part of the business-case sentence itself, so an answer could reasonably include or leave them out. The core of a correct answer is evidence 0.

records.short_answer: The paper makes the case with one cost comparison, cited from reference [4]: zoonotic disease prevention actions cost less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year. It says this presents a business case to address the heavy burden of emerging, re-emerging and endemic zoonoses in the continent and globally. The argument sits within the context of scarce resources in Africa, where the multiplicity of players needs to address risks at the interface of human, animal and environmental health. The burden is described as economic. Zoonotic outbreaks have caused billions of dollars lost and indirect losses affecting economies, with impacts reaching the tourism, agricultural and financial sectors. Across the continent they cause massive economic losses for both the government and private sector.

records.short_answer:
The authors searched the PubMed, Web of Science and Science Direct databases. Only articles in English and from online databases were considered, and the time span was 2011–2022. The last search was on 11 March 2022. The search combined three groups of terms with AND: (i) animal terms (livestock, swine, pig, cattle, poultry, pets, dogs, cats, rats and others); (ii) the Southeast Asian countries or "Southeast Asia"; and (iii) "zoonoses OR zoonotic diseases". It retrieved 2,329 articles: PubMed n = 1043, Web of Science n = 994 and Science Direct n = 292. These were imported into Endnote (version X7), where duplicates were manually identified and removed. The authors also checked that known key articles were in the results.

First screening (titles and abstracts):
- Inclusion: original English research articles (peer-reviewed), published 2011–2022 (by 11th March), presenting prevalence or outbreak data on zoonotic/livestock diseases.
- Exclusion: study not conducted in Southeast Asia, articles about avian influenza, and review articles.
- 674 duplicates were removed and 1,302 publications were excluded: not conducted in Southeast Asia (n = 339), focusing on influenza (n = 145), review articles (n = 91), book chapters (n = 4) and not related to the targeted diseases (n = 723).
- 358 articles went to full-text assessment.

Second screening (full text):
- Inclusion: cross-sectional study, random selection of individuals, and clear description of methods and results.
- 263 articles were excluded: full text unavailable (n = 23), animal selection procedure unclear (n = 156) or results not presented clearly (n = 84). The stated reasons were missing information on how farms and individuals were selected, and poor random selection, such as targeted sampling of animals showing symptoms.
- Grey literature on the articles' reference lists was cross-checked against the search results.

All four authors (TTN, TNM, XSD and HSL) worked independently and classified each article 'Yes' or 'No' for inclusion. Conflicts were settled by discussion among the four reviewers. This left 95 publications in the final qualitative synthesis.

records.question_issues: The question is answerable from the text (Section 1 on page 2, Section 3 on pages 5 to 6, Section 3.1 on page 6, Section 3.2 on page 7). Development: misuse and overuse of antimicrobials happen on a far greater scale in agriculture than in human medicine, and use in animal agriculture vastly outstrips medical use in humans. Agricultural overuse has been directly linked to the rise of AMR. The drivers named are: group antimicrobial treatment, which causes overuse and inconsistent dosing; use for disease prevention and growth promotion; metaphylactic and prophylactic use; and delivery in feed and water, which gives suboptimal dosing and environmental residues. Under antimicrobial selection, bacteria acquire resistance genes and mobile genetic elements (MGEs). Animal bacteria are one of the most important reservoirs for the horizontal transfer of resistance genes and share most of these genes and MGEs with human pathogens. Some genes (tetX, cfr, optrA) give cross-resistance to protected human last-resort antimicrobials.

Transmission to humans happens by three routes. (1) Direct infection with resistant bacteria, most commonly through consumption of contaminated meat, eggs and dairy. For example, as resistant Campylobacter spp. increase in chickens, many Campylobacter spp. from diarrhea patients are quinolone-resistant. Some resistant hospital bacteria can be traced back to animals. (2) Direct exposure to the farm environment, which shapes the human gut microbiota and resistome. Resistant plasmids spread from chicken to handlers. (3) The environment. Farm waste carrying antimicrobial residues and resistant bacteria creates new resistance reservoirs. Manure used to fertilize crops can move ARGs from animals to soil and crops and then to the human microbiome, and manured soil holds approximately 28,000 times more ARGs than un-manured soil. Animal waste contaminates water sources around farms. More than 70% of administered veterinary antibiotics are excreted into the environment, where residues select resistant environmental bacteria, and plants can absorb and accumulate them. The paper notes that the direct contribution to human infections is debated.

key_concepts.phrase: direct exposure to the farm environment

records.short_answer: AMR: resistance was rare among Salmonella from imported edible leaves but common, including MDR, among those from imported raw chicken. Of the 115 leaf isolates, three (3%) had AMR determinants, all from three curry leaf samples, and two (2%) were MDR. 97% of leaf isolates had a genotypic profile in line with the typical intrinsic resistance to aminoglycosides. Of the 231 chicken isolates, 214 (93%) had at least one mutation or resistance gene determinant, most commonly to β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines or sulphonamides, and only 17 (7%) had none. 164 (71%) were MDR, and these came from all four countries of origin. In chicken, 170 (74%) had β-lactam resistance determinants (blaCMY-2 the most common, 54%) and 222 (96%) had at least one QRDR mutation. Serovars: leaves showed a larger diversity of serovars than chicken. The paper gives the leaf count as 33, 29 or 30 in different places; chicken has 16 throughout. Curry leaves had the most diversity (23). The most common leaf serovars were S. Virchow (20.9%), S. Newport (11.3%) and S. Bareilly (7.8%). Chicken was dominated by S. Heidelberg (138, 60%), all from Brazil except one isolate of unrecorded origin, followed by S. Minnesota (9%) and S. Enteritidis (7%). All S. Heidelberg isolates had resistance genes for fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and sulphonamides, and the paper reports S. Heidelberg from Brazil as resistant to three or more antimicrobial classes. The authors say antimicrobials are less likely to be used in farming edible leaves, which may account for the larger serovar diversity in leaves.

records.question_issues: The threshold is stated plainly: isolates 5 or fewer SNPs apart, in the same ≤5 SNPs single linkage cluster, were treated as genetically related. The "pipeline" part is less clear. The body text gives no name for a relatedness pipeline. It says only that SNP typing was "derived from the genomic data as described previously (Chattaway et al., 2019; Dallman et al., 2018)". SnapperDB appears only in the reference-list title of Dallman et al. (2018). The one pipeline the Methods name, the UKHSA KmerID pipeline, identifies species and subspecies and does not assess relatedness. So "pipeline" can be answered two ways: as SNP typing by the cited method (SnapperDB, through the reference), or as the UKHSA WGS workflow as a whole. The paper also uses a 25 SNP single linkage cluster for more distant isolates. That level does not define "genetically related".

evidence.sentence: Confirmation of identity of Salmonella spp., sequence type (ST), eBURST group (eBG), serovar and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) typing were derived from the genomic data as described previously (Chattaway et al., 2019; Dallman et al., 2018).
evidence.supports: Pipeline: SNP typing derived from the WGS data by the previously described methods

evidence.sentence: The relationship between isolates within an individual eBG or ST was assessed by pairwise SNP differences: isolates with ≤5 SNPs difference from each other were considered to be indistinguishable and to have a recent common ancestor (Mook et al., 2018; Waldram, Dolan, et al., 2018a).

records.short_answer: SNP typing was derived from the genomic data as described previously (Chattaway et al., 2019; Dallman et al., 2018). The Dallman et al. (2018) reference is SnapperDB. Within an eBG or ST, relatedness was assessed by pairwise SNP differences. Isolates with ≤5 SNPs difference were considered indistinguishable and to have a recent common ancestor. Isolates in the same ≤5 SNPs single linkage cluster were therefore considered genetically related. The Discussion describes this as a 5 SNP cluster.

records.question_issues: The question is answerable, with two caveats. (1) The genotype-phenotype match for quinolones (gyrA T86I in 96% of the isolates with phenotypic quinolone resistance) is reported only for all Campylobacter isolates together, C. jejuni and C. coli (Results p.6, Discussion p.9, Figure 3). The paper gives no match rate for C. jejuni alone. For C. jejuni it gives only two separate rates: 100% phenotypic resistance to CIP, ENR and NAL, and gyrA T86I in 95.2%. Turning 95.2% of 21 into "20 of 21" is arithmetic the text does not print, so the answer leaves it out. (2) "Genotypic markers" is broad. The only fluoroquinolone marker the paper reports is the gyrA T86I point mutation; it reports no fluoroquinolone resistance gene. Per-isolate detail appears only in Figures 2 and 3, which are images.

records.short_answer: Genotype and phenotype correspond closely for fluoroquinolones. All 21 C. jejuni isolates were phenotypically resistant to ciprofloxacin, enrofloxacin and nalidixic acid (CIP, ENR, NAL). The genotypic marker, the gyrA T86I mutation (associated with quinolone resistance), was detected in 95.2% of C. jejuni and was among the most consistently identified resistance markers in C. jejuni. Across all Campylobacter isolates, gyrA T86I was found in 96% of the isolates with phenotypic quinolone resistance. The authors call this a correspondence between fluoroquinolone resistance and gyrA mutations (T86I) (96%) and conclude that phenotypic and genotypic resistance correlate.

Assembly quality was checked with QUAST (Galaxy version 5.2.0), and assemblies with sequence identity > 95% were kept for further analyses. These steps ran on Galaxy at https://usegalaxy.org.au. The assemblies were then analysed with web-based tools. Antimicrobial resistance genes were detected with ResFinder version 4.1, using its default thresholds of 90% sequence identity and 60% minimum length; the paper describes these thresholds as being "to identify chromosomal point mutations". MobileElementFinder V1.0.3 was used to identify mobile genetic elements and their relationship to ARG and VF. Virulence genes were detected with the Virulence Factor Database, using a conservative threshold of blastp E-value 1e-10 and query coverage > 40%.

Part of the argument is drawn in Figure 1, which is a diagram. Only its legend text can be quoted, so any loop drawn in the image cannot be checked from the text.

records.short_answer:
The paper never calls it a cycle. Instead it describes a "transmission continuum" (Figure 1 legend), a "complex web" of transmission pathways that runs in both directions. All of it comes from cited studies.
1. Animals to the environment. Discharge from bovine and poultry slaughterhouses and farms introduces ESBL-producing microorganisms into aquatic ecosystems, which helps them spread among animal and human populations. Stored dairy cow manure can serve as a reservoir for resistance genes. Antimicrobial use in food-producing animals indicates AMR in the environment.
2. Animals and the environment to humans. Multidrug-resistant pathogens reach humans through the consumption of animal-derived foods. Fish and shrimp are reservoirs that threaten human health through raw seafood. blaCTX-M transfer suggests a role in transfer to human gut E. coli after contaminated fish is eaten. The paper also cites the zoonotic potential of ESBL-producing bacteria.
3. Humans back to the environment and to food. Effluent contaminated with human feces, and wastewater from hospitals and healthcare facilities, spread ESBL producers. The Figure 1 legend describes the aquatic ecosystem as a reservoir fed by farm, industrial and hospital sewage. Food handlers can contaminate animal-origin foods.
4. Shared genetics. Plasmid backbones are nearly identical among chickens, cattle and swine and are similar to plasmids from humans. ST10 is found in meats, in healthy individuals and in human blood cultures, and also in animals and animal-origin food. Resistance patterns of isolates from UTI patients resemble those of isolates from meat and animals.
The paper concludes that clonal lineages found in humans, animals and environments call for surveillance within a One Health framework. It also reports a Reunion Island study suggesting animals might not be the primary reservoir of ESBL E. coli in humans.
records.synthesis_statement: The paper frames ESBL E. coli spread as a web or "transmission continuum" linking farms, food industries, food handlers and an aquatic reservoir fed by farm, industrial and hospital sewage [9, 10, 11, 12]. Animals and farms release resistant bacteria into the environment through manure and through slaughterhouse and farm discharge, and antimicrobial use in food animals indicates AMR in the environment [3, 6, 13]. From there the bacteria spread to animal and human populations [6], including through raw seafood and contaminated fish [4, 5]. Animals also pass them to humans through animal-derived foods, and the paper cites their zoonotic potential [14, 19]. Humans feed them back into the environment through effluent contaminated with human feces and hospital wastewater [7, 8], and back into food through food handlers and human carriers [17, 18]. Shared genetics tie the compartments together: isolates from animals and food resemble those from human infections [0], plasmids are nearly identical across chickens, cattle and swine and similar to plasmids from humans [1], ST10 occurs in meats, healthy people, human blood cultures and animals [15, 16], and resistance patterns of UTI isolates resemble those from meat and animals [20]. The paper concludes that lineages across humans, animals and environments require One Health surveillance [21]. It also notes a Reunion Island study suggesting animals might not be the primary reservoir for human ESBL E. coli [2].

(p1) and "Extensive antimicrobial usage..." (p5) were missing from B. B's blaCTX-M fish sentence (p3) was missing from A. All three are verbatim and relevant, and all were kept. D3, evidence both agents missed, now added: the Figure 1 legend sentence containing "transmission continuum" (p4), "This evidence highlighted ... including food and human carriers." records.short_answer: In 2021–2022, C. jejuni and C. coli from humans and animals showed high to extremely high resistance to fluoroquinolones. In human isolates in 2022, overall ciprofloxacin resistance was 69.1% in C. jejuni and 70.6% in C. coli. The abstract gives a range of 33.1% (lower in Iceland and Norway) to 100%, and the key findings give 20.6% to 96.6% for human C. jejuni among EU countries. The implication is that fluoroquinolones can no longer be recommended for treating Campylobacter infections in humans. Ciprofloxacin is not advised because of the risk of treatment failure, unless prior testing can confirm susceptibility. Fluoroquinolones are no longer an obvious option for severe human campylobacteriosis in Europe, and macrolides are now the main first-line treatment. As a result, even low levels of resistance to other critically important antimicrobials are a cause for concern in public health.

records.short_answer:
OHAMRS integrates human and animal health AMR data at Kenya's national AMR data repository, the Central Data Warehouse (CDW), and collates the data in a single digital platform. It has two core digital components:
(1) interoperability middleware (Open Interop), which integrates data from various sources and connects the CDW to the OHAMRS portal;
(2) a DHIS2 web portal, which analyses and visualises AMR surveillance data from the human and animal health sectors.
Animal health data flow from SILAB into the CDW. The customisable dashboards show data from both sectors and update in near real time as new data are submitted to the CDW. There are 42 dashboards, including 17 for human and animal health priority pathogens, a One Health intersectoral analysis dashboard and a One Health AWaRe classification dashboard. The components are scalable for future inclusion of other One Health sectors (environment, food/feed, aquaculture). Environmental data are not yet included, and the paper proposes adding them.

records.short_answer: The 17 surveillance sites report AMR data to the CDW in three ways. (1) A LIMS linked to the CDW, which transmits data directly in near-real-time: 43% of sites. (2) The national standard MS-Excel tool developed by NPHL, with files sent monthly to NPHL for upload to the CDW: 38% (the "MS-Excel template"). (3) WHONET data files sent to NPHL on a weekly or monthly basis: 19%.

records.short_answer:
BiSeq and bsseq offer "a very limited subset" of what methylPipe/compEpiTools do. Most such tools were developed and tested for finding DMRs on RRBS data. The text says they could manage WGBS data, but Table 1 marks BiSeq and Bsseq "-" for WGBS data.

The authors tested three WGBS tasks: profiling ROIs in one dataset, DMRs between 2 conditions, and DMRs between multiple conditions.
- BiSeq uploads the entire dataset into memory. It failed to load a whole WGBS dataset even with 80 GB (only chromosome 1 loaded), so it performed none of the three tasks.
- bsseq only provides a smoothing-based method to identify DMRs, with no additional functions. On the 2-group DMR comparison it returned an error after about 3 days, the time DSS took to finish.
- In Table 1, BiSeq and Bsseq are "-" for multi-sample WGBS data and NA for pairwise WGBS DMR analysis, meaning it is not supported.
- methylPipe was optimized for the analysis of multiple WGBS datasets. Pairwise DMRs took 20 min with 1 core on chromosome 1 and 45 min with 10 cores genome-wide. DMRs among 8 WGBS methylomes took 40 min on chromosome 1 with a single core, which is manageable even on a laptop.

No compared tool matched the complete set of functions in methylPipe and compEpiTools. The authors call methylPipe the first package to analyse multiple WGBS experiments while also being compatible with targeted or low-resolution DNA methylation data.

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text, with two points of interpretation. (1) "Statistical algorithms" can be read narrowly or broadly. The narrow reading covers only the DMR tests (Wilcoxon for two groups, Kruskal-Wallis for multiple samples). The broad reading also covers the binomial test that calls the seed Cs, the multiple-testing correction, and Fisher's method for combining the p-values of merged regions. The evidence covers both. (2) The paper gives only one explicitly genome-wide resource figure, for a two-sample comparison: 45 min with 10 cores and a max 28GB RAM peak on a cluster. The other figures are for chromosome 1 only: 20 min, 1 core, 4GB for two samples, and 40 min, 1 core, 4.9GB for 8 methylomes. For the 8-methylome analysis on a cluster with 10 cores the paper says only "a similar time", gives no RAM figure, and does not state whether that run is genome-wide. In the extracted text the sentence that introduces the Wilcoxon/Kruskal-Wallis tests has no full stop before "Briefly". It is quoted as printed, run on into the next sentence.

records.short_answer: methylPipe's findDMR function identifies DMRs with paired non-parametric tests: Wilcoxon to compare two groups of samples, and Kruskal-Wallis to compare multiple samples. The tests run inside a dynamic sliding window. Each window is seeded by a cytosine that the binomial test calls methylated and that meets user-defined cutoffs for sequencing depth and methylation difference. The consolidateDMRs function then applies a multiple-testing correction to the p-values. It merges significant regions that lie closer than a user-adjustable threshold and combines their p-values with Fisher's method. A genome-wide DMR identification between 2 WGBS samples took 45 min with 10 cores, with a max 28GB RAM peak on a cluster. On chromosome 1 alone, the same two-sample analysis took 20 min with 1 core (max 4GB RAM peak). DMR identification among 8 WGBS methylomes took 40 min on chromosome 1 with a single core (max 4.9GB RAM peak), and a similar time on a cluster with 10 cores. Parallelization adjusts automatically to the available number of cores and RAM.

records.short_answer: According to the paper, HTS-flow offers a web interface (GUI) designed for users without bioinformatics skills, the typical wet-lab scientist. It gives them enough control by choosing a few critical parameters, for example the maximum number of mismatches in alignment or the significance threshold for the peak caller, while leaving the rest as defaults. In Table 1, HTS-flow has "default parameters provided" and the "possibility to tweak some parameters". HTS-flow also runs predefined, easily customizable modular scripts and builds in standard Bioconductor annotation (TxDb, BSgenome). The authors say its automation is higher than in the other tools, mainly because of the integration with the SMITH LIMS and the optional parameter tweaking. Galaxy offers the "possibility to tweak all the parameters". The paper says this high flexibility decreases a lot the automation and limits Galaxy to an audience with a good knowledge of the tools and good IT skills. Galaxy is intended also for non-programmers but is mainly restricted to skilled bioinformaticians for complex tasks. Its pipeline output is not standardized, and expert users must add annotation libraries by modifying pipelines. At the other extreme, QuickNGS achieves high automation at the expense of flexibility, because parameters cannot be set.
