records.question_issues: Answerable from the text. Two scope notes, neither making it unanswerable. (a) "Functional significance" is open ended, and the paper states the finding at three levels (organismal tumour onset, cellular transformation, and the transcriptional mechanism), so a complete answer should cover all three. (b) "Liver tumor development" covers initiation and progression, which the paper separates: initiation is impaired by V394D, while the aggressiveness of tumours once formed is unchanged. The paper does not test whether the MYC-MIZ1 interaction is required to maintain an established tumour. The paper's own wording also varies in strength, "an essential role of the MYC/MIZ1interaction in repression in tumor initiation" on page 2 against "MIZ1-dependent repression plays an important role" on page 9; tumours still arise in tet-MYC-VD mice, only later, so the requirement is for efficient initiation and not absolute. One transcription note: evidence 15 is one printed sentence that the text layer splits across the page 6 to page 7 column break, with figure panel labels between the halves, so a single-page string search will not find it whole; it was checked by hand against both halves.

evidence.sentence: We further show that cellular transformation, and thus initiation of liver tumorigenesis, were impaired in mice harboring a MYC mutant unable to associate with the corepressor protein MIZ1 (ZBTB17).
evidence.supports: Abstract statement of the functional significance: the MYC-MIZ1 interaction is needed for cellular transformation and thus for initiation of liver tumorigenesis. Names MIZ1 as the corepressor (ZBTB17).

evidence.sentence: As in other tissues (19, 24), MYC-VD showed reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC in the liver, owing to an essential role of the MYC/MIZ1interaction in repression in tumor initiation.
evidence.supports: Introduction summary: the interaction has an essential role in repression in tumour initiation in the liver. The text layer prints 'MYC/MIZ1interaction' without a space.

evidence.sentence: To study the interplay between MYC activity, transcription, and chromatin organization in liver tumors, we used a tet-MYC/LAPtTA mouse model as originally described (Supplementary Fig. S1A; refs. 22, 23) but based on two different c-MYC transgenes, tet-MYC-WT and tet-MYC-VD, the latter expressing the MYC V394D mutant defective in MIZ1 binding (19).
evidence.supports: What V394D is: a MYC mutant defective in MIZ1 binding, carried as the tet-MYC-VD transgene in the liver model.

evidence.sentence: Relative to tet-MYC-WT, tet-MYC-VD animals showed delayed tumorigenesis (Fig. 1B).
evidence.supports: In vivo consequence of losing MIZ1 binding: delayed liver tumour onset.

evidence.sentence: The median survival was 5 weeks for tet-MYC-WT and 13 weeks for tet-MYC-VD–expressing mice.
evidence.supports: Size of the delay, from the Figure 1 legend: median survival 5 weeks for WT against 13 weeks for VD.

evidence.sentence: Once formed, however, MYC-WT- and MYC-VD–induced tumors appeared equally aggressive, moribund animals showing comparable liver weights (Fig. 1H) and tumor load (Supplementary Fig. S2A).
evidence.supports: The interaction is not required for the aggressiveness of tumours once formed, which localises its role to initiation.

evidence.sentence: To address MYC function at a pretumoral stage, we puriﬁed LAPtTA/tet-MYC-WT and VD fHBs by magnetic cell sorting with an E-cadherin antibody (28).
evidence.supports: Grounds the answer's "Already at a pretumoral stage" clause and identifies the "both populations" of the RT-PCR sentence that follows (evidence 7) as tet-MYC-WT and tet-MYC-VD fetal hepatoblasts.

evidence.sentence: RT-PCR analysis revealed similar MYC mRNA levels in both populations (Supplementary Fig. S1B), showing comparable activation of a MYC-induced gene (Smpdl3b) but defective repression of Cdkn1a by MYC-VD, as expected (Supplementary Fig. S2F; ref. 29).
evidence.supports: At a pretumoral stage the mutant activates normally but fails to repress Cdkn1a, isolating repression as the lost function.

evidence.sentence: MYC-WT and MYC-VD led to similar increases in the number of fetal hepatoblasts recovered per embryo (Supplementary Fig. S2G), suggesting equivalent proliferative activities.
evidence.supports: The interaction is not needed for MYC's proliferative function.

evidence.sentence: RASG12V was expressed at similar levels and enhanced proliferation of cells with either MYC-WT or MYC-VD (Supplementary Fig. S3D and S3E) but the latter showed marked defects in cellular transformation, as assayed either in vitro by sphere formation in methylcellulose (Fig. 1J) or in vivo by subcutaneous tumor growth in CD1-nude mice (Fig. 1K).
evidence.supports: The mutant is defective in transformation of hepatoblasts in vitro and in vivo, while proliferation is unaffected.

evidence.sentence: When cultured in semi-solid medium, however, cells expressing the MYC-ER VD mutant showed a marked decrease in sphere-forming ability relative to the MYC-ER WT controls (Supplementary Fig. S3F).
evidence.supports: The same transformation defect in an independent MYC-ER system in BNL CL.2 liver progenitor cells.

evidence.sentence: Remarkably, knockdown of MIZ1 with either of two different shRNAs (#8 and #9) decreased sphere-forming efﬁciency of MYC-ER WT to levels comparable with those of MYC-ER VD, ablating the difference between the two forms of MYC.
evidence.supports: MIZ1 knockdown phenocopies the V394D mutation, showing the transformation defect runs through MIZ1.

evidence.sentence: Hence, the deﬁcit in cellular transformation of VD mutant was entirely attributable to its interaction with MIZ1 (29).
evidence.supports: Attribution of the transformation defect specifically to the MYC-MIZ1 interaction.

evidence.sentence: Taken together, the above data indicate that while retaining normal proliferative activity, MYC-VD is defective in cellular transformation, affecting most likely the frequency of tumor initiation in vivo.
evidence.supports: The paper's functional conclusion: the interaction acts on transformation and on the frequency of tumour initiation, not on proliferation.

evidence.sentence: In particular, secondary response genes were similarly deregulated in C!T and C!Tvd, regardless of whether they were induced or repressed (Fig 3D, i and ii).
evidence.supports: Secondary response genes are unaffected by the mutation, which is part of the selectivity of the defect. The arrow is mis-encoded as '!' in the text layer ('C!T' means C to T).

evidence.sentence: The same was true for the primary MYC-induced genes (Fig 3D, iii), conﬁrming that MYC-VD is as effective as WT in transcriptional activation (18).
evidence.supports: Gene activation by MYC is intact without MIZ1 binding, so the phenotype is not a general loss of MYC function.

evidence.sentence: Instead, primary MYC-repressed genes showed weaker downregulation in C!Tvd relative to C!T (Fig 3D, iv): among these, 285 genes were repressed with a 2-fold lower efﬁciency in MYC-VD relative to MYC-WT tumors (Fig. 3E; Supplementary Table S3), enriching for functional categories including cell adhesion/response to wounding (Fig. 3F), as previously reported in different cellular compartments (18, 31).
evidence.supports: The molecular defect of V394D: selectively weaker repression of primary MYC-repressed genes, 285 genes at 2-fold lower efficiency, enriched for cell adhesion/response to wounding. One printed sentence that the text layer splits across the page 6 to page 7 break.

evidence.sentence: As in other tissues (19, 24), tet-MYC-VD in the liver showed signiﬁcantly reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC.
evidence.supports: Discussion statement of the in vivo result.

evidence.sentence: Expression proﬁling of MYC-VD–driven tumors showed a selective impairment in the downregulation of a subset of the primary MYC-repressed genes identiﬁed upon tet-MYC shut down.
evidence.supports: Discussion restatement of the selective repression defect.

evidence.sentence: Hence, MIZ1-dependent repression plays an important role in MYC-induced liver tumorigenesis.
evidence.supports: The paper's own statement of the functional significance of the interaction in liver tumorigenesis.

evidence.sentence: In line with the fact that MYC-repressed transcriptional programs appear to be largely tissue-speciﬁc, the requirement for the MYC-MIZ1 interaction appears to differ among the tumor types studied so far, including suppression of TGFb-mediated senescence in T-cell lymphomas (19), maintenance of stemness in medulloblastoma (24) and, possibly related to the latter, tumor initiation in the liver (this work).
evidence.supports: Assigns the role of the interaction in the liver to tumour initiation and contrasts it with its roles in other tumour types.

evidence.sentence: tet-MYC-VD is impaired in liver tumor induction compared with tet-MYC-WT.
evidence.supports: Figure 1 legend title, stating the in vivo finding in one line.

evidence.sentence: Tet-MYC-VD is deﬁcient in MYC-dependent gene repression.
evidence.supports: Figure 3 legend title, stating the transcriptional finding in one line.

records.short_answer: The V394D mutant (MYC-VD), a MYC mutant defective in MIZ1 binding, shows that the MYC-MIZ1 interaction is required for MYC to transform liver cells and thus for initiation of liver tumorigenesis, and not for MYC-driven proliferation, for transcriptional activation, or for the aggressiveness of tumours once formed. (1) Tumour onset: tet-MYC-VD animals showed delayed tumorigenesis, with median survival 13 weeks against 5 weeks for tet-MYC-WT, and tet-MYC-VD in the liver showed significantly reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC; once formed, MYC-WT- and MYC-VD-induced tumours appeared equally aggressive, with comparable liver weights and tumour load. (2) Cellular level: MYC-WT and MYC-VD led to similar increases in the number of fetal hepatoblasts recovered per embryo, suggesting equivalent proliferative activities, but MYC-VD showed marked defects in cellular transformation, in vitro by sphere formation in methylcellulose and in vivo by subcutaneous tumour growth in CD1-nude mice, and MYC-ER VD cells showed a marked decrease in sphere-forming ability. Knockdown of MIZ1 with either of two different shRNAs (#8 and #9) decreased sphere-forming efficiency of MYC-ER WT to levels comparable with MYC-ER VD, so the deficit in cellular transformation of the VD mutant was entirely attributable to its interaction with MIZ1. The authors conclude that while retaining normal proliferative activity, MYC-VD is defective in cellular transformation, affecting most likely the frequency of tumour initiation in vivo. (3) Transcriptional mechanism: the defect is selective for repression. Secondary response genes were similarly deregulated in both genotypes, and MYC-VD is as effective as WT in transcriptional activation, whereas primary MYC-repressed genes showed weaker downregulation in MYC-VD tumours, with 285 genes repressed with a 2-fold lower efficiency in MYC-VD relative to MYC-WT tumours, enriching for functional categories including cell adhesion/response to wounding. Already at a pretumoral stage, in tet-MYC-WT and tet-MYC-VD fetal hepatoblasts purified by magnetic cell sorting, the two populations showed comparable activation of the MYC-induced gene Smpdl3b but defective repression of Cdkn1a by MYC-VD. Hence MIZ1-dependent repression plays an important role in MYC-induced liver tumorigenesis, and the requirement for the MYC-MIZ1 interaction differs among tumour types: suppression of TGFb-mediated senescence in T-cell lymphomas, maintenance of stemness in medulloblastoma, and tumour initiation in the liver in this work.
records.notes:
Single paper, conceptual question. The answer is assembled from the paper's own statements across Abstract (p1), Introduction (p2), Results (pp3 to 7) and Discussion (p9), plus two figure legend titles.

Verification. Every one of the 22 evidence sentences was checked against /Users/valeriobianchi/projects/Mentori-reanalysis/data/ground_truth_v2/paper_text/48_myc_oncogene.pymupdf.txt with a script that normalises only line breaks and line-break hyphenation. 21 matched contiguously on the page stated. The one exception is evidence 15, which is a single printed sentence that the text layer splits across the page 6 to page 7 column break ("... with a 2-fold lower" ends page 6; "efﬁciency in MYC-VD relative to MYC-WT tumors ..." begins page 7, with figure panel labels between). Both halves were confirmed by hand at pymupdf lines 655 to 656 and 871 to 874, and it is filed under page 6 where it begins.

Text-layer artefacts kept exactly as printed. The ﬁ ligature is U+FB01 in "efﬁciency", "deﬁcit", "conﬁrming", "proﬁling", "identiﬁed", "signiﬁcantly", "tissue-speciﬁc", "deﬁcient". The hex check confirms "efﬁciency" is "ef" + U+FB01 + "ciency", so neither "effi" nor "e" plus ligature is correct. The dash in "MYC-VD–induced", "MYC-VD–expressing" and "MYC-VD–driven" is U+2013 as printed. The right arrow is mis-encoded as "!", so "C!T" and "C!Tvd" mean C to T and C to Tvd. "MYC/MIZ1interaction" in evidence 1 is missing its space in the source and is quoted that way. "TGFb" stands for TGF-beta and "RASG12V" for RAS with superscript G12V, both flattened in the text layer.

Joins made under the rules: "knock-/down" to "knockdown" (evidence 10), "MYC-/VD" to "MYC-VD" (evidences 7 and 12), "trans-/genes" to "transgenes" and the wrap of the token "tet-MYC/LAPtTA" after its slash (evidence 2), "senes-/cence" (evidence 19), "Sup-/plementary" and "includ-/ing" (evidence 15). Nothing else was altered. Evidence 6 is printed one word per line in the pymupdf layer ("showing / comparable / activation / of / a / MYC-induced / gene"); joining the line breaks with spaces gives the quoted sentence, and the pypdf extraction of the same passage agrees.

Not used as evidence: the Figure 1B axis labels on page 4 give n = 41 tet-MYC-WT, n = 20 tet-MYC-VD, n = 40 control and P < 0.0001 for the survival curve, and panel 1H gives P = 0.23 for liver weight, but these are isolated label fragments and not sentences. The Figure 3E panel label "VD-Sensitive genes (285)" on page 7 is consistent with the 285 in the main text. No figure-image-only content is needed: every number in the short answer is in running text or a figure legend.

records.disagreements:
A and B agreed on answer_type (extractive), on question_answerable (true), and on 13 evidence sentences, with identical page attributions and the same transcription caveats for the page 6/7 split sentence and "MYC/MIZ1interaction". Five points of difference, each resolved against the text.

1. Evidence coverage. B carried four Results sentences A omitted: the page 3 definition of the tet-MYC-VD transgene as the V394D mutant defective in MIZ1 binding, the pretumoral Cdkn1a repression defect, the equal fetal hepatoblast numbers, and the RASG12V transformation assays. All four are verbatim and answer the question, so all are kept. A carried no sentence B lacked.

2. Sentences both missed. I added four, all verified verbatim: the page 5 MYC-ER VD sphere-forming decrease (evidence 9), the page 6 statement that secondary response genes were similarly deregulated in both genotypes (evidence 13), the page 9 Discussion sentence "As in other tissues (19, 24), tet-MYC-VD in the liver showed signiﬁcantly reduced tumorigenic potential relative to wild-type MYC." (evidence 16), and the two figure legend titles (evidences 20 and 21), which state the in vivo and transcriptional findings in one line each.

3. A rule violation in B's short answer. B wrote "secondary response genes behave the same" while quoting no sentence that says so. Resolved by quoting the sentence (evidence 13) rather than deleting the clause, since it is load-bearing for the selectivity of the defect.

4. Scope of the negative claim. A wrote that the paper does not test whether the interaction is required for maintenance of an established tumour; B wrote that it is "not for tumour maintenance or aggressiveness". A is right and B overreaches: the paper shows aggressiveness of formed tumours is unchanged (evidence 5) but never tests MIZ1 dependence of maintenance. A's narrower wording is in question_issues.

5. Quotation fidelity in prose. B's short answer re-rendered the Introduction phrase as "MYC/MIZ1 interaction" with a space, against the source "MYC/MIZ1interaction". The final short answer does not re-quote that phrase, and evidence 1 keeps the printed form.

6. Key concepts. A chose "corepressor protein MIZ1 (ZBTB17)", "attributable to its interaction with MIZ1"; B chose "frequency of tumor initiation in vivo", "as effective as WT". Resolved by taking eight phrases that span the three levels of the answer (onset, cellular transformation, mechanism) and re-checking each one word for word inside its cited evidence sentence.

7. The "efficiency" ligature. Neither agent got it wrong, but the two plausible mis-renderings ("effi" plus ligature, and "e" plus ligature) were both tested against the file and both fail; the source is "ef" + U+FB01 + "ciency".

records.question_issues: The running text gives the counts only approximately: "equivalent numbers (ca. 1,200-1,400)" of MYC-induced and repressed genes (Introduction, p2) and "each over 1,000 genes" (Discussion, p9). Exact counts exist only in the Fig. 2D and 2E Venn diagrams, whose labels survive in the text layer detached from their regions: induced 1,426 / 254 / 903 and repressed 1,373 / 461 / 926 (pymupdf lines 676-688). The text does not say which number belongs to which region. Two text statements support one reading: most T to Toff (primary) DEGs also scored in C to T while larger numbers of C to T DEGs were MYC-independent (p5), and primary induced and repressed genes are "categories 2, 3 and 5, 6, respectively" (p5), i.e. two regions each. On that reading 1,426 and 1,373 are the secondary (C to T only) regions, giving primary induced = 254 + 903 = 1,157 and primary repressed = 461 + 926 = 1,387. The Fig. 3E Venn labels (707, 219, 66, 395) also sum to 1,387 primary repressed genes. Both exact totals are inferred from figure labels, not stated in text; the figure image is needed to confirm. A system answering from the figure may give 1,157 and 1,387; the author should decide whether the key is the stated range or these figure-derived counts. Supplementary Table S1 (gene lists) is not in the paper text. v2.4 (11 October 2026, Q49): decided for the figure-derived counts. The region assignment does not need the figure image. The Fig. 3C labels (p7) give C→T totals of 2,081 + 248 = 2,329 = 1,426 + 903 induced and 1,878 + 421 = 2,299 = 1,373 + 926 repressed, and only this reading fits them. The Fig. 3E labels 707 + 219 + 66 + 395 = 1,387 split the primary repressed set.

records.question_issues: The question is loosely phrased ("how does this relate to") and leaves "gene categories" undefined. The paper reports the two findings in adjacent Results subsections: "Genomic MYC-binding profiles are not predictive of MYC-dependent regulation" and "MYC influences promoter-loading of RNA Pol II at both activated and repressed loci". The Figure 4 title links them explicitly: binding does not discriminate, while RNA Pol II changes correspond to the DEG categories. "Gene categories" can be read two ways: as the paper's regulatory categories (primary versus secondary genes, classes 1/4 versus 2,3/5,6) or as activated versus repressed genes. The evidence covers both readings. Much of the supporting data is only in figures (Fig. 4A-F, Supplementary Figs. S5, S6), but the main text states the conclusions, so the question can be answered from the text. "C!T" and "T!Toff" are the PDF text layer's mis-encoding of the arrow in C→T and T→Toff, and they are quoted as printed.

records.short_answer: MYC influences RNA Pol II loading on both activated and repressed genes. Up- or downregulation of gene expression is paralleled by equivalent changes in RNA Pol II binding at promoters. During the C→T transition, primary and secondary genes (classes 2/5 and 1/4) show similar variations in Pol II binding. During the T→Toff transition, only primary MYC-dependent genes (classes 2,3/5,6) are affected. Pol II abundance changes consistently on gene bodies as well as on promoters, but stalling indices are not consistently affected in any regulatory category. Whether regulated by MYC in a primary or secondary manner, activated and repressed genes show generally consistent changes in Pol II loading and elongation. MYC-binding profiles, by contrast, are not predictive of MYC-dependent regulation. Peak presence, localization relative to the TSS and binding intensity do not distinguish primary from secondary MYC-responsive genes. Increases in binding neither discriminate MYC-dependent from -independent responses nor correlate with the extent of changes in mRNA levels. Enhancer recruitment does not discriminate them either. Primary repressed genes are less frequently and more weakly bound than nonregulated genes, and primary induced genes show the opposite. So genome-wide MYC binding alone does not discriminate primary from secondary targets and no simple rule links it to regulation, whereas changes in RNA Pol II activity correspond to the DEG categories.

records.short_answer:
PDBinder does only slightly worse on apo (unbound) structures than on holo (ligand-bound) structures:
- MCC: 0.313 holo, 0.271 apo
- PPV: 0.413 holo, 0.372 apo
- Sensitivity: 0.295 holo, 0.251 apo
- Specificity: 0.983 holo, 0.984 apo
- ROC AUC (Figure 1 legend): 0.780 holo, 0.767 apo

That is a 13% drop in MCC and a 10% drop in PPV. Q-SiteFinder drops 35% in MCC and 28% in PPV.

On robustness, the authors say performance "suffers only a modest decrease" from holo to apo and that apo performance is "quite similar" to holo. Their explanation is that the method considers the conformation of groups of three residues only. The ligand can alter the overall structure of the binding pocket, but the local conformation of these small subsets of residues is mostly preserved. They call this extremely important for real-world applications, where the location of the binding site is unknown because the protein has been crystallized without a ligand.

records.question_issues: The paper never names a step "Spatial Clustering". The section is headed "Clustering of the predictions", and the text calls the step "spatial filtering", "clustering radius" and "spatial clustering". It is a filter on predictions: it drops every predicted residue that has no other prediction within a set radius. It does not group residues into clusters. The only parameter given is the radius: 10.0 Å, chosen from tests between 1.0 and 20.0 Å in 1 Å steps. The paper does not say how the distance is measured (by atoms or by Cα). Other "cluster" hits do not answer this question: the BLASTClust sequence clusters (page 10), the Methods search for the binding-pocket definition from 3.0 to 10.0 Angstrom in increments of 0.5 (page 10), and the probe clusters of other methods.

records.short_answer: Spatial clustering filters PDBinder's predictions. On the training set the propensity value alone gave about 40% correct predictions. Binding sites are contiguous regions of the surface, so PDBinder discards spatially isolated predictions: any prediction without at least one other prediction within a defined radius is dropped. The authors tested radii from 1.0 Å to 20.0 Å in increments of 1 Å. The best clustering radius was 10.0 Å, close to the mean binding-site radius in the training set (8.97 ± 0.20 Å, 99% confidence interval). This threshold raised the positive predictive value by 5.4% and the MCC by 0.018, with a loss of 1.4% in sensitivity. The Table 1 results use a single propensity threshold for all amino acids together with spatial clustering at a 10 Angstrom threshold. With residue-specific thresholds, adding spatial clustering did not recover the slightly worse average performance (data not shown).

records.short_answer: A successful 4C-seq experiment should always show a strong enrichment of contacts with DNA fragments flanking the viewpoint on the linear chromosome, in particular fragments co-occupying the same TAD. Preferably >60% of the reads map to the chromosome containing the viewpoint (the cis chromosome), with most reads mapping within 1 Mb of the viewpoint. Self-ligation of the viewpoint fragment and undigested DNA can heavily skew these metrics, so they should be assessed after exclusion of the top fragments (fragMappedCisCorr and cov1Mb). The viewpoint should also capture many different fragments: >40%, preferably >60%, of mappable fragment ends within 100 kb of the viewpoint should be captured at least once (capt100Kb > 40%). Low-complexity libraries (capt100Kb < 40%) often result from bad template quality rather than insufficient sequencing depth. With (previously frozen) primary tissue, the cis percentage frequently drops to ~50%. That drop indicates random ligations, but the local coverage around the viewpoint is often still good enough to draw reproducible conclusions.

records.question_issues: The question asks for "the minimum number", but the paper gives no single threshold. It says "roughly 50,000–100,000 cis-mapped 4C reads are sufficient". The correlation data behind that range are in Supplementary Fig. 2, which is not in the text, so no exact cut-off can be checked. An answer of 50,000 alone or 100,000 alone only partly matches. records.short_answer:
The two papers address different layers, and neither compares itself with the other.

nf-core (here the nf-core/sarek 3 pipeline) saves storage and cost through pipeline design and cloud set-up:
- Storage: intermediate files are CRAM instead of BAM. CRAM stores only differences to the reference, and work-directory storage for pre-processing dropped by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage. The default number of interval groups is set to 21, because more scattering gave no runtime benefit but increased storage. Together the two changes cut storage requirements by two-thirds plus a further factor of 5.
- Cost: the abstract credits the 70% cost reduction to the CRAM format (less storage) and more intra-sample parallelization (less runtime) together. Input FastQ files can be split and mapped in parallel, which cut the median mapping runtime to 37% at a plateau of 12 shards. Costs were evaluated on AWS Batch using spot instances. The saving is stated four ways: a 70% cost reduction (abstract), a 69% reduction (introduction), costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and to 50% (Discussion). Table 2 gives $68.04 per normal sample for 2.7.2 against $20.82 for 3.1.1, about $20 per germline analysis. Users can cut costs further by choosing cheaper AWS regions and capping the spot price.

Snakemake offers engine-level features:
- Scheduling: a mixed integer linear program (MILP) replaced the earlier greedy scheduler. It runs at the start of execution and whenever a job finishes, and selects jobs without exceeding resources such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. Its goals are fast execution, preferring high-priority jobs and quickly deleting temporary output files. The MILP's four criteria are job priority, number of used cores, deleting temporary files as soon as possible, and reducing the lifetime of temporary files that cannot yet be deleted.
- Transparency: the ability to judge whether an analysis is methodologically valid. Snakemake tracks input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each job and makes them available in self-contained, interactive HTML based reports that show provenance and runtime statistics and are portable and archivable.

Comparison: both act on disk storage, sarek through file format and scattering defaults, Snakemake through scheduling that deletes temporary files early. Only sarek reports measured cloud cost savings; only Snakemake describes provenance reporting for transparency.
records.synthesis_statement: The nf-core/sarek paper reduces storage at the pipeline level by adopting CRAM, which stores only differences to the reference and cut work-directory storage by 65%, from 170.4 TB to 59.7 TB, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage [0, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. It sets the default number of interval groups to 21, because more scattering did not reduce runtime further but increased storage, and the two changes together cut storage by two-thirds and a further factor of 5 [9, 10, 11, 12]. It also shortens runtime by intra-sample parallelization, splitting input FastQ files and mapping them in parallel, which cut the median mapping runtime to 37% at a plateau of 12 shards [0, 39, 40], and the abstract credits the 70% cost reduction to the storage and runtime gains together [0, 1]. It evaluated costs on AWS Batch with spot instances [13, 15], and states the saving as a 70% reduction, a 69% reduction, a reduction to approximately 30% and a reduction to 50% [1, 2, 14, 17], with $68.04 against $20.82 per normal sample in Table 2 and about $20 per germline analysis [3, 16]. Users can reduce costs further through cheaper AWS regions and a spot price cap [18]. Snakemake instead schedules jobs with a mixed integer linear program, which replaced a greedy scheduler [24, 30], run at the start of execution and whenever a job finishes [20], within resources including hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores [19]. It aims for fast execution, high-priority jobs and quick deletion of temporary files [21, 22, 23], and its MILP criteria are priority, used cores, deleting temporary files as soon as possible and shortening the lifetime of temporary files not yet deletable [25, 26, 27, 28, 29]. For transparency, the ability to judge whether an analysis is methodologically valid [31, 32, 33], Snakemake tracks each job's inputs, outputs, parameters, software and code and presents them in self-contained, interactive HTML reports that show provenance and runtime statistics and are portable and archivable [34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. Both address disk storage, sarek through file format and scattering defaults [6, 11], Snakemake through scheduling that deletes temporary files early [23, 28]; only sarek reports measured cloud cost savings [14, 16], and only Snakemake describes provenance reports [34, 35, 36].

The fastp paper (2018) never mentions MultiQC (a grep for "MultiQC" in the fastp text returns nothing). The MultiQC paper (2016) came out before fastp and gives only a count of supported tools ("22 common bioinformatics tools"), without naming fastp. The complementarity can only be inferred by setting each paper's description of its own tool side by side: fastp does the preprocessing in one pass and writes HTML and JSON QC reports per run, and MultiQC gathers per-sample logs and QC reports from many tools into one report across samples. Any claim of a fastp module in MultiQC, or of direct integration, comes from outside these texts. The question is also open-ended ("how does ... complement"), so it can reasonably be framed in more than one way.

records.short_answer: Neither paper mentions the other, so the complementarity is inferred from what each paper says about its own tool. In the past, multiple tools were used for FASTQ quality control and preprocessing, and reading and loading the data multiple times made preprocessing slow and I/O inefficient. fastp is an all-in-one FASTQ preprocessor. It performs quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and other operations in a single scan of the FASTQ data. For each run it writes HTML and JSON reports. The HTML report shows quality control for pre- and post-filtered data on a single page, and the JSON holds all the data visualized in the HTML report. MultiQC fills a different gap. Nearly all logs and reports are produced on a per-sample basis, so MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single report visualizing output from multiple tools across many samples. Its shared plots allow comparison between samples. It supports 22 common tools (aligners, processing tools and QC programs) and functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. In a pipeline, then, fastp provides the preprocessing and a per-run QC report, and MultiQC provides the cross-sample, cross-tool view. Neither paper states that MultiQC parses fastp output.

key_concepts.phrase: single scan of the FASTQ data

records.synthesis_statement: fastp combines quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering, per-read quality pruning and other operations into a single scan of the FASTQ data [1,2,7], which avoids the multi-tool approach that had to read and load the data multiple times [0,16]. For each run it generates HTML and JSON reports [3,5]. A single HTML page shows quality control reports for pre- and post-filtered data, which allows direct comparison of quality statistics altered by preprocessing [4,6], and the JSON contains all the data visualized in the HTML report [5]. MultiQC addresses the fact that logs and QC reports are produced on a per-sample basis [9]: it scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single report visualizing output from multiple tools across many samples, with shared plots for comparison between samples [8,10,11,14]. It exports parsed data and functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [13,15]. Read together, fastp supplies the preprocessing and a per-run QC report, and MultiQC supplies the aggregation and visualization across samples and tools [3,4,8,10,15]. The MultiQC paper gives only a count of 22 supported tools [12], and neither paper names the other tool or states that MultiQC reads fastp's reports.

records.short_answer: All three provide software through Conda (Bioconda) environments or Docker and Singularity containers, and all three run across platforms including clusters/HPC schedulers and cloud. Sarek installs all its tools in Conda and pushes them to DockerHub, so they are available from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers "to ensure reproducibility"; containers let it install on all POSIX compatible systems, and through Nextflow it runs on Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS. Snakemake deploys a software environment per rule via the Conda package manager, or pulls a container image and runs the job using Singularity, which makes the environment portable across operating systems and increases reproducibility; it scales to cluster middleware, grid computing and cloud computing. In nf-core, module tools are typically accessible through (bio)conda with corresponding Docker and Singularity containers from Biocontainers, enabling portability and reproducibility for each module; nf-core/sarek, written in Nextflow, is portable to cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers.
records.synthesis_statement: The shared method is software deployment through Conda environments (Bioconda in Sarek and nf-core), with Docker or Singularity containers as the alternative: Sarek installs all its tools in Conda and pushes them to DockerHub [0, 1, 2], Snakemake deploys an environment or container per rule [5, 6, 7] and nf-core provides one per module [10]. Each paper credits this with reproducibility and/or portability [1, 3, 8, 10]. All three also run across cluster and cloud environments: Sarek and nf-core/sarek through Nextflow [4, 11], and Snakemake through cluster middleware, grid and cloud computing [9].

records.question: What common technical methodologies do Sarek, Snakemake, and the nf-core framework share to ensure reproducibility and portability across different computing environments?

records.question_issues:
The question is phrased as a hypothetical ("How could integrating..."). The paper filed as 03_nfcore_framework is not a general paper on the nf-core framework. It is the nf-core/sarek 3 paper (NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics 2024). That paper reports the integration as already done (fastP introduced with release v3.0, CRAM intermediates, tuned interval scattering) and measures its effects, so the answer comes from measured results. The "data management optimizations" belong to Sarek 3, not to nf-core as a framework. The phrase is vague; here it is read as CRAM storage, FastQ sharding, interval scattering, and a dedicated process in place of splitFastq().

What each paper contributes:
- 01_sarek (Sarek 2.5.2) gives only the baseline resource profile, from one 90X/90X run on a single 48-thread node. The Sarek 3 comparison is v2.7.2 (in places v2.7.1) against v3.1.1 on AWS Batch, so the two sets of numbers are not one before-and-after measurement.
- 04_fastp gives tool-level speed and splitting features. It has no measurements made inside Sarek.

03 states its headline figures inconsistently:
- Cost: "70% cost reduction" (abstract), "69% reduction" (introduction), "to approximately 30%" (results) and "to 50%" (discussion).
- CPU hours: reduced by "approximately 70%" (results, whole pipeline on AWS) and by "66%" (discussion, attributed to the fastP step plus interval splitting).
- Baseline version: 2.7.2 in the introduction and Table 2, 2.7.1 on page 8.

The question is open-ended, so answers may reasonably emphasise different measured effects.

records.short_answer:
Baseline: the original Sarek WGS run on a 90x/90x tumour/normal dataset took 48 hours and 21 minutes and 1790 CPU h, of which mapping, merging and deduplication took 1081 CPU h. Total storage including temporary data was 3.7 TB. The paper recommends 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and at least 4 TB of free storage.

fastp: it does quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data. It is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt and can split its output into multiple files for parallel processing.

fastP in nf-core/sarek 3 (introduced with release v3.0) shards the FastQ files with optional adapter trimming in one step:
- Alignment can run on smaller machines, and the computation is faster.
- Median mapping runtime fell to 37%, reaching a plateau at 12 shards.
- Storage rose because sub-FastQs are written to disk, and mapping CPU hours stayed about the same.
- Running the split as a dedicated process in place of splitFastq() gives resource assignment, automatic retries on job failure and resume.
- Doing trimming, QC and sharding in one step, together with more tailored interval splitting, reduced the needed CPU hours by 66%.

Data management:
- CRAM intermediates cut pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB).
- Average pre-processing CPU hours were 3252.37 with CRAM against 3,761.07 with BAM, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage.
- Runtime gains stop beyond 21 interval groups, and reducing scattering cuts storage by a further factor of 5.

Overall on AWS:
- One normal sample went from $68.04, 46h8m and 1118.4 CPU hours (2.7.2) to $20.82, 12h4m and 342.5 CPU hours (3.1.1).
- The results text reports single-sample CPU hours reduced by approximately 70%, runtime by 84%, and costs to approximately 30%.
- Elsewhere the paper gives the cost saving as 70%, 69%, or costs reduced to 50%.

key_concepts.phrase: reduction of the median runtime to 37%
reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%

records.synthesis_statement: The original Sarek WGS workflow was recommended to run on 16 cores, 128 GB RAM and at least 4 TB of free storage [0]. A 90x/90x tumour/normal run took 48 hours and 21 minutes and 1790 CPU h, mapping, merging and deduplication took 1081 CPU h, and total storage including temporary data was 3.7 TB [2, 3, 29]. That workflow already used scatter-gather to spread load across CPU cores [1]. fastp performs quality control, adapter trimming and filtering in a single scan, avoiding the slow, I/O-inefficient repeated reading of data [4, 5]. It is 2–5 times faster than Trimmomatic or Cutadapt and can split its output for parallel alignment [6, 7, 8, 9]. In nf-core/sarek 3, fastP shards FastQ files with optional adapter trimming in one step, so alignment runs on smaller machines and computation is faster [10, 11]. Median mapping runtime fell to 37%, with a plateau at 12 shards [12]. Sharding increased storage and left CPU hours about the same [13, 14]. Running the split as a dedicated process gives resource assignment, automatic retries and resume [16]. Together with tailored interval splitting, the single fastP step reduced CPU hours by 66% [15]. Storing intermediates as CRAM cut pre-processing work-directory storage by 65% (170.4 TB to 59.7 TB) and lowered average CPU hours from 3,761.07 to 3252.37, at the cost of a 34% increase in memory [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Scattering gives no runtime benefit beyond 21 interval groups, and reducing it cuts storage by a further factor of 5 [22, 23]. On AWS, one normal sample went from $68.04, 46h8m and 1118.4 CPU hours to $20.82, 12h4m and 342.5 CPU hours [30]. The paper reports the overall effect as approximately 70% fewer CPU hours and 84% less runtime [25]. It gives the cost saving variously as costs reduced to approximately 30%, a 70% or 69% reduction, or costs reduced to 50% [24, 26, 27, 28].

records.question_issues: Partial premise mismatch. The paper filed as 03_nfcore_framework is the nf-core/sarek 3 paper ("Scalable and efficient DNA sequencing analysis on different compute infrastructures aiding variant discovery"). It describes one nf-core pipeline written in Nextflow, not the nf-core framework in general. Its parallelization strategies work at the pipeline level by splitting the data: FastQ sharding with fastP, scatter/gather over genomic interval groups, and variant callers run in parallel. Job execution is left to Nextflow and the HPC schedulers or cloud vendors beneath it, and the paper describes no scheduling algorithm of its own. The Snakemake paper describes scheduling inside the engine (a MILP over pending jobs, resource hand-off to middleware, DAG partitioning into group jobs). The two papers therefore describe different layers, and the contrast holds only on those terms. Both papers contribute evidence.

records.short_answer:
nf-core/sarek, a Nextflow pipeline from nf-core, gets its parallelism by splitting the data. The FastQ files are split into shards with fastP and mapped in parallel. Mapping runtime plateaus at 12 shards, with the median runtime reduced to 37%. Genomic regions are processed in parallel after duplicate marking, and small regions are grouped to reduce the number of jobs. Scatter/gather across genomic regions is used for BQSR and variant calling, and the variant calling tools all run in parallel. Interval-group parallelization has clear limits: there is no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups. Job execution is left to Nextflow, which runs on several cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers. Splitting runs as a dedicated process, so it gets regular job submission with resource assignment, automatic retries and resume.

Snakemake does the job scheduling itself. At the start of execution, and whenever a job finishes and new jobs become pending, it selects the subset of jobs to run without exceeding resources such as hard drive space, I/O capacity and CPU cores. It does this by solving a mixed integer linear program (MILP), which replaced the greedy scheduler of its first releases. Four criteria are applied in lexicographical order: job priority first, then the number of used cores (the extent of parallelization), then deleting temporary files as soon as possible, then reducing the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass. By default all jobs have the same priority, so the MILP maximizes used cores while removing as many temporary files as possible. On a cluster or cloud, Snakemake passes resource requirements to the middleware. By default it submits each job separately, but it can partition the DAG of jobs into subgraphs submitted together as a single cluster or cloud job. Scaling to a platform only requires changing command line parameters.
records.synthesis_statement: nf-core/sarek parallelizes by splitting the data inside the pipeline. It shards FastQ files with fastP and maps them in parallel, with runtime gains plateauing at 12 shards [0, 1, 2]. It processes genomic regions in parallel, grouping small ones to reduce job count, with scatter/gather for BQSR and variant calling [3, 4, 5, 6], and it runs the variant callers in parallel [7]. Interval-group parallelization gives no further benefit beyond 21 interval groups [8, 9]. Job execution is handed to Nextflow and the cloud vendors or HPC schedulers beneath it, and splitting runs as regular job submission with resources, retries and resume [10, 11]. Snakemake instead solves scheduling in its own engine. Each time jobs become pending, it selects which ones to run within resource limits by solving a MILP, which replaced an earlier greedy scheduler [14, 15, 16, 17]. The MILP ranks four criteria: priority, then used cores (parallelization), then temporary file deletion, then the lifetime of temporary files that cannot be deleted in this pass, and by default maximizes used cores while removing temporary files [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24]. On clusters and clouds it passes resource requirements to the middleware [25]. It submits jobs separately by default but can partition the DAG into subgraphs submitted as one job [26, 27]. Scaling to another platform only changes command line parameters [12, 13].

records.question_issues: Answerable from the text of all three papers, with four caveats. (1) Only SeqKit and Cutadapt use the word "bottleneck". SeqKit names file I/O and record parsing; Cutadapt names alignment in theory and reading and parsing input in practice. fastp gives the slowness of earlier tools (high-level languages, limited multi-threading, reading data multiple times) as its motivation, but it never calls any of these a bottleneck. (2) The Cutadapt paper (a 2011 technical note) describes one speed measure only: the alignment algorithm is written in C as a Python extension module. It says reading and parsing take more than half the time but gives no strategy for that, and it does not mention multi-threading. So Cutadapt has little content for the "optimization strategies" part. (3) The papers are independent. Only fastp compares itself with one of the others (Cutadapt), and it gives two figures for its advantage over other tools: 2–5 times faster in the abstract and 3–5 times longer for the other tools in the Results, plus Table 1. The throughput figures in the papers come from different hardware and datasets, so they cannot be compared directly across papers. (4) The fastp text layer prints C++ as "Cþþ" and "=" as "¼". The evidence keeps these as printed; the printed paper says C++ (C/C++).

records.short_answer:
fastp is developed in C/C++ (printed "Cþþ" in the text layer) with multi-threading. It says earlier tools were slow because most were written in Python or Java with limited multi-threading, and because they read and loaded data multiple times. Its strategies:
- multi-threaded parallel processing, with reads packed in groups of N = 1000 and each pack consumed by one thread in a pool
- all operations in a single scan of the FASTQ data
- a duplication array and a counting array in place of a hash table, for faster access

fastp reports being 2–5 times faster than other FASTQ preprocessing tools such as Trimmomatic or Cutadapt (abstract). In its speed evaluation, with all tools run on a single thread, the other tools take 3–5 times longer than fastp (Results). In Table 1, fastp SE takes 6 min (129397.9 reads/s) and Cutadapt SE 18 min (43132.6 reads/s).

SeqKit is implemented in Go. It names file I/O, and sequence record parsing, as the main bottleneck. Its strategies:
- its own parsing package, bio, with performance similar to klib (kseq.h)
- a custom buffered file reader instead of Go's "bufio", which increased speed and lowered memory use
- CPU-intensive processes parallelized by Goroutines, with a default of two threads (three or more gave no further significant improvement)
- a slice indexed by ASCII code instead of a map for reverse complement, a ~20× speedup
- lower memory use by not loading all records into memory, by MD5 digests, and by a two-pass read mode with a FASTA index

Cutadapt is mainly written in Python, but for speed its alignment algorithm is implemented in C as a Python extension module. In theory its run time is dominated by alignment, O(nk). In practice, reading and parsing the input files take more than half of the time. It trims about 1 million reads per minute (0.06 ms per read) on a single core of a 2.66 GHz Intel Core 2 processor.
records.synthesis_statement: The three tools use different languages: fastp is developed in C/C++ [3, 5], SeqKit in Go [13], and Cutadapt mainly in Python, with its alignment algorithm in C as a Python extension module for speed [27]. fastp and SeqKit both parallelize. fastp uses a thread pool that consumes packs of 1000 reads [6, 7, 8]. SeqKit runs CPU-intensive processes as Goroutines [16] and defaults to two threads, because three or more gave no further significant improvement [25, 26]. Cutadapt reports its speed on a single core [30]. They target different bottlenecks. fastp blames high-level languages, limited multi-threading and repeated loading of data [0, 1], answers with a single scan of the data [2], and uses arrays in place of a hash table for faster access [9]. SeqKit names file I/O and record parsing as the bottleneck [14, 24]. It answers with its own parsing package [15], a custom buffered reader [17, 18], a slice in place of a map with a ~20× speedup [19, 20], and memory savings from streaming, MD5 digests and an indexed two-pass mode [21, 22, 23]. Cutadapt's time is dominated by alignment in theory, O(nk), and that is the part moved into C [27, 28], yet in practice reading and parsing input take more than half of the time [29]. fastp reports being 2–5 times faster than tools including Cutadapt [4]. In its Results, with all tools run on a single thread, the other tools take 3–5 times longer [10, 11], and in its Table 1 Cutadapt SE takes 18 min against fastp's 6 min [12].

records.question_issues: The question can be answered in more than one reasonable way. "Technical challenges" is not defined, so several selections of evidence would each give a correct answer. It also assumes a sequential STAR, then Salmon, then DESeq2 pipeline that none of the three papers describes. STAR (06) mentions neither Salmon nor DESeq2. Salmon (07) mentions neither STAR nor DESeq2: it can take "pre-computed alignments provided in SAM or BAM format" without naming an aligner, and its own DE benchmark does not use DESeq2. DESeq2 (08) mentions neither STAR nor Salmon. Its benchmark reads "were aligned using the TopHat2 aligner [65], and assigned to genes using the summarizeOverlaps function" (08_deseq2 p19). It is presented for per-gene counts of reads "unambiguously mapped" or "uniquely assigned" to a gene, and it sets these apart from algorithms that assign reads to transcripts probabilistically, which is the approach Salmon takes. So the papers do not state how the three tools connect. The answer can only set side by side how each paper handles its own technical challenges and what input and normalization DESeq2 accepts. All three papers contribute evidence.

records.short_answer:
STAR (mapping) targets the non-contiguous transcript structure, relatively short read lengths, increasing sequencing throughput and multiple copies of related genomic sequences. Its method is a sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching. This detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without a priori knowledge of junctions. MMPs serve as anchors that are extended, which allows alignments with mismatches. Poly-A tails, library adapter sequences and poor sequencing quality tails are identified. The search finds all distinct genomic matches for multimapping reads, and STAR reports every alignment scoring within a user-defined range below the highest score.

Salmon (quantification) targets technical biases from fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can lead to high false positive rates in differential expression studies. It quantifies either by quasi-mapping raw reads to a transcriptome index, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed alignments in SAM or BAM format. Its model accounts for positional biases in coverage, 5′ and 3′ sequence-specific biases, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution, with parameters learned in the online phase. It estimates the conditional probability that a fragment came from each transcript to which it multimaps. It also estimates abundance uncertainty due to random sampling and multimapping. The paper says GC bias correction improves the reliability of subsequent differential expression analysis. In the paper's own DE tests (t-tests of log2(TPM + 1), not DESeq2), Salmon's estimates gave markedly higher sensitivity at the same false discovery rate than kallisto's and eXpress' estimates on the Polyester simulated data. They also gave fewer false-positive DE calls when 30 GEUVADIS samples were compared across sequencing centers, where few or no true differences are expected.

DESeq2 (downstream) starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously mapped to a gene, that is, per-gene counts. Size factors estimated by the median-of-ratios method account for differences in sequencing depth. Gene-specific normalization factors for technical biases such as GC content or gene length, or estimates of average transcript length, can be supplied. DESeq2 contrasts its per-gene counts with algorithms that use probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts. None of the papers describes STAR or Salmon output being passed to DESeq2.
records.synthesis_statement: STAR addresses non-contiguous transcripts, short reads, high throughput and multicopy sequences [0, 1]. It uses sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, followed by seed clustering and stitching [2], and detects splice junctions in a single alignment pass without prior junction knowledge [3]. It extends MMP anchors to allow mismatches and identifies poly-A tails, adapters and poor-quality tails [5, 6]. It finds all genomic matches for multimapping reads and reports alignments within a user-defined score range of the best [4, 7]. Salmon targets the technical biases of fragmentation, amplification and sequencing, which, uncorrected, can cause high false positive rates in differential expression studies [8, 10]. It quantifies from quasi-mapping of raw reads, without intermediate alignment files, or from pre-computed SAM/BAM alignments [14, 15]. It models positional, 5′/3′ sequence-specific, fragment-level GC, strand-specific and fragment-length effects [16]. It assigns multimapping fragments to transcripts probabilistically and estimates the resulting abundance uncertainty [11, 17]. The paper reports that GC correction improves the reliability of subsequent DE analysis [9]. In the paper's own DE tests, Salmon's estimates gave markedly higher sensitivity at the same FDR and fewer false-positive calls [12, 13]. DESeq2 starts from a count matrix of reads unambiguously or uniquely assigned to genes [18, 19, 23]. It normalizes for sequencing depth with median-of-ratios size factors [20, 21]. It accepts supplied gene-specific normalization factors for GC content, gene length or average transcript length [22, 25]. It contrasts its per-gene counts with probabilistic read-to-transcript assignment [24].

key_concepts.phrase: probabilistic assignments of reads to transcripts

records.question: In the context of RNA-seq analysis, how do the mapping and quantification methods of STAR and Salmon address technical challenges before downstream differential expression analysis in DESeq2?

records.question_issues:
The question can be answered only in part, and the answer is lopsided. It assumes that both tools deal with the same "technical artifacts in RNA-seq data", but the papers describe different artifacts handled at different stages.

Cutadapt (10_cutadapt) removes adapter sequence, and optionally low-quality read ends, from the reads before read mapping. It is framed around small RNA sequencing (454, Illumina and SOLiD data). Salmon (07_salmon) removes nothing from the reads. It models fragment-level sampling biases during quantification (positional, 5'/3' sequence-specific, fragment GC, strand, fragment length) and corrects for them through effective transcript lengths.

Neither paper mentions the other or compares itself with the other, so the comparison has to be assembled from each paper's own description.

On downstream implications, Cutadapt says only two things: just the relevant part of the read is passed on to further analysis, and a leftover colour could cause a spurious mismatch during read mapping. It reports no measured effect on quantification or differential expression. Salmon reports quantitative effects on differential expression (DE).

Salmon gives different values for the same results in different places. For DE sensitivity, the main text says 53% to 250% higher, while the Figure 1c legend says 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress. For false-positive DE calls, the main text says "fewer", while the Figure 1d legend says "fewer than half as many". All of these are quoted.

records.short_answer:
Cutadapt edits the reads themselves, before read mapping.
- What it targets: in small RNA sequencing the reads are longer than the RNA, so they contain parts of the 3' adapter.
- How it finds the adapter: error-tolerantly, using 'regular' or slightly modified semi-global alignments.
- What it does with the read: it can either trim or discard reads in which an adapter occurs. It trims the read when the error rate is below the allowed maximum, and reads must be discarded entirely when the adapter is a sign of contamination.
- Other trimming: it can also trim low-quality read ends using the same algorithm as BWA.
- Colour space: it also removes the colour preceding the adapter.
- Stated implications: only the relevant part of the read is passed on to further analysis, and removing that colour avoids a spurious mismatch during read mapping.

Salmon (in quasi-mapping mode) takes raw, unaligned reads and performs quantification directly, without generating intermediate alignment files. It handles artifacts inside quantification.
- What it models: positional biases in coverage, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ ends of fragments, fragment-level GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution.
- How: these models are learned in the online phase, including a foreground and background GC-bias model, and are used to re-estimate the effective length of each transcript.
- Read errors: when alignments are the input, it models substitution and indel rates in bins along each read.
- Stated implications: uncorrected biases can confound downstream analyses and lead to high false positive rates in differential expression. GC-bias correction improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the reliability of DE analysis.

Salmon's reported DE results:
- Sensitivity 53% to 250% higher at the same FDRs. The Figure 1c legend instead gives 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress.
- Fewer false-positive DE calls. The Figure 1d legend says fewer than half as many.
- A ~2.6-fold decrease in genes called DE.
- Isoform switching seen under kallisto or eXpress estimates is eliminated.
records.synthesis_statement:
The two tools handle different artifacts at different stages, and neither paper compares itself with the other.

Cutadapt acts on the reads themselves, before read mapping. The artifact is 3' adapter sequence in reads that are longer than the small RNA [0, 1, 5]. Cutadapt finds the adapter error-tolerantly with semi-global alignments and trims the read when the error rate is below the allowed maximum [5, 9, 10]. It can instead discard reads in which an adapter occurs, as when the adapter signals contamination [4, 6], and it can also trim low-quality ends [7]. Its stated downstream consequences are that only the relevant part of the read goes on to further analysis and that, in colour space, removing the preceding colour avoids a spurious mismatch during read mapping [2, 3, 8].

In quasi-mapping mode, Salmon takes raw, unaligned reads and quantifies them directly, without intermediate alignment files [16]. During its online phase it learns models of positional, 5′/3′ sequence-specific and fragment GC bias, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution [14, 15, 18]. It corrects for these biases by re-estimating effective transcript lengths [19]. With alignments as input, it models substitution and indel rates in bins along each read [20]. Its stated motivation is that other quantifiers lack rich bias models, and that uncorrected biases cause high false positive rates in differential expression and confound downstream analyses [12, 13, 17].

With GC-bias correction, Salmon reports more accurate abundance estimates and more reliable DE analysis [11]. DE sensitivity at the same FDR is 53% to 250% higher in the main text, and 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress in the Figure 1c legend [21, 22]. Salmon also reports fewer false-positive DE calls (fewer than half as many in the Figure 1d legend), a ~2.6-fold decrease in genes called DE, and elimination of the isoform switching seen under kallisto or eXpress estimates [23, 24, 25, 26].

key_concepts.phrase: high false positive rates in differential expression

records.question_issues: Partly a false premise. The question assumes the papers describe how fastp and Cutadapt integrate with MultiQC, and none of them does. The MultiQC paper (2016) never names fastp or Cutadapt. It says only that MultiQC supports "22 common bioinformatics tools including aligners, processing tools and QC programs" without listing them, and the only QC tools it names are FastQC, Qualimap and RSeQC. The fastp paper (2018) never mentions MultiQC. The Cutadapt paper (2011) mentions neither MultiQC nor any log, report or visualisation output. The answer can therefore only be pieced together from what each paper says on its own. fastp and Cutadapt clean the reads, and fastp also writes its own HTML and JSON QC report. MultiQC collects per-sample log files and QC reports from supported tools into one cross-sample report at the end of a pipeline. Any claim that MultiQC parses fastp or Cutadapt output comes from outside knowledge and is not in these texts. All three papers contribute evidence. Cutadapt's contribution is limited to its trimming and filtering role.

records.short_answer:
None of the papers describes a direct integration. Each describes a complementary role.

fastp: performs quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data. It generates its own reports in HTML and JSON formats, with statistics for pre-filtering and post-filtering data. The JSON contains all the data visualised in a standalone HTML report.

Cutadapt: a command-line adapter trimmer. It finds and removes adapters, can trim or discard reads in which an adapter occurs, and can trim low-quality read ends. It solves a small but important task within sequencing pipelines. In the older multi-tool combination it was used for adapter trimming, alongside FASTQC for quality control.

MultiQC: targets the problem that logs and QC reports are produced on a per-sample basis. It scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single summary report visualising results across all samples, through submodules that contribute only when they find logs. At the time of writing it supported 22 common bioinformatics tools, including processing tools and QC programs, and it functions as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines.

None of the papers states that MultiQC parses fastp or Cutadapt output specifically.
records.synthesis_statement: fastp does quality control and preprocessing in a single scan of the FASTQ data [0]. Cutadapt finds and removes adapters, trims or discards reads that contain one, and trims low-quality ends, a small but important task within sequencing pipelines [1, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]. fastp also writes its own per-run HTML and JSON reports covering pre-filtering and post-filtering data, and the JSON holds all the visualised data [2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. MultiQC addresses the fact that tool logs and QC reports are produced per sample [12]. It scans directories for log files and QC reports and combines output from multiple tools across all samples into a single summary report, through submodules that contribute when they find logs [13, 14, 15]. Its 22 supported tools include processing tools and QC programs [16], and it serves as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [17]. The papers do not state that fastp or Cutadapt output is among what MultiQC parses [16].

key_concepts.phrase: single scan of the FASTQ data

records.short_answer:
STAR trades memory for speed. It runs a sequential maximum mappable seed (MMP) search in uncompressed suffix arrays, applied only to the unmapped portions of each read, then a clustering/stitching/scoring step. The binary SA search scales logarithmically with reference genome length. Uncompressed SAs are faster than compressed SAs but use more memory: STAR requires 27 GB of RAM for the human genome. One SA is shared among all threads, so RAM does not grow with thread count, and throughput scales close to linearly with the number of cores. Its sparse-SA option cuts peak RAM to 15.6 to 16.0 GB (Table 1) at the cost of a 25% decrease in mapping speed.

SeqKit treats file I/O as the bottleneck and keeps memory use low. It parses FASTA/Q with its own lightweight bio package, using a custom buffered file reader in place of Go's bufio, which increased speed and lowered memory usage. It parallelises CPU-intensive processes with Goroutines, though more than two threads gave no significant further gain. It stores complementary sequences in a slice indexed by the byte's ASCII code instead of a map, a ~20× speedup. Most subcommands do not load all records into memory. Deduplication represents sequences by an MD5 digest, and sample, split, shuffle and sort read files twice in two-pass mode with a FASTA index. Its peak memory is determined by the length of the longest sequence record.
records.synthesis_statement: STAR gets its speed from a sequential maximum mappable seed search in uncompressed suffix arrays, applied only to unmapped portions of the read and followed by clustering and stitching, with binary search scaling logarithmically with genome length [0,1,2,3,4]. It accepts higher memory use for that speed: uncompressed SAs beat compressed ones, but STAR requires 27 GB of RAM for the human genome, and sparse SAs lower peak RAM to 15.6 to 16.0 GB at a 25% speed cost [5,6,7,9,10]. Its threads share one SA, and throughput scales close to linearly with cores [8,11]. SeqKit instead treats file I/O as the bottleneck and optimises parsing and memory, with its own bio package and a custom buffered reader that increased speed and lowered memory usage [12,13,15,16]. It avoids loading all records, uses MD5 digests for deduplication, and reads files twice in two-pass mode with a FASTA index, so peak memory is determined by the longest sequence record [19,20,21,22,23,25]. For CPU-bound work it uses Goroutines, with no significant gain beyond two threads, and a slice lookup table to store complementary sequences that gave a ~20× speedup over a map [14,17,18,24].

logarithmic scaling of the search time

records.question_issues: Both listed papers contribute. Neither paper compares itself with the other, so the answer sets the two methods sections side by side. "Biological markers" fits the Ethiopia paper directly (serum antibodies against PPRV). The Cameroon paper names no marker. Its readout is the variation in skinfold thickness after intradermal bovine and avian tuberculin (DB, DA), so that skin reaction has to stand as the bTB "marker". The Cameroon paper reports its 4 mm prevalence figures inconsistently. The abstract gives CIDT 1.8% (0%–3.6%) at 4 mm and the simple IDT 0.6% (0%–1.2%) at 4 mm. The Results text and Table-2 reverse this: SITT ≥4 mm 3/160 = 1.8%, CIDT ≥4 mm 0.6%. Table-2 and the opening Results sentence give 1 CIDT positive at 4 mm. The next Results sentence and the Discussion say "Three positive reactions" for CIDT at 4 mm but keep 0.6%. 0.6% matches 1/160. All versions are quoted. The Results call 3 mm a "WOAH recommended threshold", while Table-1 lists only the >4 mm WOAH cut-off. The CIDT 3 mm value (6.8%, 11/160) agrees everywhere.

records.short_answer: Cameroon (bTB): 160 live cattle were tested with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test (CIDT) and the simple intradermal tuberculin test (SITT), as described in the WOAH Manual. The initial skin thickness was measured, and then bovine PPD (AN5 strain, 20,000 IU/mL) and avian PPD (D4 ER strain, 25,000 IU/mL) were injected intradermally in the cervical region. Results were read 72 h later. The marker is the variation in skinfold thickness with bovine tuberculin (DB) and with avian tuberculin (DA). Under the WOAH grid, DB >2 mm with DB–DA >4 mm is positive, 1–4 mm inconclusive and <1 mm negative. SITT is positive at >4 mm. A 3 mm threshold was also applied. CIDT at 3 mm found 11 positives (6.8%, 95% CI 4.35%–9.41%), and the 3 mm threshold increased detection sensitivity compared with the WOAH 4 mm threshold. At 4 mm the paper is inconsistent. Table-2 and the Results give SITT 1.8% (3/160) and CIDT 0.6% (1 positive in Table-2, "three" in the text). The abstract gives CIDT 1.8% and simple IDT 0.6%. Ethiopia (PPR): 384 serum samples from sheep and goats were obtained from jugular blood. They were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA (ID Screen PPR Competition ELISA, ID.vet; sensitivity 94.5%, specificity 99.4%). ODs were read at 450 nm and expressed as S/N%: ≤50% positive, 50%–60% doubtful, >60% negative. Seroprevalence was 32.1% in nonvaccinated, 68.8% in vaccinated (seroconversion) and 45.5% in animals of unknown vaccination status.
records.synthesis_statement: The Cameroon bTB study tested 160 live cattle with the comparative intradermal tuberculin test under the WOAH Manual, and also with the simple intradermal test [0, 1, 6]. It measured initial skin thickness, injected bovine and avian PPD intradermally in the neck and read the result 72 h later [2, 3, 4]. Its marker was the variation in skinfold thickness to bovine versus avian tuberculin, against mm cut-offs (DB–DA >4 mm positive for CIDT, >4 mm for SITT), with a 3 mm threshold also applied [5, 9]. CIDT at 3 mm gave 6.8% (11/160) [11, 13, 14]. At 4 mm the values 1.8% and 0.6% are assigned to SITT and CIDT differently in the abstract and in the Results and Table-2 [7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14]. The 3 mm threshold increased sensitivity [15]. The Ethiopia PPR study instead used serology: 384 sheep and goat sera, separated from jugular blood, were tested for PPRV antibodies by competition ELISA [16, 17, 18]. The ID Screen kit had 94.5% sensitivity and 99.4% specificity [19]. OD at 450 nm was expressed as S/N%, with ≤50% positive, >60% negative and 50%–60% doubtful [20, 21, 22]. Seroprevalence was 32.1% nonvaccinated, 68.8% vaccinated and 45.5% unknown status [23, 24, 25]. So the bTB study reads a skin reaction to tuberculin in live cattle, and the PPR study measures antibodies in serum [5, 16].

records.question_issues: Neither paper mentions the other's disease, so neither states any relation between the Serengeti rabies control challenges and LSD vaccine efficacy. The question can only be answered by setting the two papers side by side, and several framings are reasonable. The two papers also measure different things. The rabies paper (15_rabies_tanzania) measures vaccination delivery: coverage, its spatial heterogeneity, logistical lapses and incursions. It reports no vaccine efficacy figure. The LSD review (20_lsd_review) reports vaccine protection: goat pox vaccine 60 to 70%, Lumpi-ProVacInd 100% (attributed to ICAR scientists, with no primary data), sheeppox vaccine only partial cross-protection, and about 96% cross-protection among capripoxviruses. It does not analyse coverage heterogeneity or incursions. Its only delivery figures are 15 million doses for around 200 million cattle in India and ring vaccination within 5 km of outbreaks. Any causal link, for example that high efficacy cannot make up for patchy coverage, is an inference neither paper makes. Both papers contribute evidence. v2.3 (11 October 2026, F5): corrected; the review does address disease entry (border areas, infiltration, points of incursion); only heterogeneity in coverage is absent.

evidence.sentence: These effects led to outbreaks following years when vaccination campaigns missed many villages, whereas when heterogeneity in coverage was reduced, incidence declined to low levels (<0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually and no human deaths) and short vaccination lapses thereafter did not lead to resurgence.

evidence.supports: Rabies challenge: spatial heterogeneity in coverage raises incidence.

evidence.supports: Rabies challenge: incursions drive residual transmission.

evidence.supports: Rabies challenge: coverage target rarely reached.

evidence.sentence: Returning to our three initial hypotheses for why rabies continues to circulate despite control efforts, we conclude that: 1) spatial heterogeneity in dog vaccination was detrimental for control, and vaccination was only effective in interrupting endemic circulation when implemented consistently, underlining the importance of monitoring fine-scale coverage to promptly identify and address gaps; 2) mean coverage over the district was relatively low, but once heterogeneity was addressed, rabies was controlled nonetheless – a promising result given hard-to-reach populations with fast demographic rates; 3) Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district are frequent and now represent a major source of residual transmission.

records.short_answer: Neither paper links the two diseases, so the answer is a comparison of what each reports. In the Serengeti, the rabies control challenges concerned delivering the vaccine, and the paper gives no efficacy figure. Campaign coverage ranged from 8-37% (mean 22%), and only 3% of village campaigns reached the recommended 70% target. Campaigns missed villages and lapsed due to logistical constraints, and increased heterogeneity in coverage led to increased incidence. Fast demographic rates mean many dogs must be vaccinated annually. Incursions reached 50% of cases in 2022 and are now a major driver of continued transmission, so elimination will require expanded vaccination. Once heterogeneity in coverage was reduced, vaccination controlled rabies despite not reaching the 70% target. The LSD review reports how well the vaccines protect. The goat pox vaccine gives 60 to 70% protection, and ICAR scientists report 100% efficacy for Lumpi-ProVacInd. The attenuated sheeppox vaccine gives only partial cross-protection, and SPPV vaccines had varying success. The capripoxviruses share approximately 96% cross-protection. On delivery, the review gives only 15 million doses for around 200 million cattle in India, ring vaccination within a 5-km radius of outbreaks, and an annual vaccination schedule with a booster dose. It does not discuss heterogeneity in coverage, but it does address disease entry: ring vaccination was prioritized in border areas of different states to limit the spread to surrounding states, and the review calls vaccination the singular means to thwart the onset, recurrence and infiltration of the disease and asks for genomic data from various points of incursion.
records.synthesis_statement: The rabies paper finds that control in the Serengeti was limited by how vaccination was delivered: campaigns missed villages and increased heterogeneity in coverage raised incidence [0, 1, 8]; coverage was low (8-37%, mean 22%) and only 3% of village campaigns reached 70% [3, 4]; campaigns lapsed due to logistical constraints [5]; fast demographic rates require annual vaccination [7]; and incursions (50% of cases in 2022) drive residual transmission, so elimination will require expanded vaccination [2, 8, 9]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, vaccination controlled rabies below the 70% target [0, 6, 8]. The rabies paper reports no vaccine efficacy figure. The LSD review reports vaccine protection: goat pox vaccine 60 to 70% [10], Lumpi-ProVacInd 100% according to ICAR scientists [11], sheeppox vaccine only partial cross-protection with varying success [12, 13, 14], good protection against virulent field strains in general [15], and approximately 96% cross-protection among capripoxviruses [16]. On delivery, it reports only 15 million doses for around 200 million cattle in India [17], ring vaccination within 5 km of outbreaks to limit spread to surrounding states [18] and an annual vaccination schedule with a booster dose [19], and it calls vaccination the singular means to thwart the onset, recurrence and infiltration of the disease [20], with LSDV genomic data from various points of incursion guiding vaccine strategies [21]. Neither paper states a link between the two diseases, so the papers support a comparison: the LSD review reports how well the vaccines protect, and the rabies paper reports coverage and delivery problems (low and heterogeneous coverage, missed villages, fast demographic turnover, incursions). The LSD review touches two of these only briefly, vaccine supply short of demand (15 million doses for around 200 million cattle, and vaccine makers asked to increase output) [17, 22] and spread between states (ring vaccination prioritized in border areas) [18], and it does not discuss heterogeneity in coverage.
