records.question_issues: Partly answerable, and the two papers do not cover the same things. 12_hpai_netherlands is a field study of clinical signs and mortality by poultry type and age on 92 commercial farms. 19_hpai_canada is a short commentary. It gives no clinical signs for Canadian birds and no data broken down by poultry type. For birds it reports only scale: millions of wild and farmed birds infected, severe seabird mortality, mass mortality events in wild birds, and over 7 million birds culled. Its only clinical description is for infected mammals: severe neurological signs, encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. That statement is not limited to Canada, and its citations cover Europe and Canada. So the clinical comparison cannot be made like for like. The question's framing also fits neither paper exactly. The Netherlands data cover H5N8, H5N6 and H5N1 of clade 2.3.4.4, and the paper names 2.3.4.4b only for H5N1 from 2021 onwards. The Canada paper calls its virus HPAI H5N1. It names clade 2.3.4.4b only for the UK outbreaks that came first and for genotypes detected in mammals worldwide. It never says outright that the Canadian 2022 outbreaks were 2.3.4.4b. Neither paper uses the phrase "ecological crisis". The Netherlands paper also gives two different values for the same results. Duck nervous and locomotor signs are 67.7% in the text but 66.7% (14 of 21) in Table 5. The MR > 3 percentages are 83/80/54% in the text and 82.6/80.0/53.8% in Table 6. Both versions are quoted.

records.short_answer:
Netherlands (92 commercial poultry farms; H5N8, H5N6 and H5N1 of clade 2.3.4.4): the clinical picture differed by poultry type and age.
- Ducks: neurological, locomotor and reproductive tract signs were common. Nervous and locomotor signs were seen on 67.7% of duck farms (66.7% in Table 5), against 48.4% of meat-type and 15.0% of layer-type farms. Reproductive tract signs were seen on 100% of duck farms. Egg production fell in all five breeder duck flocks, and reduced feed and water intake was seen mainly in ducks.
- Chickens: mucosal membrane and skin signs, including cyanosis and hemorrhagic conjunctiva, were seen on 55.0% of layer-type and 67.8% of meat-type farms, against 4.7% of duck farms. Respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry: 61.3%, against 37.5% in layers and 23.8% in ducks.
- Age: juveniles (chickens and ducks) showed neurological and locomotor signs more often than adults. Diarrhea occurred more often in adult chickens and juvenile ducks.
- Mortality: it increased exponentially within four days before notification. An MR > 3 was reached on 83% of layer-type, 80% of meat-type and 54% of duck farms (82.6/80.0/53.8% in Table 6), and these differences were not statistically significant. Mortality remained limited in ducks, where notification relied more on drops in feed or water intake or egg production.
- Over time: outbreaks in ducks decreased in 2020–2022 against 2014–2018, and outbreaks in meat-type poultry increased.

Canada, 2022 (HPAI H5N1): the paper reports scale and species range, not clinical signs in poultry. It names clade 2.3.4.4b only for the UK outbreaks and for genotypes found in mammals.
- Birds: millions of wild and farmed birds were infected. Seabird mortality was particularly severe on the Atlantic Coast. Infected wildlife was found in all provinces and territories, with mass mortality events in a broad range of wild bird species. Over 7 million birds were culled.
- Mammals: skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins were infected. Most infected mammals had severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Mammalian-adaptation mutations (PB2-E627K, E627V, D701N) were found in the brains of carnivores in Europe and Canada.

Comparison: the Dutch study measures differences in clinical signs between poultry types and age groups. The Canadian commentary describes infection and mortality across wild birds, farmed birds and mammals, and its only clinical picture is severe neurological disease in mammals.
records.synthesis_statement: In the Dutch commercial poultry sector, the clinical manifestation of clade 2.3.4.4 HPAI depended on poultry type and age [0, 1]. Ducks most often showed nervous and locomotor signs and reproductive tract signs [2, 3, 6], along with drops in egg production and reduced feed and water intake [7, 8, 9]. Chickens mainly showed mucosal membrane and skin signs, and respiratory signs were most frequent in meat-type poultry [1, 4, 5]. Juveniles showed neurological and locomotor signs more often than adults [10, 11], and diarrhea was more frequent in adult chickens and juvenile ducks [12]. Mortality rose exponentially within four days before notification [13]. Ducks reached MR > 3 less often than chickens (54% against 83% and 80%), but these differences were not statistically significant [14, 15, 16]. Mortality remained limited in ducks, so notification relied more on drops in feed or water intake or egg production [17, 18]. Over time, duck outbreaks decreased and meat-type poultry outbreaks increased [19]. The Canadian commentary instead describes HPAI H5N1 in 2022 across wild and farmed birds [21]. It reports severe seabird mortality on the Atlantic Coast, mass mortality in a broad range of wild bird species in all provinces and territories, over 7 million birds culled, and a substantial impact on both wildlife and the poultry industry [22, 23, 24, 25]. It also reports infection in many mammal species. Most infected mammals had severe neurological signs and died from encephalitis or meningoencephalitis, and mammalian-adaptation PB2 mutations were found in carnivore brains [26, 27, 28, 29]. Neurological disease appears in both papers: in ducks and juvenile poultry in the Netherlands [2, 10], and in infected mammals in the Canada paper [28]. The Canada paper gives no clinical signs for birds by poultry type, so it offers nothing to set against the Dutch data on that point [21, 24].

records.question_issues:
(1) Partly false premise, "in the same region". The PPR study (16_ppr_ethiopia) was done in the Borena zone of Oromia Regional State, in southern Ethiopia (ev 19). The brucellosis study (17_brucellosis_ethiopia) was done in the Liban Zone of the Somali region (ev 20). Both are pastoral settings, but they are different regions.
(2) The PPR paper sampled only sheep and goats, so it gives nothing to compare with the camel results. Camels appear only on the brucellosis side.
(3) PPR risk factors come from the nonvaccinated population (Table 4). The paper also analyses seroconversion in vaccinated animals, where species and body condition were significant. That is vaccine response, not infection risk, and it is left out.
(4) Inconsistencies inside the papers:
(a) PPR age. The text compares older animals with "adult animals" (ev 2), but in Table 4 the reference category is Young (ev 6).
(b) PPR veterinary services. The text says poor access raised the risk, OR 2.6 (ev 5). Table 4 uses Poor as the reference and gives OR 2.6 to Good (ev 8). In the univariable Table 3, seropositivity was higher with good services, 37/85 (43.5%), than with poor services, 38/149 (25.5%) (ev 21). The direction of this effect cannot be settled from the paper.
(c) Brucellosis RFM in small ruminants. The text gives OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42) (ev 12). Table 2 gives 8.2 (2.4–29) (ev 13).
(d) Brucellosis RFM in camels. The text gives only the CI, 12.7–60 (ev 15). Table 4 gives OR 35 (ev 16). The univariable camel RFM CI is printed as "5.9–8" for OR 22, which cannot be correct as printed.
(e) The brucellosis abstract and conclusion name herd size as a risk factor "in animals" (ev 9, 18). For camels, however, herd size was not significant (OR 1.9, p = 0.33; ev 17). It was significant only in small ruminants.

records.short_answer:
Herd or flock size is the only risk factor the two studies share.
- Brucellosis: small ruminants from a large herd were 5.01 times more likely to be infected (OR 5.01, 95% CI 1.2–21.4).
- PPR: sheep and goats in medium-sized flocks were more likely to be seropositive (OR 15.4, 95% CI 3.1–77.3). Large flocks were not significant (OR 1.5, p = 0.551).
- Camel brucellosis: herd size was not significant (OR 1.9, p = 0.33).

The other brucellosis risk factor is reproductive: a herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM).
- Sheep and goats: OR 9 (95% CI 1.9–42) in the text, but 8.2 (2.4–29) in Table 2.
- Camels: in the multivariable model, history of RFM was significantly associated with seropositivity, OR 35 (12.7–60). In the univariable analysis, pregnancy, history of abortion and RFM were all significant.

The other PPR risk factors, in nonvaccinated sheep and goats, are age, animal origin and veterinary services status.
- Age: older animals had OR 7.3.
- Origin: purchased animals had OR 4 and gifted animals OR 8.3, compared with animals born in the flock.
- Veterinary services: OR 2.6. The text says poor access raised the risk, but Table 4 lists Poor as the reference category, so the direction is unclear.

The PPR study did not sample camels. The two studies were not in the same region: the PPR study was in the Borena zone of Oromia Regional State, southern Ethiopia, and the brucellosis study was in the Liban Zone of the Somali region.
records.synthesis_statement:
Herd or flock size is the only risk factor the two studies share. For brucellosis, small ruminants from a large herd had OR 5.01 [9, 10, 11]. For PPR, medium-sized flocks had OR 15.4, and large flocks were not significant [1, 4, 7]. Herd size was not significant for camel brucellosis (OR 1.9, p = 0.33) [17].

The other brucellosis risk factor is reproductive: a history of retained fetal membranes. In small ruminants the text gives OR 9 and Table 2 gives 8.2 [12, 13]. In camels, history of RFM was significant in the multivariable model, with OR 35 [15, 16]; pregnancy, abortion and RFM were significant in the univariable analysis [14].

The PPR risk factors with no counterpart in the brucellosis study are age, animal origin and veterinary services status [0, 1]:
- older animals, OR 7.3 [2, 6];
- purchased animals, OR 4, and gifted animals, OR 8.3 [3];
- veterinary services status, OR 2.6, with the text and the tables pointing in opposite directions [5, 8, 21].

The studies were done in different regions: the Borena zone of Oromia for PPR and the Liban Zone of the Somali region for brucellosis [19, 20].

records.short_answer: fastp detects adapters automatically, without needing their sequence. For single-end data it assembles the high-frequency read tails: it computes k-mers of the first reads, takes k-mers with occurrence frequency >0.0001 as adapter seeds, and extends the seeds into the complete adapter with a tree-based algorithm. For paired-end data it finds the overlap of each read pair and treats the bases outside the overlap as adapter. A user can still give an adapter sequence: for single-end data that turns automatic detection off, and for paired-end data the given sequence is used for sequence matching only when no good overlap is found. Cutadapt works from adapter sequences the user supplies. It computes optimal semi-global alignments (regular or slightly modified) between each read and all given adapters, keeps the alignment with the greatest number of matching characters, computes the error rate e/l, and trims the read if that rate is below the allowed maximum. A minimum read-adapter overlap can be specified to reduce random hits. The fastp paper calls Cutadapt sequence-matching-based and says it requires at least 3 bp of matching, whereas fastp's overlap analysis can trim adapters with even only one base in the tail.

key_concepts.phrase: finding the overlap of each pair

records.short_answer:
Nawalpur 2022 outbreak (13_lsd_nepal): morbidity was 28.02% (431/1,538) and mortality 3.06% (47/1,538). Case fatality was 10.90% (47/431); the Results text gives it as 10.9%. The predominant signs were nodules in the skin (97% of case farms), reduced milk production (87%) and lameness (55%). Dry cattle had the highest morbidity (47.62%), and dry cattle, including pregnant cows, and cattle heifers were the most affected. Case fatality was highest in heifers (15.56%) and milking cattle (12.95%). In univariable analysis, outbreaks were linked to importing animals from disease prevalent regions, sharing feed and water, herd size and clinical signs in neighbouring farms. In the multivariable model only symptoms in neighbouring farms remained significant (odds ratio 88.45, 95% CI 13.27–589.36, p <0.001). Vectors (mosquitoes, houseflies, tabanus flies, ticks) were found on almost every farm, and the movement of animals between farms spread the infection. The animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD. The study recommends animal movement control and quarantine (the government mandates a 21-day quarantine), biosecurity protocols during nearby outbreaks, a practical vector control strategy, and vaccination of susceptible animals with more than 80% coverage.

Review (20_lsd_review, Kaur et al.): LSD has significant morbidity but a low fatality rate. Mortality is typically less than 10%, and morbidity can reach 100%. The disease is characterised by fever, lymph node enlargement, anorexia, depression, agalactia, emaciation and skin nodules of 10–50 mm, which can cause a significant decrease in milk output, abortion in pregnant heifers and sterility in bulls. Vectors are the most common mode of transmission (blood-sucking arthropods). Breed, age and gender do not appear to have a significant impact on severity, though Bos taurus may be more prone to severe disease and calves often show more severe signs than adult cattle. Larger farms with intensive housing and shared feeding and watering facilities can contribute to transmission. Prevention relies on vaccination, movement management, quarantine, tick management and biosecurity through vector control. The review calls vaccination the singular means to prevent the disease.

Contrast: Nawalpur's mortality of 3.06% is within the review's typical range of under 10%. Its morbidity of 28.02% is well below the review's ceiling of 100%. Nawalpur shares the review's skin nodules and drop in milk production, and Nawalpur reports lameness in 55% of case farms. Morbidity was highest in dry and pregnant cattle, whereas the review singles out calves and Bos taurus for more severe disease. Shared feed and water and herd size, the farm-level risks the review lists, were associated only in the univariable analysis. In the multivariable model they were overshadowed by symptoms in neighbouring farms. Both papers point to vectors and recommend the same prevention measures: movement control, quarantine, biosecurity, vector control and vaccination. The review calls vaccination the singular means of prevention, yet the Nawalpur animals were not yet vaccinated.
records.synthesis_statement: The Nawalpur outbreak had 28.02% morbidity, 3.06% mortality and 10.90% case fatality [0, 5], which the authors summarise as morbidity below 30% with a low mortality rate [13]. This fits the review's profile of significant morbidity with a low fatality rate, where mortality is typically below 10% [18, 19]. Nawalpur's morbidity is well below the review's statement that morbidity can reach 100% [0, 19]. Skin nodules and reduced milk production appear in both papers [1, 3, 20], and Nawalpur also reports lameness in 55% of case farms [3]. In Nawalpur, morbidity was highest in dry cattle (47.62%), and dry cattle, including pregnant cows, and heifers were the most affected [2, 4]. The review instead says breed, age and gender do not appear to significantly affect severity, and it singles out Bos taurus and calves for more severe disease [23, 24]. The review lists larger farms and shared feeding and watering facilities as contributors to transmission [25]. In Nawalpur, herd size and shared feed and water were associated with outbreaks only in the univariable analysis [6, 8]. In the multivariable model they were overshadowed by symptoms in neighbouring farms (odds ratio 88.45, p <0.001) [7, 8, 9, 10]. Both papers point to vectors: vectors were present on almost every Nawalpur farm and acted as a predisposing factor [11, 12], and the review calls vectors the most common mode of transmission [21, 22]. The prevention strategies coincide (movement control, quarantine, biosecurity, vector control and vaccination) [14, 16, 26, 27, 29]. The review calls vaccination the singular means of preventing the disease [28]. The Nawalpur animals were not yet vaccinated against LSD, and the study calls for vaccine coverage above 80% [15, 17].

key_concepts.phrase: mortality rate is typically less than 10%

records.question_issues:
Answerable, but the two papers are different kinds of source, so the comparison is uneven. 19_hpai_canada is a commentary with no data analysis. Its human risk factors are exposure circumstances (direct exposure to poultry, exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10–14 days). Its animal-side risks are spillover to mammals, mammalian-adaptive mutations and reassortment. It sets out explicit surveillance recommendations. 17_brucellosis_ethiopia is a cross-sectional serosurvey with logistic regression, so its risk factors are measured associations. It has no surveillance programme as such. It recommends molecular detection, One Health epidemiological studies to isolate and characterise circulating strains, and a One Health control strategy, so "surveillance priorities" fits the brucellosis paper only loosely.

The brucellosis paper is internally inconsistent in four places:
(a) The human RFM-disposal effect is 26-fold in the Discussion and OR 26 (4.0–45.6) in Table 5 (univariable). Table 6 (multivariable) gives 37.4 (5.1–18.5), a CI that does not contain its own point estimate. The Results text gives only "95% CI: 4.0–45, p = 0.001". The positive percentage for the same 3/16 is 19 in Table 5 and 23 in Table 6.
(b) The Discussion calls assisting calving or birthing a significant multivariable association (OR = 8; 95% CI = 0.6–127). Table 6 gives p = 0.11, and the Results call the univariable result (OR 3.6, p = 0.16) not statistically significant.
(c) The sevenfold household-seropositive-animal effect is presented in the Discussion without qualification, but the Results give p = 0.72.
(d) The small-ruminant RFM OR is 9 (1.9–42) in the Results text but 8.2 (2.4–29) in Table 2. The camel RFM multivariable result has no OR in the text; Table 4 gives OR 35 (12.7–60,).

Three evidence sentences run across a page break (indices 1, 24 and 41). They are quoted joined, without the page footer and running header, under the page where they start. The Table 6 quotation (index 29) follows the extraction order of the pymupdf text, where the "Assist birthing or / Calving" label is split around the "No" cells. The pypdf text gives the same cells.

records.short_answer:
HPAI H5N1 in Canada (19_hpai_canada, a commentary)

Human risk factors:
- All severely affected human cases had direct exposure to poultry.
- Clinicians should consider HPAI after exposure to birds or sick wildlife in the previous 10–14 days.

Animal-side risks:
- Wild birds are a source of novel influenza viruses.
- Avian infections create abundant opportunities for spillover to mammals, particularly wild mammals.
- Mutations in the HA, PB2 and NA genes are linked to mammalian adaptation. PB2-E627K, E627V and D701N were found in the brains of carnivores in Europe and Canada.
- The spillover raises the risk of reassortment with swine or human influenza viruses.

Surveillance priorities:
- Enhanced surveillance among humans, by strengthening public health and laboratory capacity to detect, report and investigate cases.
- Coordination of surveillance and reporting among the human and animal health sectors.
- Strategic surveillance with the animal health sector, focused on the regions and populations at highest risk.
- Continued in vitro and in vivo analysis of circulating strains.
- Reporting suspect cases to local public health.
- Awareness among frontline practitioners.

Gaps: surveillance of sick and dead wildlife is limited, and preparedness in the human health care sector is limited. The animal health sector is already engaged in surveillance, and CFIA, PHAC and provincial authorities monitor the disease.

Brucellosis in the Somali region of Ethiopia (17_brucellosis_ethiopia, a serosurvey)

Animal risk factors are herd size and herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM):
- Small ruminants from a large herd: OR 5.01 (95% CI 1.2–21.4).
- RFM in small ruminants: OR 9 in the text, 8.2 in Table 2.
- RFM in camels: OR 35 in Table 4.

Human risk factor: disposing of RFM, or handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials (p = 0.001). The Discussion calls this a 26-fold higher risk. Table 5 gives OR 26 and Table 6 gives OR 37.4.

Factors that were not significant or are reported inconsistently:
- Raw milk consumption (76.4% of participants; OR 5.7, p = 0.06) was not significant.
- Seropositivity was seven times higher in households with seropositive animals, but p = 0.72.
- Assisting calving or birthing is called significant in the Discussion (OR = 8), but Table 6 gives p = 0.11.

Environmental drivers: drought driven by climate change moves livestock, which concentrates animals, facilitates spillover and is expected to sustain endemicity.

Priorities:
- Molecular detection of the prevalent Brucella spp. strains before any vaccination programme.
- One Health epidemiological studies to isolate and characterise circulating Brucella spp. in humans and livestock.
- A coordinated One Health control strategy that respects the sociocultural dynamics of pastoral communities.

Comparison

Both papers place human risk in contact with animals: poultry, birds and wildlife for HPAI, and reproductive material from livestock for brucellosis. HPAI's priority is coordinated human and animal surveillance. Brucellosis's priorities are characterising the circulating strains and One Health control adapted to pastoral communities.

records.question_issues: None of the four papers compares itself with the others, so no paper states the contrast. It has to be built from separate descriptions: the computational handling of sequencing outputs in MultiQC (05_multiqc) and SeqKit (09_seqkit), and the field data collection in the Cameroon bovine TB study (14_bovine_tb_cameroon) and the Ethiopia brucellosis study (17_brucellosis_ethiopia). Neither field study states "requirements" for data collection. Each only reports the procedures it used (questionnaires, animal records, sampling, sample coding, spreadsheet entry), so "requirements" has to be read as those procedures. Neither field study uses sequencing, MultiQC or SeqKit. The question is loosely framed and could reasonably be answered more than one way, for example tool features against field procedures, or automated high-throughput processing against manual collection. All four listed papers contribute evidence.

records.short_answer:
MultiQC and SeqKit are tools for data that already exists as sequencing analysis files. MultiQC scans analysis directories for log files and QC reports and creates a single summary report across all samples. It saves parsed data as tab delimited text, YAML or JSON, parses data for thousands of samples within minutes, and through plugins can insert LIMS metadata and store summary results in a database. This lets it act as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines. SeqKit has nineteen subcommands for FASTA/Q manipulation (converting, searching, filtering, deduplication, splitting, shuffling, sampling). They take plain or gzip-compressed inputs and outputs from standard streams or local files, and SeqKit converts FASTA/Q to and from tabular format.

The two zoonotic disease studies had to collect their data in the field from people and animals. In Cameroon (bovine TB), an interviewee-administered questionnaire gathered data from 90 cattle professionals. It was pre-tested and closed-ended, written in English and French, and could be translated into the participant's local language. It covered sociodemographics, herd management, cattle-wildlife interaction, knowledge of zoonotic TB and farm bTB status. Sex, age and body condition score were recorded for each tested animal at the time of the test. Data were organised in Microsoft Excel and analysed in IBM SPSS Statistics. In Ethiopia (brucellosis), a structured questionnaire collected biodata on tested animals and animal attendants: sex, age, herd size, animal movement, parity, herd history of abortion and RFM, and physiological status. Blood samples and exposure information (raw milk consumption, assisting calving, disposing of aborted fetuses) were collected from animal owners. In total 450 camel, 300 small ruminant and 250 human samples were collected. A bar code system, built from the first letters of region, zone, district and PA, labelled human and animal samples to minimise error. Field and laboratory data were entered into Microsoft Excel and analysed with R-3.3.0. None of the papers states this contrast itself.
records.synthesis_statement: MultiQC works on existing analysis output. It aggregates log files and QC reports into a single summary report [0], exports parsed data as tab delimited text, YAML or JSON [1], parses thousands of samples within minutes [2], links to a LIMS and a database through plugins [3] and serves as a central collection point at the terminus of analysis pipelines [4]. SeqKit converts, searches, filters, deduplicates, splits, shuffles and samples FASTA/Q files [5] with nineteen independent subcommands [6] that read and write plain or gzip-compressed streams or files [7], and it converts FASTA/Q to and from tabular format [8]. The field studies instead collect their data from people and animals. In Cameroon, a pre-tested closed-ended questionnaire in English and French, translatable into local languages, gathered sociodemographic, herd management, wildlife interaction and zoonotic TB knowledge data from 90 cattle professionals [9, 11, 12]. Animal sex, age and body condition score were recorded at testing [10], and the data were organised in Excel and analysed in SPSS [13]. In Ethiopia, a structured questionnaire collected animal and attendant biodata [14, 15], and blood samples and exposure information were collected from animal owners [16]. There, 450 camel, 300 small ruminant and 250 human samples were collected [17] and labelled with a bar code system built from region, zone, district and PA letters to minimise error [18, 19], and field and laboratory data were entered into Excel and analysed in R [20].

records.question_issues: The question is open-ended ("how do ... differ"). Several reasonable answers are possible, each stressing different axes: workflow language, software deployment, traceability, user interface, versioning and scaling. None of the three papers compares itself with the other two. HTS-flow (2016) does not mention Nextflow, Sarek or Snakemake. Sarek compares Nextflow only with Bpipe. Snakemake places Nextflow and itself in the same DSL category. The comparison therefore has to be assembled from each system's description of itself. "Nextflow-based systems like Sarek" can be answered only from the Sarek paper. Nextflow has no paper of its own in the set and is described only as Sarek's implementation language, plus briefly in the Snakemake paper's taxonomy. The question calls Snakemake an NGS workflow system, but its paper ("Sustainable data analysis with Snakemake") presents a general data-analysis workflow manager, a mild framing mismatch. The Snakemake text is version 3 of the article, so some features it describes (e.g. execution plugins) may postdate the other two papers.

records.short_answer:
Sarek is implemented in Nextflow, a workflow language designed for bioinformatics. Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF and Kubernetes, with native support for Google Cloud and AWS. To ensure reproducibility, all Sarek required tools are installed in Conda and then pushed to DockerHub, so Sarek and its dependencies are available from a Conda environment or as Docker or Singularity containers. Nextflow downloads the specified pipeline version from GitHub, together with its container and the reference files from AWS-iGenomes. Sarek follows the nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, restarts incomplete runs from any stage and ships with a suite of tests to verify the installation. A complete run was executed by a single command.

Snakemake specifies workflows as rules in a domain specific language (DSL). Its DSL extends Python, while Nextflow's extends Groovy. Dependencies between jobs are inferred automatically. Software stack management is integrated into Snakemake itself: each rule can declare a Conda environment, or a container image run with Singularity. Snakemake can also automatically generate a containerized version once a workflow is production ready. It tracks the input files, output files, parameters, software and code of each executed job and makes them available in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports. Scaling to a specific platform needs only a change of command line parameters, using execution plugins (e.g. SLURM, LSF, Kubernetes, Amazon AWS Batch).

HTS-flow is designed to work together with a LIMS (SMITH), so raw NGS data become visible in it automatically. Analyses run through a web interface designed for users without bioinformatics skills (the typical wet-lab scientist). It works with predefined, easily customizable modular scripts, deposited to Github for versioning. It allows complete traceability of datasets, accompanying metadata and analysis scripts. Reproducibility rests on standard Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb and BSgenome), outputs in standard locations as Bioconductor R data objects, and identical workflows for data from various sources.
records.synthesis_statement: Sarek and Snakemake both define workflows in code. Sarek is implemented in the Nextflow workflow language [0], and Nextflow and Snakemake both specify workflows in a DSL, built on Groovy and Python respectively [8, 9]. Snakemake decomposes workflows into rules and infers dependencies between jobs automatically [10, 11]. HTS-flow instead couples a LIMS to a web interface for users without bioinformatics skills [20, 21, 24, 29]. The interface sits over predefined, easily customizable modular scripts [25]. Both code-based systems get reproducibility by packaging software, at different levels. Sarek encapsulates all its dependencies in Docker or Singularity containers or a Bioconda-built Conda environment [2], and pulls a specified pipeline version from GitHub with its container and reference files [5]. Snakemake builds software stack management into the engine, with a Conda environment or a Singularity-run container for each rule [12, 13, 14], and can generate a containerized version of a workflow [15]. HTS-flow instead bases reproducibility on standard Bioconductor annotation packages (TxDb, BSgenome) and Bioconductor R data objects [27, 28]. It versions its scripts on Github [26] and analyses data from various sources with identical workflows [23]. For traceability and robustness, Sarek relies on nf-core portability and documentation guidelines, error reporting with restart from any stage, and installation tests [3, 4, 6]. Snakemake tracks the files, parameters, software and code of every job and reports them in self-contained, interactive, HTML based reports [16, 17]. HTS-flow provides complete traceability of datasets, metadata and analysis scripts, with raw data made visible automatically from the LIMS [20, 22]. For execution, Nextflow supports Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, LSF, Kubernetes, Google Cloud and AWS [1]. Snakemake scales through execution plugins and needs only a change of command line parameters [18, 19]. HTS-flow's automation comes mainly from integration with the SMITH LIMS [29].

records.question_issues: Neither paper refers to the other. The Kenya paper (45_kenya_amr_digital) never mentions ISSE and reports no evaluation of OHAMRS against any framework. The ISSE paper (35_isse_framework_amr) never mentions Kenya or OHAMRS. Any "alignment" is therefore the answerer's mapping of what paper 45 describes onto the levels paper 35 defines; neither paper states it. "Levels of surveillance" is ambiguous in three ways: (a) ISSE's five evaluation levels (the abstract calls them "evaluation components"); (b) ISSE's separate Table 3 scale of six OH integration levels (0 to 5) for data collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination; (c) Kenya's administrative "national, county, and surveillance site levels". This record reads it as (a) and uses (b) only for the data-collection gap. Neither paper places OHAMRS at a specific ISSE level or integration score, and the Kenya paper reports no outcome or impact data, so nothing maps to ISSE Level 5. Both listed papers contribute.

records.short_answer: Neither paper makes this comparison, so the alignment is inferred from the two papers. ISSE evaluates a One Health surveillance system at five levels: (1) integrate a OH approach, (2) produce OH information and expertise, (3) generate actionable knowledge, (4) influence decision-making, (5) positively impact outcomes. Level 1 also scores six levels of OH integration for data collection, analysis, interpretation and dissemination. Mapped onto these: Level 1, OHAMRS integrated human and animal health AMR data, through interoperability middleware and a DHIS2 web portal. Level 2, the portal analyses and visualises those data, but the environment, food/feed and aquaculture sectors are only planned for future inclusion, and antimicrobial consumption and use data still need to be incorporated; ISSE Level 2 asks whether data are collected from animals, humans and the environment, and the top data-collection integration levels require environmental or AMU data. Level 3, 42 dashboards (17 for priority pathogens, 8 for drug-resistance indicators, plus a One Health intersectoral dashboard) present, interpret and disseminate actionable information at national, county and surveillance site levels. Level 4, OHAMRS is meant to inform policymaking, and its success will be gauged by use in evidence-based decision-making, so this is expected, not shown. Level 5, the Kenya paper reports no outcome impacts. ISSE suggests focusing on evaluation levels 1 and 2 in the first 3–5 years of a new or recently integrated system.
records.synthesis_statement: ISSE evaluates a One Health AMR/AMU surveillance system at five levels: integrating a OH approach, producing OH information and expertise, generating actionable knowledge, influencing decision-making and positively impacting outcomes [0, 1, 4, 6, 7, 8]. Level 1 also scores six levels of OH integration for data collection, analyses, interpretation and dissemination [2]. OHAMRS integrated human and animal health AMR data through interoperability middleware, which is what ISSE Level 1 examines [1, 10, 11]. It analyses and visualises those data in a DHIS2 web portal, relevant to ISSE Level 2 [4, 11]. Its data coverage does not yet include the environment, food/feed or aquaculture sectors, or antimicrobial consumption and use data [12, 19], whereas ISSE Level 2 asks whether environmental data are collected and the higher data-collection integration levels require environmental or AMU data [3, 5]. Its 42 dashboards, including a One Health intersectoral dashboard, present, interpret and disseminate actionable information at national, county and surveillance site levels, the subject of ISSE Level 3 [6, 13, 14, 16]. OHAMRS is meant to inform policymaking, and its success will be gauged by use in evidence-based decision-making, the subject of ISSE Level 4 [7, 15, 17, 18]. The Kenya paper reports no impacts on AMR or AMU, the subject of ISSE Level 5 [8]. For a new or recently integrated system, ISSE suggests focusing on evaluation levels 1 and 2 in the first 3–5 years [9].

records.short_answer:
28_otu_vs_asv ran the same data through VSEARCH (clustering into OTUs) and DADA2 (error correction into exact ASVs). Both pipelines gave comparable results that generally allow the same interpretations. Even so, community composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% at phylum level, based purely on the pipeline.

Findings in 28_otu_vs_asv:
- **Spurious OTUs.** OTU approaches overestimate diversity and produce spurious OTUs. The study saw this too, but relative abundance thresholds easily mitigated it: a cutoff as little as 0.001% removed enough spurious or rare taxa to fall within the ranges produced by the ASV pipeline. The ASV pipeline outputs fewer to no spurious variants and is precise to a single base.
- **Alpha diversity.** Trends were similar, and the OTU pipeline typically reported slightly higher diversity. The two pipelines diverged for the psychrophilic PWASS samples, where the inverse Simpson index differed at times by a factor greater than two.
- **Community composition.** Pipeline choice significantly influenced reported composition. Over more than 170 days, the dissimilarity between pipelines was greater than the dissimilarity between treatments. The ASV pipeline showed the influence of time and co-substrate more clearly.
- **Consequences.** These differences could lead to different conclusions and could interfere with downstream analyses such as network analysis. On the reduced dataset they would suggest that the pipeline affects composition more than any treatment, a conclusion with no foundation in experimental reality.
- **Comparability.** OTUs are analysis-specific and give no direct comparability with other studies. ASVs are directly comparable between studies.

Findings in 29_16s_best_practices (a review):
- OTUs are clustered at an arbitrary threshold (often 3%) and have no innate biological meaning.
- De novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies, and closed-reference clustering loses information that lies outside the database.
- ASVs significantly reduce clustering artifacts, allow valid comparison, are not restricted by reference databases and need relatively light computation.
- One concern with ASVs is possible diversity inflation from multiple ASVs generated from a single bacterial genome.

23_swine_cultivation does not compare the two approaches.

key_concepts.phrase: de novo OTUs cannot be compared between studies

records.synthesis_statement: Both papers say OTUs come from clustering, are analysis-specific and cannot be compared directly between studies [0, 4, 5, 23, 26]. They also say ASVs come from error correction, resolve single-base differences and are directly comparable [0, 6, 13, 22, 27, 28]. 29 adds that OTUs have no innate biological meaning and that clustering affects biological interpretation [24, 25]. 28 measured the effect on interpretation. Overall, the two pipelines allow the same interpretations [1, 14], but phylum-level composition differed by 6.75% to 10.81% [2, 9]. Diversity estimates diverged for the PWASS samples [8, 15]. Pipeline choice significantly influenced composition, and the dissimilarity between pipelines exceeded the dissimilarity between treatments [17, 18, 20]. These differences could lead to different or unfounded conclusions [3, 21]. The papers place the diversity bias differently. 28 reports that OTU approaches overestimate diversity with spurious OTUs and that abundance thresholds mitigate this [7, 10, 11, 12]. 29 records the concern that ASVs may inflate diversity through multiple ASVs per genome [30]. 29 also says ASVs need lighter computation [31].

records.short_answer:
The three papers tackle efficiency at different levels.

nf-core/sarek 3 (the pipeline in the paper filed as nf-core), at the workflow level:
- Uses the CRAM format instead of BAM to reduce storage. Work-directory storage drops by 65%, from 170.4 TB (BAM) to 59.7 TB (CRAM), at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage.
- Increases intra-sample parallelization. FastQ files are split into shards with fastP, which combines sharding and adapter removal into one step, so alignment can run on smaller machines. Mapping runtime plateaus at 12 shards, with the median runtime reduced to 37%. Genomic regions are processed in parallel, with no further runtime benefit beyond 21 interval groups.
- Is written in Nextflow, so it is portable to several cloud vendors and common HPC schedulers.
- Single-step preprocessing plus tailored interval splitting reduces the needed CPU hours by 66%.
- The paper states the cost effect four ways: a 70% cost reduction in commercial clouds (abstract), a 69% reduction in compute costs (Introduction), cloud computing costs reduced to approximately 30% (Results) and costs reduced to 50% compared with previous releases (Discussion).

fastp, inside one preprocessing tool:
- Avoids reading and loading data multiple times, which is slow and I/O inefficient, by doing quality control, adapter trimming, quality filtering and per-read quality pruning in a single scan of the FASTQ data.
- Is designed for multi-threading parallel processing: each pack of reads is consumed by one thread in the pool.
- Can split output into multiple files for parallel processing, by file lines or by file numbers.
- Is 2–5 times faster than tools such as Trimmomatic or Cutadapt. With a single thread it took 6 min (SE) and 13.3 min (PE).

methylPipe, at the data-storage level:
- Keeps WGBS data on disk as Tabix-indexed compressed files that are accessed directly from disk. This reduces disk space (269 MB and 380 MB compressed versus 372 MB and 554 MB uncompressed for IMR90 and H1) and saves memory.
- By contrast, BiSeq and M3D upload the entire dataset into memory and failed even with 80 GB.
- Parallelizes demanding tasks such as DMR identification and adjusts automatically to the available cores and RAM. DMR identification between 2 WGBS samples took 20 min with 1 core on chromosome 1 (max 4GB RAM) and 45 min with 10 cores genome-wide (max 28GB RAM).

The direct link between the tools: sarek uses fastp to shard FastQ files and remove adapters in one step.
records.synthesis_statement: All three papers use parallel processing, at different levels. nf-core/sarek increases intra-sample parallelization by sharding FastQ files and processing genomic regions in parallel, on cloud or HPC infrastructure made portable by Nextflow [0, 3, 4, 6]. fastp is designed for multi-threading inside one tool and can split its output into multiple files for parallel processing [18, 19, 20, 23]. methylPipe parallelizes demanding tasks such as DMR identification and adjusts to the available cores and RAM [25, 30]. Both sarek and fastp cut repeated passes over the data. fastp performs all operations in a single scan, avoiding slow, I/O-inefficient repeated reading [15, 16]. sarek adopted fastP because it combines FastQ sharding and adapter removal in one step, and single-step preprocessing with tailored interval splitting reduced CPU hours by 66% [5, 12]. On storage, sarek moved to CRAM files, cutting work-directory storage by 65% at the cost of a 34% increase in memory usage [7, 8, 9]. methylPipe instead keeps data on disk as Tabix-indexed compressed files read directly from disk, saving both disk space and memory [24, 26, 27, 28], unlike BiSeq and M3D, which load the entire dataset into memory and failed with 80 GB [29]. Reported gains: for sarek, the median mapping runtime fell to 37% [10] and the cost reduction is given as 70%, 69%, to approximately 30% and to 50% in different sections [1, 2, 11, 14]. fastp is 2–5 times faster than other FASTQ preprocessing tools [17, 21, 22]. methylPipe ran a genome-wide 2-sample DMR analysis in 45 min with 10 cores [31].

records.synthesis_statement: QMP addresses RMP bias directly: it combines sequencing with a microbial load assay and produces an absolute abundance matrix [0, 3], so it follows whether taxa thrive or wither and shows real community dynamics [1, 2], minimizing compositionality effects [9]. Against QMP, RMP ignored absolute growth or decline and biased trajectories [4, 7, 8, 10], exaggerated the variation explained by individual, segment and DPH [5, 11], and overestimated or missed taxon–taxon correlations [6, 12]. Culturomics works on a different limitation of sequencing-based profiling: it recovers taxa missed for low relative abundance, shallow sequencing depth, incomplete lysis or unfavorable PCR amplification [14, 16], adding 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs across the four time points [15] and isolating core ASVs and novel species [20], which shows a more diverse microbiota [13]. Its Bacteroides example touches the compositional problem: relative abundance fell below detection while culture suggested absolute abundance might not decrease, as other taxa may have proliferated more [17, 18, 19]. The livestock review adds only that culturomics combined with shotgun metagenomics may give a more exhaustive picture of the gut [21].

records.question_issues:
The question is broad and open-ended, so it can reasonably be answered in more than one way. A grader should accept any correct selection that covers all three papers. The premise holds only in part, and the three papers do not measure the same thing, so the answer can only set them side by side.
(1) 41_salmonella_wgs_amr is a WGS study with one poultry source: raw chicken imported into England. It contrasts that source with edible leaves imported from Asia, and compares the chicken isolates across their four countries of origin (Brazil and Thailand are the main ones).
(2) 42_campylobacter_wgs_thailand is a WGS study of 26 isolates from commercial broilers and native chickens in southern Thailand. It reports AMR prevalence by species (C. jejuni vs C. coli), not by poultry source. Its only source contrast is that most C. coli came from native chickens, plus the authors' interpretation about environmental exposure. Its geographic comparison is limited to SNP similarity with human genomes from Taiwan and to sequence types reported in Thailand.
(3) 43_esbl_ecoli_food is a narrative review, not a WGS or genomic study. All of its poultry and regional findings (Pakistan, Hong Kong, China, Canada, conventional vs organic farms) are citations of other studies.
None of the papers compares its own figures with the other organisms, so a ranking across organisms would go beyond the evidence. On transmission the papers offer patterns and interpretation (clustering within consignments, SNP distances, shared sequence types, plasmid similarity, environmental acquisition), not measured transmission rates. The ≤0.5% link to UK human cases in paper 41 cites the authors' earlier report (Alikhan et al., 2022), not this study's data.

records.short_answer:
Salmonella (41, WGS of imported raw chicken):
- Chicken vs leaves: 214 (93%) chicken isolates were resistant to at least one antimicrobial agent and 164 (71%) were MDR. Among isolates from edible leaves imported from Asia, three (3%) were resistant and two (2%) were MDR. Leaf isolates showed a low level of resistance irrespective of the country of origin.
- Origin: most chicken isolates came from Brazil (165, 71%) or Thailand (51, 23%), and MDR isolates came from all four countries of origin.
- Country differences: the most frequent serovar, S. Heidelberg from Brazil, was resistant to three or more antimicrobial classes, and all S. Heidelberg isolates had resistance genes for fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines and sulphonamides. Five of six S. Agona isolates from Thailand were resistant to five classes of antibiotics, while S. Agona from Brazil had no resistance genes. All Thai S. Enteritidis isolates had gyrA[87:D-Y], and 10 of them also carried blaTEM-135.
- Overall: 170 (74%) chicken isolates had beta-lactam resistance determinants (plasmid-encoded blaCMY-2 in 124, 54%), and 222 (96%) had a QRDR mutation.
- Transmission: 60% of consignments carried the same genetically related strain (within a 5 SNP cluster) with an identical AMR profile. In the authors' earlier report, Salmonella types from Brazilian raw chicken corresponded to ≤0.5% of UK human salmonellosis cases between 2004 and 2019.

Campylobacter (42, WGS of 21 C. jejuni and 5 C. coli from commercial broilers and native chickens in Thailand):
- Genotypes: blaOXA was present in all isolates. gyrA mutations were found in 95.2% of C. jejuni and 80.0% of C. coli, and tet(O) in 76.2% and 80.0%.
- Phenotypes: all C. jejuni were resistant to ciprofloxacin, enrofloxacin and nalidixic acid. Three of the 5 C. coli were resistant to all 8 tested antimicrobials.
- Source differences: C. coli showed higher heterogeneity in ARG, and most C. coli came from native chickens. The authors attribute this to native chickens' greater exposure to the environment, which enables acquisition of ARG from other bacterial species.
- Transmission: no mobile genetic elements were detected. Similar STs came mainly from the same host species, but one broiler isolate and one native-chicken isolate of ST460 differed by only 602 SNP. C. coli genomes were close to human genomes from Taiwan (1,161 and 1,280 SNP). Two ST (51 and 464) have been published in both humans and chickens in Thailand.

ESBL E. coli (43, a review citing other studies):
- Prevalence: ESBL/pAmpC E. coli occur in all stages of broiler production. MDR E. coli from healthy commercial poultry carry IncC and IncFIA plasmids.
- Sources and regions: in Pakistan, the incidence was high in commercial chickens and lower in wild birds. Conventional farms have more ESBL E. coli than organic farms. Commercial chicken meat in Hong Kong had an estimated 80% prevalence, with frequent blaCTX-M-1. In China, ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae came predominantly from frozen chicken meat. Canada saw a decrease between 2012 and 2017, linked to the 2014 ban on preventive ceftiofur use in chickens.
- Transmission: plasmid backbones can be nearly identical among chickens, cattle and swine and are similar to human plasmids.
records.synthesis_statement:
AMR in Salmonella was far more common in poultry than in the non-poultry source. Among isolates from imported raw chicken, 93% were resistant and 71% were MDR, against 3% resistant among isolates from edible leaves; the authors suggest the drivers of resistance selection operate differently in poultry production [1, 2, 3, 12]. Resistance in the chicken isolates varied by country of origin:
- MDR isolates came from all four countries [4, 5].
- The most frequent serovar in imported chicken, S. Heidelberg, came from Brazil and was MDR [6, 13].
- Thai and Brazilian S. Agona differed (five classes vs none), and Thai S. Enteritidis all carried gyrA[87:D-Y], with 10 of 15 also carrying blaTEM-135 [7, 8].
- Leaf isolates stayed low in resistance whatever their origin [11].

In Thai chicken Campylobacter, blaOXA was found in every isolate, and gyrA and tet(O) were frequent in both species [17, 18]. C. coli carried more heterogeneous ARG and came mostly from native chickens; the authors link this to native chickens' greater environmental exposure [26, 27, 28].

For ESBL E. coli, the review reports cited findings:
- presence in all stages of broiler production [29, 37];
- more ESBL in commercial chickens than in wild birds (Pakistan), and on conventional than on organic farms [31, 32];
- an estimated 80% prevalence in commercial chicken meat in Hong Kong, and in China ESBL-producing Enterobacteriaceae found predominantly in frozen chicken meat [35, 36];
- a decline in Canada after the 2014 ceftiofur ban [33, 34].

On transmission:
- 60% of Salmonella-positive chicken consignments carried one genetically related strain with an identical AMR profile [14], and Brazilian chicken types matched ≤0.5% of UK human cases in an earlier report [15].
- Campylobacter STs clustered mainly by host, but a broiler isolate and a native-chicken isolate of ST460 differed by 602 SNP. Some genomes or STs were close to, or shared with, human isolates from Taiwan and Thailand, and no mobile genetic elements were found [21, 22, 23, 24, 25].
- ESBL plasmid backbones can be nearly identical among chickens, cattle and swine, with similarities to plasmids isolated from humans [38].

I took every evidence sentence programmatically from the pymupdf page text. The script joined word-break hyphens at line ends and turned line breaks into single spaces; it changed nothing else. Paper 41's special characters are kept as printed: non-breaking spaces (U+00A0), thin spaces (U+2009) and soft hyphens (U+00AD, e.g. "Seventy-­one", "blaCMY-­2"). Also kept: the U+2212 minus in "535−536" (paper 42) and the "ﬂ" ligature in ciproﬂoxacin.
Inconsistency within paper 41: the abstract says 74% of chicken isolates came from South America, while the Results give Brazil 165 (71%) and Thailand 51 (23%). Both sentences are quoted.
Paper 42 gives the C. coli phenotypes twice. The abstract says "Most C. coli isolates were resistant to all tested antimicrobials" and the Results say "Three out of the 5 ... all 8 tested". These are consistent, and both are quoted.
I left out paper 41's comparisons with Dutch and other literature data. Paper 43's figures are all cited from other studies.

records.question_issues: The question is broad and open-ended ("how do ... incorporate technology"), so there is more than one reasonable selection of evidence and level of detail. This record keeps to passages that name technologies, digital or data platforms, or analytic methods applied to detection and response. Much of 37_data_driven_one_health is a commentary: its machine-learning surveillance capability is mostly proposed ("can be used", "would allow"), and the only quantitative result is a cited study (Mollentze et al., 70.8%). The third listed paper, 45_kenya_amr_digital, is about antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance, not zoonotic disease. It describes a digital One Health platform (OHAMRS) that facilitates detection of resistant pathogens, so it bears only on the general technology point and says nothing about detecting or responding to zoonotic disease. The question names only GOHF and "data-driven approaches", so whether paper 45 belongs in the answer is debatable. Its evidence is included and labelled as AMR. Paper 34 prints "a two-folder higher detectability" (sic); it is kept as printed.

records.synthesis_statement: GOHF incorporates technology at implementation: software and web platforms, mobile phones, tablets and apps support surveillance, prevention, control and preparedness [0]. Its examples are text-based monitoring for novel influenza A [1], and smartphone apps such as WVS for rabies data and KABS, which expedites detection of zoonotic diseases and triggered a One Health anthrax investigation [2, 3, 4, 5]. Smartphone-based laboratory diagnostics for H5N1 are another example [6, 7]. In its surveillance and laboratory domains, interoperable platforms and standardized data sharing give early warning signals, speed outbreak detection and support coordinated response [8, 9, 10]. The data-driven approach builds on One Health surveillance and data sharing for early detection and coordinated response [11] and adds machine learning modelling capability [12]. That capability is used to project disease progression and predict outbreak magnitude and timing [13]. It is also used to predict animal-to-human viral spillover, citing a model that correctly identified 70.8% of human viruses with high or very high zoonotic potential [14, 15]. Big-data machine learning and classical statistics would complement traditional surveillance and predict outbreaks at lower economic cost [16, 17]. In an AMR context rather than a zoonotic one, Kenya's OHAMRS integrates human and animal health data. It uses interoperability middleware, a DHIS2 web portal and 42 near-real-time dashboards to aid detection of resistant pathogens [18, 19, 20, 21, 22].

records.short_answer: Dairy cows (25_dairy_cow_feed, rumen microbiome): the networks show three types of relationship. (1) Direct: the cow genome directly affects both rumen microbial abundances and feed efficiency traits. (2) Indirect through microbes: the cow genome (Chr3: 116.5 Mb) indirectly affects RFI, mediated by the abundance of Syntrophococcus, Prevotella and an unknown genus of Class Bacilli. (3) Through DMI: the cow genome (Chr7: 52.8 Mb and Chr11: 6.1–6.2 Mb) affects the abundance of Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group mediated by DMI, so the direction may be DMI →ASV, the opposite of the ASV →DMI usually assumed. The authors propose that the host controls microbes through passage rate, constant supply of substrates, pH and temperature. The cow genome exerts moderate control over feed efficiency and low to moderate control over rumen microbial abundances. Pigs (26_gut_meat_quality, a review): genetic background, in addition to diet composition, might impact gut microbiota composition. Heredity of the microbiome was estimated for carcass composition and meat quality traits. Swine breeds differ in their microbial community (Duroc, for example). Gut microbiome and genetics are two important factors affecting IMF, and the gut microbiome plays a crucial role in differing fattiness across pig breeds. Mice given Jinhua pig microbiota had elevated lipid and triglyceride levels. The review does not separate direct from indirect genetic effects, and 22_pig_mags does not address host genetics.
records.synthesis_statement: In dairy cows the host genome acts directly on both rumen microbial abundances and feed efficiency traits [0, 7, 12]. It also acts indirectly on RFI through the abundance of Syntrophococcus, Prevotella and an unknown Bacilli genus [0, 3, 8, 12], and it affects Rikenellaceae RC9 gut group abundance through DMI [0, 4, 5, 9, 12], suggesting a DMI →ASV direction [10]. The authors propose passage rate, substrate supply, pH and temperature as ways the host controls microbes [6, 11]. Genomic control is moderate for feed efficiency and low to moderate for microbial abundances [2]. In pigs, the review states that genetic background might impact gut microbiota composition [13], that microbiome heredity was estimated for carcass and meat quality traits [14], with microbial correlations to meat color and firmness [15], and that breeds such as Duroc have distinct microbial communities [16]. Gut microbiome and genetics both affect IMF [17], the microbiome plays a crucial role in breed differences in fattiness [18], and microbiota from Jinhua pigs, a breed with higher IMF than Landrace, raised lipid and triglyceride levels in mice [19, 20].

records.question_issues: The question can be answered, but its framing does not fit the papers, so the comparison is uneven. (1) "Global reviews and regional case studies": only 36_integrated_amr_surveillance is a review. It is a scoping review of 14 antibiotic-resistance (ABR) surveillance systems, all in high-income countries, and it found no operating integrated system in LMICs. 37_data_driven_one_health and 38_one_health_africa are commentaries, not case studies. Paper 37 uses historical examples, partly from Australia (Hendra virus). Paper 38 describes African Union coordination bodies and frameworks, not an operating integrated surveillance system. (2) The topics differ: 36 is about antibiotic resistance; 37 and 38 are about zoonotic diseases. (3) Economic benefits are uneven. 36 reports no monetary benefit. It says integration has a financial and social cost, that intersectoral coordination is costly and usually unfunded, and that integration outcomes are rarely documented. The outcomes it does report are non-monetary (less antibiotic use; ceftiofur use stopped and resistance fell). Only 37 gives quantified savings (over €1 million for West Nile virus surveillance and response; 26% of laboratory operating cost), and these are cited from other sources in its Table 1 (Paternoster et al.; World Bank), not measured in the paper. 38's only figure is a general prevention cost-benefit argument (prevention costs less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year) plus outbreak losses, not a benefit measured for integrated surveillance. (4) Only 36 gives a detailed typology of organisational models. 37 and 38 describe coordination mechanisms. A correct answer has to show these asymmetries rather than present a symmetric comparison.

records.short_answer:
Organisational models.
- Global review (integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance): 14 integrated antibiotic-resistance surveillance systems, all operating in high-income countries; the review found no operating integrated system in LMICs. It sets out integration along two dimensions, information integration and structural integration, and groups the systems into four distinct clusters:
  - Group 1 (six systems) mainly operates in silos, with data analysed separately by each sector.
  - Group 2 (four systems: DANMAP, NORM/NORM-VET, SWEDRES/SVARM, NARMS) has a high level of integration at both structural and informational levels.
  - Group 3 (CIPARS, SONAAR) is supervised solely by the human health sector.
  - Group 4 (ZoMo, FINRES-Vet) is supervised by the food safety sector, with the animal health sector for ZoMo.
  At governance level, four systems are supervised by a multi-sectoral body and five separately by each sector. Some authors consider governance more effective when there is an intersectoral committee (DANMAP) or a single supervising organisation (CIPARS). The level of resources and the regulatory framework appeared to play a major role in how integrated surveillance was set up and organised.
- The data-driven One Health paper describes:
  - an inter-agency technical working group set up after the 2008 Hendra virus outbreak in Australia;
  - multisectoral partnerships, in contrast to preparedness and surveillance plans that in most countries are often developed by a single sector;
  - data-driven coordinated surveillance with machine learning modelling capability.
- The One Health in Africa paper describes the African Union's interagency One Health Coordinating Group on Zoonotic Diseases, the Africa CDC Framework for One Health Practice in National Public Health Institutes (coordinated surveillance and data sharing), and a continental strategy at national, regional and continental levels. It notes gaps in political commitment, skilled workforce, domestic financing and legal frameworks, and that many countries lack formal and funded One Health programs.

Economic benefits.
- The review reports no monetary benefit. Integration is associated with a financial and social cost; intersectoral coordination remains costly and funding is usually lacking; integration outcomes are poorly described and rarely available. The outcomes it reports are non-monetary: less antibiotic use in animals and humans, and the poultry sector stopped using ceftiofur, after which resistance to it in salmonella fell.
- The data-driven One Health paper cites returns of over €1 million in savings from integrated West Nile virus surveillance and response, and 26% savings in operational cost from hosting human and animal health laboratories under one roof. It says coordination can save costs by preventing duplication and provides a positive return on investment, that analytically driven prediction costs much less than response, and that the Ebola economic losses in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia could have been prevented by a more resilient and integrated health system. It also says data on financing and cost projections are limited.
- The One Health in Africa paper says zoonotic disease prevention costs less than 1/20th the value of lives lost each year (a business case), set against outbreak losses of billions of dollars.
records.synthesis_statement: The organisational models differ in scale and detail. The global review classifies 14 high-income-country antibiotic-resistance systems by information and structural integration into four clusters: siloed (Group 1), highly integrated (Group 2), and led by the human health sector (Group 3) or the food sector (Group 4) [0, 2, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. It found no operating integrated system in LMICs [19]. Resources and the regulatory framework shape how systems are organised [1], and governance is seen as more effective with an intersectoral committee or a single supervising organisation [13]. Paper 37 describes an inter-agency working group, multisectoral partnerships set against single-sector planning, and data-driven surveillance with machine learning [20, 21, 25, 26]. Paper 38 describes a continental model: an AU coordinating group, an Africa CDC framework in national public health institutes, and a multi-level strategy [32, 36, 37, 38, 39]. It also notes gaps in financing and funded programmes [31, 35]. On economics, the review stresses the costs of integration (a financial and social cost; costly, underfunded coordination) and finds outcomes poorly documented, reporting only non-monetary benefits [3, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. Paper 37 cites over €1 million in West Nile virus savings and a 26% cut in laboratory operating cost, and argues for a positive return on investment, cheaper prediction and avoided losses [22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30], while noting that cost data are limited [27]. Paper 38 makes a prevention business case (less than 1/20th the value of lives lost) against outbreak losses of billions of dollars [33, 34].

records.question_issues: The question assumes the three papers describe how DNA methylation and chromatin-structure tools complement transcriptomic analysis of oncogene targets. None of them says so. 46_methylpipe and 50_4cseq_protocol are methods papers that never mention MYC or oncogene targets. 48_myc_oncogene uses RNA-seq and ChIP-seq (MYC, RNAPII, H3K4me3, H3K27ac) but no DNA methylation data and no 4C or other chromosome conformation data. The answer can only put the papers side by side. The methods papers say what their tools measure and how those data combine with RNA-seq. The MYC paper reports what RNA-seq plus binding data could not explain. That methylation or 4C data would resolve MYC targets better is an inference the papers do not make. The question has more than one reasonable answer, since 'complement' could mean data integration, regulatory mechanism or target prioritisation. All three listed papers contribute.

records.short_answer: The papers do not state the link, so the answer comes from reading them together. In the MYC liver carcinoma model (48), chromatin immunoprecipitation was combined with gene expression profiling. MYC binding at a locus was insufficient to predict gene regulation. RNA-seq analysis following tet-MYC shutdown, more than DNA binding, narrowed down the genes primarily regulated by MYC. Neither MYC binding nor recruitment to enhancers (assigned by nearest-neighbor analyses) discriminated primary from secondary targets, and no simple rule linked promoter/enhancer association by MYC with gene regulation. The stalling index alone was insufficient in assessing RNA Pol II dynamics. The determinants of which MYC-bound genes are deregulated largely remain to be understood, and likely include promoter-dependent cues. methylPipe/compEpiTools (46) add DNA methylation, which is often combined with RNA-seq and TF ChIP-seq. They accommodate any combination of DNA methylation data, histone marks, TF binding and RNA-seq expression. They identify enhancers and RNAPII stalling/elongation dynamics, compute the stalling index, and match enhancers to the most proximal genes. Variation in methylation at intermediate or high-CpG density promoters is associated to differential expression of the downstream gene. 4C-seq (50) adds chromatin structure. It identifies regulatory chromatin loops between enhancers and promoters, through which enhancers regulate expression of distal target genes. It has been used to study enhancer hijacking in disease, and its tracks can be displayed together with ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq data. None of the papers applies methylation or 4C-seq data to MYC targets.
records.synthesis_statement: In the MYC-driven liver carcinoma model, chromatin immunoprecipitation was combined with gene expression profiling [0], and RNA-seq after tet-MYC shutdown, more than DNA binding, identified the genes primarily regulated by MYC [3]. MYC binding alone was insufficient to predict gene regulation [1]. Binding at promoters or at enhancers (assigned to genes by nearest-neighbor analyses) did not discriminate primary from secondary targets [5, 6]. The stalling index alone was insufficient to assess RNA Pol II dynamics [7]. What decides which MYC-bound genes are deregulated largely remains to be understood and likely includes promoter-dependent cues [2, 8]. The study's chromatin data were ChIP-seq profiles of MYC, RNAPII, H3K4me3 and H3K27ac [4]. methylPipe/compEpiTools add DNA methylation, which is often combined with RNA-seq and TF ChIP-seq [9], and integrate it with histone marks, TF binding and RNA-seq expression [13]. They identify enhancers and RNAPII stalling/elongation dynamics [10, 11] and match enhancers to the most proximal genes stratified by TF binding [14]. Their promoter CpG-content concept links methylation at intermediate or high-CpG promoters to differential expression of the downstream gene [12]. 4C-seq adds chromatin structure: it identifies regulatory loops between enhancers and promoters [16], through which enhancers regulate distal target genes [15]. It has been applied to enhancer hijacking in disease [17], and its tracks can be displayed with ChIP-Seq and RNA-Seq data [18]. None of the three papers applies methylation or 4C-seq data to MYC targets. That rests on reading all three papers, not on any one sentence.

records.question_issues: The question is broad ("shared methods and technical considerations"), so more than one reasonable answer set exists. The three papers differ in kind. (1) 22_pig_mags runs shotgun metagenomics on pig faeces, builds MAGs and screens them against CARD with CARD-RGI. (2) 41_salmonella_wgs_amr uses WGS of cultured Salmonella isolates, called with a customized Genefinder algorithm. Its isolates come from imported raw chicken and from edible leaves; leaves are not an animal source and raw chicken is a food product, so the premise "food animal environments" fits only in part. (3) 33_amr_food_animals is a review. It reports other studies' methods (metagenomics, plasmid metagenomics, PCR, qPCR, high-throughput sequencing, WGS, culturing) and runs no pipeline of its own. Overlaps across all three are limited to sequencing-based detection of resistance genes. Illumina short-read sequencing is stated in 22 and 41 only. Trimmomatic read trimming is shared by 22 and 41 only. Attention to mobile genetic elements appears in 22 and 33. Technical considerations are paper-specific: short-read binning limits in 22, WGS versus phenotype in 41, plasmid metagenomics for MGEs in 33. All three papers contribute evidence. Text-layer issues: 22 prints "quality score , 15" (pypdf "score, 15"; the symbol is probably "<") and "G1C" (probably G+C). Its NovaSeq sentence has a control character U+0001 where "×" probably stood. 41 contains non-breaking spaces, thin spaces and a soft hyphen ("V1-­5"). These are quoted as printed.

records.short_answer:
Shared methods: all three papers detect resistance genes by sequencing.
- Pig gut (22): Illumina NovaSeq shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic and assembled into MAGs, and the MAGs were screened against the comprehensive antibiotic resistance database (CARD) with CARD-RGI v. 5.2.0. ARG co-location with integrase/transposase sequences was checked, using Proksee and Prokka.
- Salmonella from raw chicken and edible leaves (41): whole genome sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq 2500. Reads were trimmed with Trimmomatic, and AMR genes and chromosomal mutations were called with a customized algorithm, Genefinder. Efflux pump genes were identified by a separate method.
- Review (33): cited studies used metagenomic methods (cattle faeces, shrimp, compost), plasmid metagenomics, next-generation high-throughput sequencing (pig farm bioaerosols), PCR and qPCR (manure, swine manure wastewater, shrimp), direct culturing (compost) and whole-genome sequencing of isolates (poultry farms).
The two primary studies share Illumina short-read sequencing and Trimmomatic trimming.

Technical considerations:
(a) Binning ARGs into MAGs from short reads is extremely challenging, because ARGs are often flanked by repeat sequences and located on mobile genetic elements such as plasmids. MAG-detected ARGs are therefore assumed to be chromosomal. Only 115 ARGs were found, against 250 in a previous study of the same short reads and 897 in the co-assembly. Long-read sequencing would likely increase the number binned and improve resolution of their genomic context.
(b) WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests, but it is not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods.
(c) Insertions, integrations and transposons drive horizontal transfer of ARGs. Plasmid metagenomics focusing on mobile genetic elements (MGEs) may have great potential to identify ARGs in complex environments.

records.synthesis_statement: All three papers detect resistance genes by sequencing. Shotgun metagenomics with MAGs is used for the pig gut [0, 2]. Whole genome sequencing of Salmonella isolates is used for raw chicken and edible leaves [10]. The review reports metagenomic methods [16, 19, 23], high-throughput sequencing [18], PCR and qPCR [19, 21, 22, 23], direct culturing [23] and whole-genome sequencing of isolates [24, 25] across cattle, pig, shrimp, manure, wastewater, compost and poultry settings. The two primary studies share an Illumina short-read workflow [2, 11] with Trimmomatic trimming [3, 12]. Each then calls genes with its own tool: CARD/CARD-RGI for pig MAGs [0, 1] and the customized Genefinder algorithm for Salmonella, with efflux pump genes identified separately [13]. Mobile genetic elements are a shared concern. The pig study checks ARG co-location with integrase/transposase sequences [4, 5]. The review links transposons and integrations to horizontal ARG transfer [17] and notes plasmid metagenomics focusing on MGEs may have great potential in complex environments [20]. Binning ARGs from short reads is extremely challenging because they are often flanked by repeat sequences and located on mobile genetic elements such as plasmids [6]. MAG-detected ARGs are therefore assumed chromosomal, and fewer are found (115 versus 250 and 897) [7, 8]. Long-read sequencing is proposed as the remedy [9]. For isolate WGS, results show a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests [14], but WGS cannot totally replace phenotypic methods [15].

records.short_answer:
Salmon: it corrects for fragment GC content bias, and its model also covers positional biases in coverage, sequence-specific biases at the 5′ and 3′ end of fragments, strand-specific protocols and the fragment length distribution. These bias models are used to re-estimate each transcript's effective length. The paper says this substantially improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and the reliability of downstream differential expression analysis. Uncorrected biases can lead to high false positive rates. In DE testing, Salmon's sensitivity is 53% to 250% higher at the same FDRs (main text). The Figure 1c legend gives 53%–450% over kallisto and 210%–250% over eXpress. Salmon also makes fewer false-positive DE calls.
DESeq2: it models read counts with a negative binomial (gamma-Poisson) distribution. It assumes that genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion, and it uses shrinkage estimation for dispersions and fold changes to improve the stability and interpretability of estimates. Dispersion shrinkage helps avoid false positives caused by underestimated dispersion. LFC estimates are shrunk toward zero, more strongly when a gene carries little information, which gives a more reliable basis for quantitative conclusions than normal MLEs. Overall, shrinkage improves stability and reproducibility compared with maximum-likelihood-based solutions.
HTS-flow: the paper does not mention Salmon or DESeq2. It offers absolute and differential expression quantification for RNA-Seq as a secondary analysis. Primary analyses (quality controls, pre-processing, alignment) run per sample as soon as the raw data are tracked in the LIMS. Users without bioinformatics skills run and track analyses through a web interface. The analyses use predefined, easily customizable modular scripts that are versioned on Github. Annotation uses standard Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb, BSgenome), and outputs are R data objects that follow Bioconductor standards.

key_concepts.phrase: shrinkage estimation for dispersions and fold changes

records.synthesis_statement: Salmon corrects for sample-specific RNA-seq biases, including fragment GC bias, by re-estimating each transcript's effective length [0, 2, 3]. This improves the accuracy of abundance estimates and downstream differential expression: higher DE sensitivity at the same FDRs and fewer false-positive DE calls, where uncorrected biases can cause high false positive rates [0, 1, 4, 5, 6]. DESeq2 models counts with a negative binomial distribution and shrinks dispersions and fold changes, sharing information across genes of similar expression. This avoids false positives from underestimated dispersion, gives more reliable fold changes, and improves stability and reproducibility over maximum-likelihood solutions [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. HTS-flow names neither tool. It offers absolute and differential expression quantification for RNA-Seq as a secondary analysis that follows per-sample primary analyses started once data are tracked in the LIMS [14, 15]. These analyses are run and tracked from a web interface through predefined modular scripts versioned on Github, use standard Bioconductor annotation libraries, and produce Bioconductor-compliant R objects [16, 17, 18, 19, 20].
records.disagreements: D1 answer_type: A chose synthesis, B extractive. Resolved as synthesis, because the question asks how the three papers relate and needs a combined statement. D2 Salmon Figure 1c legend (53%–450% / 210%–250%): only A had it. Kept, because the rule says to quote all values given for the same result. D3 DESeq2 "genes of similar average expression strength have similar dispersion" (p2) and "shrunken fold-change estimates offer a more reliable basis" (p5): only B had them. Both are verbatim and relevant, so both are kept. D4 HTS-flow outputs as Bioconductor R objects: only A had it. Kept. D5 HTS-flow Bioconductor metadata libraries (TxDb, BSgenome): only B had it. Kept. D6 Both short answers said "empirical Bayes shrinkage", and A's synthesis said "negative binomial GLM". Neither phrase is in any evidence sentence, so both were removed. D7 B's short answer spelled it "customisable"; the paper prints "customizable", so that spelling is used. D8 Key concepts were re-indexed to the merged evidence order. All 21 sentences were checked by script against the pymupdf text; each is verbatim on its stated page. The HTS-flow secondary-analysis sentence spans the line break in "high-\nthroughput", where the compound's own hyphen is kept.
