records.question_issues: The question is broad, and the four papers answer it only in pieces, so more than one reasonable answer can be built from them. No paper models how spatial and host-species heterogeneity together drive viral persistence. Persistence is analysed quantitatively only in 15_rabies_tanzania. There, spatial heterogeneity means uneven dog vaccination coverage among villages, plus incursions from outside the district, and not habitat or host distribution. 12_hpai_netherlands mentions HPAI persistence in resident wild birds once, in its introduction, citing other work (ref 8). Its own host-heterogeneity findings are differences in clinical signs and mortality between poultry types and age groups, which bear on detection, not persistence. 19_hpai_canada covers spatial spread (flyways, all provinces) and host range, not persistence as such. 37_data_driven_one_health says nothing about spatial or host-species heterogeneity and contributes only to the surveillance part. The word "sentinel" appears only in 37 (sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses for West Nile virus). None of the papers designs a sentinel surveillance system, so the "implications for sentinel surveillance design" part can only be answered from the surveillance and reporting recommendations the papers make. The question says "viral pathogens" in general, but the evidence covers only HPAI and rabies, plus brief Ebola and West Nile virus examples in 37.

records.short_answer:
Spatial heterogeneity: in Serengeti district, increased heterogeneity in dog vaccination coverage among villages led to increased focal rabies incidence at the same average coverage. For example, a split of 30% and 50% coverage gave 1.4 (95% CrI: 1.3-1.6) times the incidence of homogeneous 40% coverage. Outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell to <0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and short vaccination lapses did not lead to resurgence. Incursions from unvaccinated areas outside the district, reaching 50% of cases in 2022, show regional connectivity driving residual transmission. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, epidemics can escalate by farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 spread through the four major migratory bird flyways.

Host-species heterogeneity: HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and was seen in an increasing number of wild bird species. H5N1 infected mammals including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, porpoises, sea lions and dolphins. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes. Signs differ by host: exponential increasing mortality in layers and breeder chickens, but ducks reached MR > 3 less often, and drops in feed or water intake or egg production may be their only initial signs.

Surveillance implications: monitor fine-scale coverage, because models aggregating coverage to district level failed to show impacts on incidence. Make reporting criteria different for different poultry species and age groups (the Netherlands added thresholds such as MR > 3 in chickens and 0.15% per day for two days in ducks), with early notification. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes. Focus strategic surveillance on the regions and populations at highest risk. Wildlife testing is biased towards severely infected or dead animals, so identified infections are only a minority of spillovers. Sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs (great apes with Ebola virus), can warn of risk to humans. Surveillance design should be standardised to strengthen its sensitivity for detecting new or unusual events.

key_concepts.phrase: criteria for reporting should be different
Sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds, and horses

records.synthesis_statement:
Spatial heterogeneity sustains circulation. In Serengeti district, uneven dog vaccination coverage raised focal rabies incidence at the same mean coverage (1.4 times for a 30%/50% split against homogeneous 40%), and outbreaks followed years when campaigns missed many villages [12, 13, 16, 19]. Once heterogeneity was reduced, incidence fell below 0.4 cases/1,000 dogs annually, and if persistent spatial gaps are minimal, sub-optimal coverage still has major benefits [13, 18]. Incursions linked to regional connectivity reached 50% of cases in 2022 and are now a major source of residual transmission [14, 19]. For HPAI, infected farms clustered near the coast and the larger rivers, introductions can escalate through farm-to-farm transmission in poultry-dense areas, and H5N1 dispersed through migratory flyways to all provinces and territories of Canada [5, 6, 20, 21].

Host heterogeneity also matters. HPAI persisted in residential wild birds and spread to an increasing number of wild bird species and to many mammals [0, 1, 21, 22]. Wild birds will continue to be a source of novel influenza viruses [25]. Waterfowl-adapted clade 2.3.4.4b viruses had high infectivity and transmissibility in Anseriformes compared to Galliformes [7]. Clinical signs and mortality differ by host and age: ducks reached MR > 3 less often than chickens and may show only drops in feed or water intake or egg production [2, 3, 9, 10].

For surveillance design, the papers point to the following. Monitor coverage at fine scale, since district-level aggregation hid the effects [15, 17, 19]. Set reporting criteria by species and age group, as the Netherlands did with new thresholds, together with early notification under passive surveillance [4, 6, 10, 11]. Monitor viral polymorphisms after transmission from Anseriformes to Galliformes [8]. Focus strategic surveillance on the highest-risk regions and populations [26]. Allow for the bias of wildlife testing towards severe or fatal cases, which means detected infections are a minority of spillovers [23, 24]. Use sentinel surveillance in mosquitoes, birds and horses, and animal die-offs, as early warning [27, 28]. Standardise surveillance design to strengthen its sensitivity for new or unusual events [29].

records.question_issues: Partly answerable, and the premise is partly false. None of the four papers combines metagenomics, culturomics and metabolomics. Each one uses at most one of these methods. 22_pig_mags uses shotgun metagenomics (MAGs) and predicts functional potential from gene annotation only. It does no cultivation and measures no metabolites. 23_swine_cultivation is culturomics, read out by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (culture-dependent against culture-independent) and Sanger sequencing of isolates. It uses no shotgun metagenomics. 24_chicken_microbiome pairs quantitative amplicon microbiome profiling (QMP) with untargeted serum metabolomics, and uses no shotgun metagenomics and no cultivation. 26_gut_meat_quality is a narrative review of microbiota and meat quality. It does not discuss the three methods as methods and adds only general statements about bacterial functions and metabolites (SCFAs, methanogenesis). So the 'integration' can only be assembled across papers, from what each paper says about its own approach and its limits. It is not shown within any one paper. 'Evaluate' is open-ended, so more than one reasonable synthesis, at different depths, is possible.

records.short_answer:
No single paper combines all three methods. Each paper contributes one layer, and the papers themselves say how the layers connect.

Metagenomics (22_pig_mags): MAGs connect taxonomy with potential metabolic functions such as carbohydrate degradation and short-chain fatty acid production.
- Genes for acetate, butyrate and propionate production were found in 68.5%, 18.8% and 8.3% of MAGs.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes for arabinose oligosaccharides and mixed-linkage glucans were predicted to be the most prevalent.
- 327 MAGs carry antimicrobial resistance genes.
- 82% of MAGs belong to species that lack cultured representatives. The authors say metabolic reconstruction of these MAGs may inform strategies for cultivation, and that more known species are needed.

Culturomics (23_swine_cultivation): culture-dependent (CD) and culture-independent (CI) samples were read by 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.
- CD methods detected more ASVs than CI (415, 675, 808 and 823 against 378, 482, 565 and 555 across the lactation, nursery, growing and finishing stages).
- CD methods found 244, 411, 507 and 510 ASVs that CI missed.
- 1,299 colonies were Sanger sequenced, giving 148 taxa in 28 genera. About 50% of ASVs and 75% of genera and families were culturable.
- Sequencing targeting only the V4 region underestimates diversity.
- The authors argue that CI associations and multi-omics give insights, but isolation and validation in animal models are the most convincing way to prove function. Sequencing pure cultures can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics.

Metabolomics (24_chicken_microbiome): quantitative microbiome profiling (QMP) was paired with time-course untargeted serum metabolomics.
- The metabolomics revealed six metabolite clusters.
- mmvec predicted microbe-metabolite interactions. Foregut microbiota had more connections with serum metabolites, and gut microbes were closely related to lipid and amino acid metabolism.
- 11 metabolites came specifically from the gut microbiota, and 16 came from both host and microbiota (including L-lysin and L-tyrosine).
- The authors stress that these links rest only on association analysis and need experimental validation.

Review (26_gut_meat_quality): understanding the functions of key bacteria and the host-microbiota interaction is crucial. SCFAs from gut microbiota have positive effects on muscle and fat tissue. Butyrate-producing bacteria are linked to less fat deposition, and methanogenesis functions to more efficient fat deposition.
records.synthesis_statement: Metagenome-assembled genomes go beyond taxonomy by connecting species with potential metabolic functions [4, 5]: SCFA production genes in 68.5%, 18.8% and 8.3% of MAGs [0], carbohydrate degradation [1] and antimicrobial resistance [2]. 82% of these MAGs come from species that lack cultured representatives [3]. Their metabolic reconstruction may inform cultivation, and expanding the number of known species is called for [6, 7]. Culturomics read out by sequencing detects more ASVs than culture-independent profiling, and recovers ASVs that profiling misses [8, 9, 10]. It yields isolates [11, 12], shows that about 50% of ASVs are culturable [17], and together with culture-independent sequencing it expanded known richness [18]. It also shows that V4-only profiling underestimates diversity [16]. Sequencing isolates can expand the reference genome bank for metagenomics [14]. Functions suggested by culture-independent or multi-omics data are proven most convincingly by isolation and validation in animal models, which culturing makes possible [13, 15, 19, 20]. Metabolomics adds a host-facing layer. Combined with quantitative profiling, which gives a better correlation with host changes [24], it linked absolute microbiota changes to serum metabolites [21]. It revealed six metabolite clusters [22] and, through mmvec, tied microbes to lipid and amino acid metabolism [23, 25]. It also attributed 11 metabolites to the microbiota and 16 to both host and microbiota [26]. These microbe-metabolite links are associations that need experimental validation [27]. The review likewise holds that the functions of key bacteria and the host-microbiota interaction are crucial [28]. It cites SCFAs, butyrate production and methanogenesis as functional links to fat deposition and meat quality [29, 30, 31]. No single paper integrates all three approaches.

key_concepts.phrase: connected taxonomy with potential metabolic functions
validation through pure cultures is imperative

records.question_issues: Only two of the three listed papers bear on the question. 43_esbl_ecoli_food is a review of ESBL-producing E. coli in food animals and foods. Searches for "whole genome", WGS, sequenc and phenotyp found only reference-list titles and isolated typing mentions, and nothing on WGS as a surveillance method or on WGS compared with phenotypic testing. Paper 43 therefore contributes no evidence. The word "international" is only loosely covered: paper 41 speaks of "global surveillance", and paper 42 of surveillance "from the national ... to the global scales (GLASS, WHO, 2021)" and of "Several countries" and the US NARMS integrating WGS. Neither paper evaluates international monitoring systems directly. The question is open-ended ("assess the role"), so the answer is a synthesis of the authors' own discussion statements and reported concordance results, and a correct answer could weight these differently. Paper 41 reports its own WGS-versus-phenotype agreement only qualitatively ("will publish these data elsewhere"). In paper 42 the erm(B) sentence lacks a number before "out of 16 isolates resistant to tylosin" in both text extractions, so the tylosin figure cannot be stated. Paper 42 gives the gyrA/quinolone figure twice: on p6 as "gyrA mutation at point T86I ... 96% of the isolates that exhibited phenotypic resistance to quinolone antimicrobials", and on p9 as "fluoroquinolone ... gryA mutations (T86I) (96%)" (the paper's own spelling, "gryA"). Both are quoted.

evidence.sentence: In the last decade, the development of next-generation sequencing (NGS) techniques, including whole genome sequencing (WGS), has become an essential tool for genotypic AMR surveillance from the national (Argimon et al., 2020; Joensen et al., 2021; Stubberﬁeld et al., 2019) to the global scales (GLASS, WHO, 2021).

evidence.sentence: By providing an in-depth genetic proﬁle of resistant bacteria, WGS can play a pivotal role in advancing AMR surveillance and management.
evidence.supports: WGS role in advancing AMR surveillance

evidence.sentence: Several countries with established AMR surveillance systems have started to integrate WGS results.
evidence.supports: Several countries' surveillance systems integrating WGS

evidence.sentence: For example, the US National Antimicrobial Resistance Monitoring System (NARMS) (Gilbert et al., 2007) has continually integrated WGS to address emerging resistance threats in foodborne pathogens affecting human and animal populations (Karp et al., 2017).
evidence.supports: Example: US NARMS integrating WGS

evidence.sentence: The gyrA mutation at point T86I was identiﬁed in 96% of the isolates that exhibited phenotypic resistance to quinolone antimicrobials.
evidence.supports: Genotype-phenotype agreement for quinolones (96%)

evidence.sentence: Similarly, the tet(O) gene displayed the strongest correlation with the phenotypic resistance of Campylobacter isolates to tetracycline (100%).
evidence.supports: Genotype-phenotype agreement for tetracycline (100%)

evidence.sentence: In contrast, a lower association was observed between the phenotypic resistance to macrolides and the detected genes.
evidence.supports: Lower agreement for macrolides

evidence.sentence: Speciﬁcally, the erm(B) gene, the only gene associated with erythromycin and tylosin resistance, was present in only 2 out of 9 isolates resistant to erythromycin and out of 16 isolates resistant to tylosin.
evidence.supports: Macrolide discordance figures (erm(B) in 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates)

evidence.sentence: Our ﬁndings revealed a correspondence between ﬂuoroquinolone and tetracycline resistance and the presence of gryA mutations (T86I) (96%) and tet(O) genes (100%).
evidence.supports: Discussion restatement of fluoroquinolone and tetracycline agreement

evidence.sentence: However, an equivalent correspondence was absent for macrolides and their related-ARG.
evidence.supports: Discussion restatement of macrolide discordance

evidence.sentence: The absence of concordance between resistance genes and the predicted phenotype of macrolides in our study may be due to other unexamined macrolide resistance determinants, such as mutations in ribosomal proteins L4 and L22 (Lehtopolku et al., 2011).
evidence.supports: Possible reason for discordance: unexamined determinants

evidence.sentence: Secondly, while WGS is an effective tool for predicting AMR, it is worth noting that different computational pipelines may yield considerably different results in AMR prediction (Hodges et al., 2021).
evidence.supports: Limitation: results depend on the computational pipeline

evidence.sentence: The accuracy of genotypic predictions also depends on the comprehensiveness of the reference databases.
evidence.supports: Limitation: accuracy depends on the reference databases

evidence.sentence: Our ﬁndings emphasize the importance of initiating AMR surveillance systems using WGS technology under the One Health approach to mitigate the AMR problems in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries.
evidence.supports: Recommendation for WGS-based One Health surveillance in Thailand and other LMICs

records.short_answer: Both contributing papers present WGS as augmenting phenotypic AMR testing, not replacing it. Paper 41 (Salmonella) says WGS detects AMR determinants with a high level of concordance with phenotypic tests while also assigning species, serovar and genotype. It reports a high correlation with phenotypic testing in this study and highly accurate prediction in earlier work on non-typhoidal Salmonella. It states that sequencing data complement phenotypic methods and that WGS is "not without limitations and cannot totally replace phenotypic methods". Applied to global surveillance, it can show the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy, and routine genomic sequencing will enable real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain. Paper 42 (Campylobacter, Thailand) calls WGS an essential tool for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales (GLASS). It notes that several countries with established systems, for example the US NARMS, have started to integrate WGS. In its data, genotype matched phenotype for some drugs and not others. The gyrA T86I mutation was found in 96% of quinolone-resistant isolates and tet(O) matched tetracycline resistance at 100%. Macrolides showed a lower association: erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates, possibly because of unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations. Paper 42 also warns that different computational pipelines may give considerably different results and that accuracy depends on how comprehensive the reference databases are. It recommends WGS-based AMR surveillance under One Health in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries. Paper 43 does not address WGS.
records.synthesis_statement: Both papers present WGS as a tool for AMR surveillance beyond the national level. Paper 41 says its application to global surveillance can provide information on the early emergence and spread of AMR and inform policy [1]. Paper 42 calls it essential for genotypic AMR surveillance from national to global scales and notes that several countries, including the US through NARMS, have integrated it [7, 8, 9, 10]. Paper 41 reports high concordance and correlation between WGS-based AMR prediction and phenotypic tests [0, 4, 5]. Paper 42 finds that agreement depends on the drug class: 96% for the gyrA T86I mutation with quinolone resistance and 100% for tet(O) with tetracycline, but a lower association for macrolides, where erm(B) was present in only 2 of 9 erythromycin-resistant isolates [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16]. Paper 42 attributes the macrolide discordance possibly to unexamined determinants such as L4 and L22 mutations [17], and notes that predictions vary between computational pipelines and depend on the comprehensiveness of reference databases [18, 19]. Paper 41 accordingly describes WGS as complementing phenotypic methods and states that it cannot totally replace them [2, 3]. Both papers point to routine or new WGS-based monitoring: real-time monitoring of AMR genes entering the food chain [6], and WGS-based One Health surveillance in Thailand and other low- and middle-income countries [20].

records.question_issues: Answerable, with three caveats. (1) "two such groups of organisms" suggests iNAP was shown on fungi, viruses or bacteriophages. It was not. The IDENAP input example pairs a microbial abundance data set with a plant abundance data set, and the paper describes IDENAP generally as interdomain associations between two groups of species. The question makes the link between the two papers; neither paper states it. (2) "data set limits" can be read more than one way. The paper states two limits: a minimum of eight samples as replicates, and fewer than 1000 species remaining after Step 1. The 1000-species cap holds "for most approaches". The same page offers FastSpar for SparCC on larger data sets (more than 1000 species) and suggests running larger data sets on local computation machines. An answer that gives the cap as absolute is slightly too strong. (3) The majority threshold (by default, species found in at least half of the samples, adjustable for each data set) is a filtering default rather than a limit, so an answer may or may not list it. It is not in the key concepts. "Sequencing approach" has one answer, shotgun metagenomics, which the paper also calls "amplification-free shotgun metagenomics".

evidence.sentence: Finally, shotgun metagenomics extended the picture to fungi, viruses, and bacteriophages, opening avenues for exploring inter-domain interactions.
evidence.supports: Shotgun metagenomics is the approach that extended the picture to fungi, viruses and bacteriophages

evidence.sentence: We compared sequencing approach performances (3 types of 16S short amplicon sequencing, PacBio long-read amplicon sequencing, and amplification-free shotgun metagenomics) in the characterization of microbial communities in two commercial RAS fish farms.
evidence.supports: The approaches compared; the shotgun approach is amplification-free, unlike the 16S short and PacBio long-read amplicon approaches

evidence.sentence: The shotgun metagenomics data corroborated amplicon findings and extended the picture beyond prokaryotes (75.55%) and included eukaryotes (23.97%), archaea (0.24%), and viruses (0.24%) (Additional file  6).
evidence.supports: The shotgun data went beyond prokaryotes to eukaryotes, archaea and viruses

evidence.sentence: Considering the full workflow, from microbiome data set to network result, iNAP contains the molecular ecological network analysis pipeline and interdomain ecological network analysis pipeline (IDENAP), which correspond to the intradomain and interdomain associations of microbial species at multiple taxonomic levels.
evidence.supports: IDENAP is the iNAP pipeline for interdomain associations

evidence.sentence: Our proposed iNAP pipeline integrates the molecular ecological networks (MENs) [8] and interdomain ecological networks (IDENs) [15] from microbiome abundance data, for example, species (genes/OTUs) abundance data set (Figure 1).
evidence.supports: The networks are built from abundance data

evidence.sentence: For IDENAP, two input data set files (e.g., microbial abundance data set and plant abundance data sets) should be added here and the majority for each data set can be adjusted accordingly.
evidence.supports: IDENAP input: two abundance data set files, one for each group

evidence.sentence: Since there were two data sets of species in Step 1, the network matrix should be in bipartite network mode; otherwise, an adjacent network for only one group of species would be generated (Details in Box 2).
evidence.supports: Two species data sets give a bipartite network matrix

evidence.sentence: For IDENAP, there are four kinds of network results, that is, one whole network, one bipartite network between two groups, and two adjacent networks for each of the species groups.
evidence.supports: IDENAP outputs a bipartite network between the two groups

evidence.sentence: Currently, iNAP requires a minimum of eight samples as replicates for network construction.
evidence.supports: Data set limit: at least eight samples

evidence.sentence: After this step, the remaining data set should contain less than 1000 species due to the large computational resources required for most approaches.
evidence.supports: Data set limit: fewer than 1000 species after Step 1, for most approaches

evidence.sentence: In addition, we also implemented the FastSpar method to calculate these outputs for the SparCC method, which is an efficient alternative way to handle larger data sets (more than 1000 species) [17].
evidence.supports: Exception to the 1000-species limit: FastSpar for SparCC

evidence.sentence: For larger data sets, we suggest running the association calculations on local computation machines accordingly; these steps are available in Github (https://github.com/yedeng-lab/iNAP).
evidence.supports: Data sets over the limit should be run on local machines

records.short_answer: The aquaculture study reports that shotgun metagenomics (amplification-free) extended the picture to fungi, viruses and bacteriophages, opening avenues for exploring inter-domain interactions. In iNAP, the interdomain ecological network analysis pipeline (IDENAP) builds the network between two groups. Its input is two abundance data set files, one for each group (the paper's example is a microbial abundance data set and a plant abundance data set). From these it builds a bipartite network between the two groups, along with a whole network and an adjacent network for each group. The data set limits are a minimum of eight samples as replicates and fewer than 1000 species remaining after Step 1, a cap that holds for most approaches. Larger data sets can use FastSpar for SparCC or be run on local computation machines.
records.synthesis_statement: The aquaculture study compared three types of 16S short amplicon sequencing, PacBio long-read amplicon sequencing and amplification-free shotgun metagenomics [1]. It reports that shotgun metagenomics extended the picture to fungi, viruses and bacteriophages, opening avenues for exploring inter-domain interactions [0], and that the shotgun data went beyond prokaryotes to eukaryotes, archaea and viruses [2]. For interdomain associations, iNAP provides the interdomain ecological network analysis pipeline (IDENAP) [3], which builds networks from abundance data [4]. IDENAP takes two input data set files, for example a microbial abundance data set and a plant abundance data set [5]. With two data sets the network matrix is in bipartite mode, and the results include one bipartite network between the two groups, one whole network and an adjacent network for each group [6, 7]. iNAP requires a minimum of eight samples as replicates [8], and the data set remaining after Step 1 should contain fewer than 1000 species for most approaches [9]. Larger data sets can use FastSpar for SparCC or be run on local computation machines [10, 11].
records.disagreements: D1. Aquaculture page 11 sentence ("extended the picture beyond prokaryotes"): A included it, B left it out. Kept it, because it backs up how far the shotgun data reached. A wrote "Additional file  6" with two ordinary spaces, but the pymupdf text has a no-break space (U+00A0) followed by an ordinary space. The final record keeps that exact character sequence. D2. iNAP page 2 sentence (networks built "from microbiome abundance data"): A included it, B left it out. Kept it as support for the abundance-data input. D3. iNAP page 5 sentence about running larger data sets "on local computation machines": B included it, A left it out. Kept it, because it qualifies the 1000-species cap. D4. Key concept for the pipeline: A used "interdomain ecological network analysis pipeline", B used "IDENAP". Kept A's phrase, which names the pipeline in full and occurs word for word in evidence 3. D5. B's synthesis said "beyond bacteria". That wording comes from the question, not the evidence, which says "beyond prokaryotes", so it was dropped. D6. Both A and B said the 1000-species limit applies "after majority selection". The evidence sentence says only "After this step", and the sentence that names majority selection runs across the page 4 to 5 break. The short answer and synthesis therefore say "after Step 1" (Step 1 is named in evidence 6). D7. Where the eight-sample troubleshooting row sits: A put it on page 9, B on page 10. records.notes: Every evidence sentence was checked by script against the pymupdf extraction. The only normalisations were joining words hyphenated across line breaks ("micro‑bial" with U+2011 to "microbial", "in-tradomain", "re-quires", "prokary-otes") and turning line breaks into single spaces. The pymupdf aquaculture lines also carry trailing spaces, which show up as doubled spaces when the lines are joined; those were collapsed to one space. The no-break space in "file  6" was kept. records.question_issues: The question is broad and open-ended (theme analysis): "how ... facilitate" and "what does this imply" can be answered correctly with different subsets of the mechanisms and measures the three reviews describe, so more than one reasonable answer exists. None of the papers defines "anthropogenic factors". Paper 31 lists human-driven factors (mismanagement, inadequate infection control, agricultural debris, environmental pollutants or contaminants, migration), in two wordings on page 1 (abstract and introduction). Paper 33 uses "anthropogenic activities" only once, for a single river study. Paper 40 frames the driver as the industrialization of animal agriculture. The papers give different excretion figures: 75%–90% (31), approximately 75% on page 1 and 70% on page 4 (33, both citing Mackie et al., 2006), and more than 70% (40). The mitigation "implications" are the authors' recommendations, not tested results, except two reported associations (33: restricting use linked to fewer ARB and ARGs; 40: growth-promoter bans followed by decreased consumption). All three papers contribute.

records.short_answer:
How spread is facilitated: improper management of antimicrobials, inadequate infection control, agricultural debris, pollutants in the environment and migration of people and animals infected with resistant bacteria facilitate the spread of resistance (31). Use in animals is estimated to be greater than in humans, and an estimated 50∼80% of all antibiotics are applied to animals in Africa, the European Union and United States, primarily to promote growth and prevent infection (31, 33). Growth promoters are the main reason for the large volumes used (31). Animal agriculture has shifted to widespread industrialization with intensive farming systems (40). Group antimicrobial treatment causes overuse and inconsistent dosing, and delivery through feed and water causes suboptimal dosing and downstream environmental contamination with antimicrobial residues (40).

Routes into the environment: most of the antimicrobials given are excreted, 75%–90% (31), approximately 75% on one page and 70% on another (33), and more than 70% (40). Excreted residues persist and exert selective pressure on environmental bacteria; residues alone can select resistant variants in soil and water (40, 31). Manure used as fertilizer increases resistant bacteria and resistance genes in the environment and can transfer ARGs to soil, crops and then the human microbiome; ARGs in manured soil are approximately 28,000 times higher than in un-manured soil (33, 40). Farm wastewater, runoff, contaminated water sources and farm waste, debris and pollutants spread resistance and create new resistance reservoirs (33, 40). ARGs were dispersed from farms through the air to a distance of 10 km (33). Simple waste treatments such as anaerobic digesters or lagoons did not effectively remove antibiotics (33).

Implications for mitigation: reduce unnecessary use of antimicrobials in agriculture and their dissemination to the environment, and use them only as a treatment, rarely for prophylaxis and never as growth promoters (31). Restricting antibiotic application is closely related to a decrease in ARB and ARGs (33), and growth-promoter bans gave significant decreases in consumption but have yet to reach many LMICs (40). Give more attention to residues in animal waste; develop novel technologies (nanotechnology, anaerobic digestion, biochar composting), alternatives to antibiotics (herbal plant extracts, probiotics, vaccines) and antibiotic administration (33). Control and monitor resistant bacteria spreading to the environment and integrate surveillance of humans, food products, farm animals, wildlife and ecosystems (31, 40). Better prevent and manage zoonoses, develop novel therapies, take “multi-pronged” measures across human, animal and environmental sectors, and systematically reconsider animal agricultural practices (40).
records.synthesis_statement: All three reviews tie the environmental spread of AMR to how humans use antimicrobials in agriculture. Paper 31 names mismanagement, inadequate infection control, agricultural debris, environmental pollutants and migration of infected people and animals as facilitating factors [0, 1], and paper 33 names anthropogenic activities as a contamination source in one river study [19]. Animal use exceeds human use, mainly for growth promotion and prevention [2, 6, 12]. Paper 40 places this within the industrialization of animal agriculture, which raised production efficiency but drastically impacted the environment [24, 25, 29]. Its intensive systems rely on group treatment and feed or water delivery, causing overuse, inconsistent or suboptimal dosing and downstream contamination with residues [26, 30]. Most antimicrobials given are excreted: 75%–90% in paper 31, approximately 75% or 70% in paper 33 and more than 70% in paper 40 [9, 13, 17, 37]. Excreted residues persist and select for resistance in environmental bacteria, soil and water [5, 27, 38], and residues, resistant bacteria and resistance genes circulate in the ecosystem and reach humans and animals [28]. Manure fertilization increases resistant bacteria and ARGs in soil, approximately 28,000-fold in manured soil, and can pass them to crops and the human microbiome [3, 16, 34, 35]. Wastewater, runoff, contaminated water sources and farm waste create new resistance reservoirs [20, 33, 36, 43], ARGs dispersed through the air to 10 km [14], aquaculture residues remain in aquatic environments [4], and simple waste treatments did not effectively remove antibiotics [15]. For mitigation, the papers call for reducing unnecessary agricultural use and the load reaching the environment [7, 18, 21], using antimicrobials only as treatment and never as growth promoters [8, 10], supported by the link between restricting use and fewer ARB and ARGs and by the fall in consumption after growth-promoter bans, which have yet to reach many LMICs [22, 31, 32]. They also propose waste-treatment technologies, alternatives to antibiotics and antibiotic administration [23], control and monitoring of environmental spread with integrated surveillance [11, 40], zoonosis prevention and novel therapies to cut use [39, 42], and multi-sector measures with a systematic reconsideration of animal agricultural practices [41, 44].

records.question_issues: The question is loosely framed and has more than one reasonable answer. It treats 'viewpoint' (the 4C-seq anchor restriction fragment, found only in 50_4cseq_protocol) and 'location' (the sampling site along the gastrointestinal tract, in 29_16s_best_practices and 21_livestock_gut_microbiome_review) as one design theme. No paper links the two ideas, so the 'collective' conclusion is the question's framing, not something the papers state. 50_4cseq_protocol does not discuss rumen sampling, and the microbiome papers do not discuss chromosome conformation. 25_dairy_cow_feed contributes almost nothing: it only describes how its own rumen fluid was sampled (orogastric tube, single day, cows at 66 to 105 DIM) and says nothing about why sampling location matters. 21_livestock_gut_microbiome_review only reports, from cited studies, that microbiomes differ between GIT locations, and makes no design recommendation of its own. The explicit design advice on sampling location comes from 29_16s_best_practices. 'Collective evidence' and 'importance' are open-ended, so how much to quote is a judgement call.

records.short_answer:
4C-seq (50_4cseq_protocol): the viewpoint fragment should overlap the site to be analyzed or lie within <1 kb of it. A non-blind viewpoint with a fragment end >200 bp is preferred. Distance from the viewpoint decides reproducibility. Far-cis (>5 MB) and inter-chromosomal contacts are generally not reproducible between replicates, while near-cis contacts (<1 Mb) should be quantitatively reproducible. Independent of the viewpoint's genomic location, a successful experiment shows strong enrichment of contacts flanking the viewpoint, and preferably >60% of reads map to the cis chromosome, most within 1 Mb of the viewpoint.
Gut microbiome sampling (29_16s_best_practices): choosing the sample location is an essential, and commonly complicated, design step. It must rest on the hypothesis and/or objective(s) and on the physiology of the host species and/or target tissue. The rumen microbiome is distinct from the lower GIT, so fecal sampling should not typically be considered a proxy for the ruminal microbiome. In poultry, feces from 163 birds had similar bacteria to the ceca but not in the same relative abundances. Location within poultry houses also matters, and a small pilot study answers many questions on sampling location.
21_livestock_gut_microbiome_review reports marked heterogeneity across GIT locations (sheep, cattle, goats), GIT location as a source of variation in pig microbial diversity, location-specific microbial hosts, and significant differences in predicted metagenomic profiles among GIT locations in dairy cows, sheep, goats and pigs.
25_dairy_cow_feed only describes its own sampling: rumen fluid taken with an orogastric tube on a single day, cows between 66 and 105 DIM.
records.synthesis_statement: In 4C-seq, the viewpoint must overlap the site to be analyzed or lie within <1 kb of it, and a non-blind fragment with a fragment end >200 bp is preferred [0, 1, 2, 3]. Distance from the viewpoint governs reproducibility: far-cis (>5 MB) contacts are generally not reproducible between replicates, while near-cis (<1 Mb) contacts should be quantitatively reproducible [4, 5]. Independent of the viewpoint's genomic location, success is judged by strong enrichment of flanking contacts, preferably >60% of reads on the cis chromosome [6, 7]. In gut microbiome 16S studies, choosing the sample location is an essential and commonly complicated design step that must follow the hypothesis and the host's physiology [8, 14, 15], and a small pilot study answers many questions on sampling location [17]. Easily accessible samples may not represent the location of interest [13]: the rumen microbiome is distinct from the lower GIT and intestine, so feces should not typically be a proxy for the rumen [9, 10], fecal and cecal microbiota in poultry shared bacteria but not relative abundances [11, 12], and location within poultry houses also matters [16]. Livestock studies found heterogeneity, location-specific microbial hosts and different predicted metagenomic profiles across GIT locations in cattle, sheep, goats and pigs [18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. One dairy study sampled rumen fluid directly, with an orogastric tube [24, 25].

fecal sampling should not typically be considered as a proxy
based upon the hypothesis and/or objective(s)
marked heterogeneity across different GIT locations
